a.o: Dr. Inas gave Mr. Samir no rabies treatment after a stray dog bite.
a.x: He needed rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin into the wound.
a.w: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms start. A stray dog bite where rabies is common needs treatment at once.

a.o: Dr. Inas washed Mr. Samir's bite wound with soap and water for 15 minutes.
a.x: A quick rinse under the tap is enough for a bite like this.
a.w: Long washing lowers the risk of rabies.

a.o: Dr. Inas left Mr. Samir's hand wound open instead of stitching it closed.
a.x: All dog bites should be stitched closed in the department.
a.w: Hand bites are often left open to lower the risk of infection.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked that Mr. Samir could move all of his fingers fully.
a.x: Checking his finger movement was unnecessary for a dog bite.
a.w: Bites can damage tendons.

t: Dirty wound without tetanus check
s:
Mr. Fathi, 60, a farmer, cut his shin deeply on a rusty plough this morning. The wound was full of soil and manure. He could not remember ever having a tetanus injection, and his records showed none.

Dr. Nada gave him local anesthetic and washed the wound well with lots of saline. She removed dirt and dead tissue, then closed it loosely with a few stitches.

Because the wound was dirty, she gave him co-amoxiclav for a week. She checked his sugar, which was normal, and his foot pulses, which were strong.

He asked when the stitches could come out, and she said in about ten days. His son asked whether he could keep working, and she said he could do light jobs if he kept it clean.

She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin.
h: She sent him home with a dressing and advice, without any tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Fathi home with a dirty wound and no tetanus cover.
a.x: He needed a tetanus vaccine and tetanus immunoglobulin.
a.w: A soil-dirty wound in someone with no record of vaccines is high risk for tetanus, which can be deadly.

a.o: Dr. Nada removed the dead tissue from Mr. Fathi's wound before dressing it.
a.x: Removing dead tissue only makes the wound bigger than before.
a.w: Removing dead tissue lowers infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fathi a course of antibiotics for his dirty wound.
a.x: Antibiotics were unnecessary for a wound like Mr. Fathi's.
a.w: Dirty wounds can get infected.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked the pulses in Mr. Fathi's foot as part of her exam.
a.x: The pulses in his foot were off topic for a dirty wound.
a.w: Good blood supply helps a shin wound heal.

t: Syphilis in pregnancy treated with doxycycline
s:
Mrs. Reem, 25, is 14 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her routine booking blood test showed syphilis. She had no sores or rash. She is not allergic to penicillin and has had it before for a sore throat.

Dr. Soha explained the result kindly and in private, and said it could be treated. She asked about her husband and offered him a test and treatment.

She checked her HIV and hepatitis B tests, which were negative, and planned to repeat the syphilis blood test after treatment to check it had worked.

Mrs. Reem was very upset and asked whether her baby would be harmed. She also said she was scared of needles and asked if there was a tablet instead.

Because of the fear of needles, Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks.
h: Dr. Soha prescribed doxycycline tablets for two weeks

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Reem doxycycline for her syphilis in pregnancy.
a.x: She needed a benzathine penicillin injection, with support.
a.w: Doxycycline harms the baby's bones and teeth, and does not treat the baby. Penicillin treats both mother and baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha offered Mrs. Reem's husband a test for syphilis as well.
a.x: Her husband was off topic for her own treatment in pregnancy.
a.w: Partners need testing and treatment, or she can be reinfected.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the result of Mrs. Reem's HIV test from her booking visit.
a.x: HIV tests were unnecessary for a woman being treated for this.
a.w: Syphilis and HIV often go together.

a.o: Dr. Soha planned a repeat blood test for Mrs. Reem after treatment.
a.x: One treatment always works, so repeat tests are not needed.
a.w: A repeat test shows the treatment worked.

t: Gonorrhea treated without partner notification
s:
Mr. Tarek, 22, came in with a yellow discharge from his penis and burning on passing urine for three days. His swab showed gonorrhea. He had two partners in the last month and did not always use condoms.

Dr. Ihab gave him a ceftriaxone injection the same day. He also tested him for HIV, syphilis and chlamydia, and offered a hepatitis B vaccine.

He advised him to avoid sex for a week after treatment and to use condoms in future. He booked a test of cure in two weeks.

Mr. Tarek is a university student and was embarrassed. He asked whether his partners needed to know, and said he did not want to tell them himself.

Dr. Ihab said it was up to him, and did not offer the clinic's partner notification service.
h: Dr. Ihab said it was up to him, and did not offer the clinic's partner notification service

a.o: Dr. Ihab left all of Mr. Tarek's recent sexual partners untold.
a.x: He needed help to tell his partners, or the clinic to do it.
a.w: Partners may have no symptoms but can spread the infection or get complications like infertility.

a.o: Dr. Ihab tested Mr. Tarek for other sexual infections such as HIV.
a.x: Testing for other infections was unnecessary for gonorrhea.
a.w: Sexual infections often go together.

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mr. Tarek a single ceftriaxone injection for his infection.
a.x: A course of tablets would have been better than an injection.
a.w: Ceftriaxone is the treatment for gonorrhea.

a.o: Dr. Ihab booked a test of cure for Mr. Tarek after his treatment.
a.x: A test of cure was a waste of time after a single injection.
a.w: Gonorrhea resistance is rising, so a test checks the treatment worked.

t: Dengue given ibuprofen
s:
Miss Nadine, 27, came back from Thailand five days ago. She had fever, severe aches in her muscles and bones, and pain behind her eyes. Her platelets were 62 and her white count was low. Her dengue test was positive.

Dr. Fady checked her blood pressure lying and standing, which was steady, and asked about bleeding gums, nosebleeds and belly pain, which she had none.

He advised her to drink plenty of fluids and rest. He asked her to come back the next day for a blood count, as platelets can fall further on days 4 to 6.

She works as a nurse and said the pain was the worst she had ever felt. She had paracetamol at home but said it did nothing.

He prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the pain.
h: He prescribed ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the pain

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Miss Nadine ibuprofen for the fever and aches of dengue.
a.x: Miss Nadine needed paracetamol only, with no NSAIDs at all.
a.w: NSAIDs raise bleeding risk in dengue, where platelets are already low.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Miss Nadine's blood pressure lying down and standing.
a.x: Checking her standing blood pressure was unnecessary for her.
a.w: A fall on standing can show fluid loss in severe dengue.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Miss Nadine to come back the next day for a recheck.
a.x: She could have been seen again in a week instead of tomorrow.
a.w: Platelets can fall further on days 4 to 6.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked Miss Nadine about any belly pain or vomiting.
a.x: Belly pain and vomiting were off topic for a fever like this.
a.w: Belly pain is a warning sign of severe dengue.

t: Toxic shock without the tampon removed
s:
Miss Lina, 19, came in with high fever, vomiting, diarrhea and a red rash all over like sunburn. Her blood pressure was 82/50 and her pulse 132. She was on her period. She is a student and lives in a shared flat.

Dr. Inas gave her IV fluids quickly and started IV antibiotics, including clindamycin. She called the intensive care team, who came to see her.

She took blood cultures and checked her kidney and liver tests, which were both a little raised. Her platelets were low.

Her mother arrived and asked if it was food poisoning, since her flatmate had been sick too. Miss Lina was too drowsy to answer many questions.

Dr. Inas did not ask about tampons or do an examination, writing "sepsis, source unclear".
h: Dr. Inas did not ask about tampons or do an examination

a.o: Dr. Inas didn't check for a tampon in Miss Lina, who had toxic shock.
a.x: A tampon should have been looked for and removed at once.
a.w: A retained tampon is the source of the toxin. Leaving it in keeps the toxin flowing.

a.o: Dr. Inas gave Miss Lina clindamycin along with her other antibiotics.
a.x: Clindamycin was unnecessary on top of her other antibiotics.
a.w: Clindamycin stops toxin production.

a.o: Dr. Inas called the intensive care team to see Miss Lina early on.
a.x: Intensive care was not yet needed for Miss Lina at that point.
a.w: Toxic shock can kill quickly.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Miss Lina's platelet count as part of her bloods.
a.x: Her platelet count was off topic for a woman in shock.
a.w: Low platelets are part of toxic shock.

t: Repeated infections without an HIV test
s:
Mr. Hatem, 36, came in with shingles across his chest for the second time this year. He also has white patches in his mouth that won't go away. He has lost 6 kg in three months.

Dr. Ghada started aciclovir for the shingles and nystatin for the mouth thrush. She checked his blood sugar, which was normal.

She asked about steroid inhalers and antibiotics, which he had not used.

Mr. Hatem said he had several partners in the past and does not always use condoms. He was worried about his weight but said he was "just stressed at work".

Dr. Ghada treated the shingles and thrush and sent him home, without offering an HIV test.
h: treated the shingles and thrush and sent him home, without offering an HIV test

a.o: Dr. Ghada didn't offer Mr. Hatem an HIV test after repeated infections.
a.x: He needed an HIV test offered, with other sexual infection tests.
a.w: Repeated shingles, mouth thrush and weight loss in a young man are signs of a weak immune system, often from HIV.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Hatem's blood sugar given his repeated infections.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic for a man with repeated infections.
a.w: Diabetes can cause thrush and infections.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Hatem whether he uses any steroid inhalers.
a.x: Steroid inhalers were off topic for his repeated infections.
a.w: Steroid inhalers can cause mouth thrush.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started Mr. Hatem on aciclovir tablets for his shingles.
a.x: Shingles needs no treatment and gets better on its own.
a.w: Early antivirals help healing and pain.

t: Pneumonia with a high CURB-65 sent home
s:
Mr. Medhat, 78, came in with a cough, fever and breathlessness for three days. He was confused and did not know the date. His urea was 9, his breathing rate 32 and his blood pressure 94/58.

Dr. Rehab checked his oxygen, which was 92% on air, and gave him oxygen. His chest X-ray showed pneumonia on the right.

She took blood cultures and gave him the first dose of antibiotics in the department. She asked about his home, and he lives alone in a third-floor flat.

His daughter said he hated hospitals and would be better at home. She offered to stay with him for a few days.

Dr. Rehab sent him home with oral antibiotics, with his daughter staying.
h: Dr. Rehab sent him home with oral antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rehab sent Mr. Medhat home with a CURB-65 score of 5.
a.x: He needed admission for IV antibiotics and a senior review.
a.w: Confusion, high urea, fast breathing, low blood pressure and age give a CURB-65 of 5, which means a high risk of death.

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat oxygen when his levels were found to be low.
a.x: His oxygen levels were fine and no oxygen was needed at all.
a.w: 92% in an older man with pneumonia needs support.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked about Mr. Medhat's flat and who could help him there.
a.x: His home and help there were off topic for his pneumonia.
a.w: Living alone matters for safety at discharge.

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat his first dose of antibiotics in the department.
a.x: Antibiotics could have waited until he reached the ward.
a.w: Early antibiotics save lives in pneumonia.

t: Hepatitis B baby without birth vaccine
s:
Baby Yousef was born this morning by normal delivery to Mrs. Amal, 27. Her booking blood test showed she carries hepatitis B, with a high viral load, and she took tenofovir in the last months of pregnancy. The baby weighed 3.3 kg and was feeding well.

Dr. Hamed examined the baby, who was pink and active, with a normal heart and hips. He helped Mrs. Amal with skin-to-skin contact and checked that the midwife had given vitamin K.

He told her that breastfeeding was safe with hepatitis B and that she should keep taking her tablets for a few weeks after the birth, as her liver doctor had planned.

Mrs. Amal was tired and tearful, and her husband asked whether their baby had caught the virus. Dr. Hamed said most babies are protected with the right care.

He wrote that the baby's hepatitis B vaccine would be given "with the routine vaccines at eight weeks", and did not give immunoglobulin.
h: He wrote that the baby's hepatitis B vaccine would be given "with the routine vaccines at eight weeks"

a.o: Dr. Hamed left Baby Yousef's hepatitis B vaccine until eight weeks old.
a.x: He needed the vaccine and the immunoglobulin within 24 hours.
a.w: Without a birth dose, about 9 in 10 babies of mothers with a high viral load become lifelong carriers.

a.o: Dr. Hamed told Mrs. Amal that breastfeeding Baby Yousef was safe for him.
a.x: Breastfeeding spreads hepatitis B from the mother to her baby.
a.w: Breastfeeding is safe once the baby is vaccinated.

a.o: Dr. Hamed kept Mrs. Amal on her tenofovir tablets after the birth.
a.x: Her tenofovir tablets should have stopped at the delivery.
a.w: Stopping suddenly can cause a flare; her liver doctor plans when to stop.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked that Baby Yousef had been given his vitamin K at birth.
a.x: Vitamin K was off topic for a baby whose mother has hepatitis B.
a.w: Vitamin K prevents bleeding in all newborns.

t: Fever after raw milk called flu
s:
Mr. Atwa, 44, is a farmer who keeps goats and sheep. He has had fevers on and off for three weeks, with drenching night sweats, aching joints and tiredness. He drinks raw milk from his goats. He has lost 4 kg.

Dr. Ghada examined him. His temperature was 38.6°C. She found a slightly large liver and spleen, and his right knee was a little swollen.

She checked his chest, which was clear, and his urine, which showed no infection. She asked about travel, and he had not left the village.

Mr. Atwa said two of his goats had lost their kids this year. His wife has also had fevers. He was worried about missing the harvest.

Dr. Ghada told him it was flu and to take paracetamol, without a blood culture or a brucella test.
h: told him it was flu and to take paracetamol, without a blood culture or a brucella test

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Mr. Atwa's three-week fever a simple case of flu.
a.x: He needed blood cultures and a brucella test, then doxycycline.
a.w: Raw milk, goats losing kids, wavy fevers, joint pain and a big spleen point to brucellosis, which needs long treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Atwa about any recent travel inside or outside Egypt.
a.x: Recent travel was off topic for a man with a long-lasting fever.
a.w: Travel can bring malaria and typhoid.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Atwa's urine as part of looking for the fever's cause.
a.x: Checking his urine was unnecessary for a man with a fever.
a.w: A urine infection is a common cause of fever.

a.o: Dr. Ghada examined Mr. Atwa's tummy to feel whether his spleen was large.
a.x: His spleen was off topic for a man with a long-lasting fever.
a.w: A big spleen points to a long-lasting infection.

t: Ramipril and ibuprofen carried on in a dry patient
s:
Mr. Hesham, 66, came in after three days of vomiting and diarrhea from a stomach bug that went round his family. He takes ramipril and furosemide for heart failure and metformin for diabetes. He felt dizzy when he stood up.

Dr. Ihab found his blood pressure 102/64 and his mouth dry. His blood tests showed his creatinine had risen from 95 to 170. His potassium was 5.4.

He paused the metformin and the furosemide and advised him to sip oral rehydration fluids little and often. He arranged repeat blood tests in two days.

Mr. Hesham said he had also been taking ibuprofen from the pharmacy for stomach cramps and a headache. His wife asked whether he should eat bananas for his strength.

Dr. Ihab told him to carry on with the ramipril and ibuprofen "because the heart needs them", and said bananas were fine.
h: Dr. Ihab told him to carry on with the ramipril and ibuprofen "because the heart needs them"

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept Mr. Hesham on ramipril and ibuprofen while he was dry.
a.x: He needed ramipril paused and ibuprofen stopped for now.
a.w: When dehydrated, ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs reduce blood flow to the kidneys and make kidney injury and high potassium worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab paused Mr. Hesham's metformin while he had the stomach bug.
a.x: Metformin is perfectly fine to carry on during a stomach bug.
a.w: Metformin can build up and cause lactic acidosis when the kidneys fail.

a.o: Dr. Ihab paused Mr. Hesham's furosemide until he was drinking again.
a.x: Water tablets must never be stopped in a man with heart failure.
a.w: A short pause is right while he is dry.

a.o: Dr. Ihab arranged repeat blood tests for Mr. Hesham in two days' time.
a.x: The repeat blood tests could have waited for a month or so.
a.w: Kidney function and potassium must be rechecked soon.

t: High potassium without calcium
s:
Mr. Atef, 68, has chronic kidney disease and came in feeling weak and tired. His potassium was 7.2. His heart tracing showed tall, peaked T waves and wide QRS complexes. His pulse was 52.

Dr. Nada put him on a heart monitor and repeated the potassium from a fresh sample without a tourniquet, which confirmed 7.2.

She gave 10 units of insulin with glucose through a drip, and nebulized salbutamol. She checked his sugar every hour afterwards and called the kidney team about dialysis.

His wife said he had started a potassium-sparing water tablet a month ago. He had also been drinking a lot of orange juice to "help his kidneys".

She did not give any calcium gluconate, writing "insulin will bring the potassium down quickly".
h: She did not give any calcium gluconate

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Atef no calcium for a high potassium with ECG changes.
a.x: He needed IV calcium gluconate at once to protect his heart.
a.w: Calcium does not lower potassium, but it steadies the heart within minutes and prevents a deadly rhythm.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Atef's blood sugar every hour after the insulin.
a.x: Hourly sugar checks were unnecessary after the insulin drip.
a.w: Insulin can cause low sugar for hours afterwards.

a.o: Dr. Nada repeated Mr. Atef's potassium level while treatment began.
a.x: Repeating the potassium level only wasted precious time.
a.w: A damaged sample can give a falsely high result.

a.o: Dr. Nada called the kidney team to discuss Mr. Atef's high potassium level.
a.x: Dialysis was not needed, so calling them was a waste of time.
a.w: Dialysis may be needed if medicines don't work.

t: Nitrofurantoin with weak kidneys
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 79, came in with burning and going often to pass urine for two days. She had no fever or back pain. Her urine dipstick showed nitrites and white cells. Her kidney function, checked last month, showed an eGFR of 22.

Dr. Abeer sent her urine for culture, as she had had two infections this year. She checked her temperature and her belly, which were normal.

She asked about her fluid intake, and Mrs. Fawzia said she drank little to avoid going to the toilet at night. She advised her to drink more during the day.

Mrs. Fawzia lives with her daughter and takes amlodipine, a statin and a water tablet. Her daughter asked whether her mother should take cranberry juice.

Dr. Abeer prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, the usual choice for a bladder infection.
h: Dr. Abeer prescribed nitrofurantoin for three days, the usual choice for a bladder infection

a.o: Dr. Abeer gave Mrs. Fawzia nitrofurantoin with an eGFR of 22.
a.x: She needed a different antibiotic chosen for her kidneys.
a.w: Nitrofurantoin does not reach the bladder well when the eGFR is low and can build up and harm the nerves and lungs.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mrs. Fawzia's urine to the lab for culture first.
a.x: A urine culture was unnecessary for a simple urine infection.
a.w: Repeated infections need a culture.

a.o: Dr. Abeer advised Mrs. Fawzia to drink more water through the day.
a.x: Drinking more only makes a urine infection worse than before.
a.w: Fluids help flush the bladder.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked Mrs. Fawzia's temperature as part of the visit.
a.x: Checking her temperature was unnecessary for a urine infection.
a.w: A fever suggests a kidney infection.

t: Live vaccine on high-dose steroids
s:
Adam, 4, has nephrotic syndrome and is in his first course of high-dose prednisolone, 60 mg/m² a day, which he started two weeks ago. His urine has cleared of protein and the swelling around his eyes has gone.

Dr. Rana checked his blood pressure, which was normal, and his weight, which had dropped back to normal. She asked his mother to test his urine every morning with a dipstick.

She explained that the steroids would be slowly reduced over the next weeks, and that relapses are common. She asked about chickenpox, which he had not had.

His mother said his nursery wanted his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine up to date. Adam was proud of his star chart for taking his medicine.

Dr. Rana gave Adam his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine in clinic, saying "nephrotic children need extra protection".
h: Dr. Rana gave Adam his MMR booster and chickenpox vaccine in clinic

a.o: Dr. Rana gave Adam live vaccines while he was on high-dose steroids.
a.x: His live vaccines should wait 3 months after the steroids.
a.w: High-dose steroids weaken immunity, so live vaccines can cause the very infection they are meant to prevent.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked whether Adam had already had chickenpox or its vaccine.
a.x: Chickenpox was off topic for a boy with kidney disease.
a.w: Chickenpox can be dangerous in children on steroids.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked Adam's mother to dipstick his urine every day at home.
a.x: Home urine tests are unreliable and should not be relied on.
a.w: Home tests find relapses early.

a.o: Dr. Rana warned Adam's mother that relapses of his illness are common.
a.x: Warning her about relapses was far too worrying for the mother.
a.w: Most children with nephrotic syndrome relapse.

t: Infected blocked kidney sent home
s:
Mrs. Heba, 34, came in with severe pain in her right side going down to her groin. She had a fever of 38.9°C and shivers. Her pulse was 118 and her blood pressure 104/68. Her urine showed blood and white cells.

Dr. Fouad gave her IV fluids, pain relief and IV antibiotics after blood and urine cultures. A CT scan showed a 6 mm stone in her right ureter, with a swollen kidney above it.

He checked that she was not pregnant, and her test was negative. Her white count was 19 and her creatinine normal.

She has two young children and her husband was at work. She asked whether she could go home since the pain was better after the medicines.

He sent her home with oral antibiotics and painkillers, and booked a urology clinic appointment in two weeks.
h: He sent her home with oral antibiotics and painkillers, and booked a urology clinic appointment in two weeks

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent Mrs. Heba home with an infected, blocked kidney.
a.x: She needed urgent drainage of the kidney and IV antibiotics.
a.w: An infected kidney behind a stone is a urological emergency. Antibiotics alone cannot clear it, and sepsis can kill.

a.o: Dr. Fouad did a CT scan of Mrs. Heba's kidneys to look for a stone.
a.x: The CT scan was unnecessary for a woman with a urine infection.
a.w: CT finds stones and blockage.

a.o: Dr. Fouad checked for pregnancy before Mrs. Heba had her CT scan.
a.x: A pregnancy test was off topic for a woman with kidney pain.
a.w: Pregnancy changes scans and treatment.

a.o: Dr. Fouad took blood and urine cultures from Mrs. Heba before antibiotics.
a.x: Taking cultures first only wasted time before the antibiotics.
a.w: Cultures guide treatment.

t: Blood pressure cuff on a fistula arm
s:
Mr. Sabri, 62, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week through a fistula in his left arm. He was admitted with a chest infection. He was alert, his oxygen 95% and his potassium normal.

Dr. Inas checked his fistula, which had a strong buzz. She wrote "no blood or cuffs on left arm" on his chart and stuck a sign above his bed.

She started antibiotics, adjusted for his kidney function, and asked the dialysis unit to see him on his usual day.

Mr. Sabri said his fistula is "his lifeline" and that he guards it carefully. His son asked if the infection would affect his dialysis.

That night, the new nurse could not get a reading on his right arm, so Dr. Inas told her to "just use the left arm this once".
h: Dr. Inas told her to "just use the left arm this once"

a.o: Dr. Inas allowed a blood pressure cuff on Mr. Sabri's fistula arm.
a.x: That arm should never be used; a leg cuff was the safe way.
a.w: A blood pressure cuff can block a fistula, and a clotted fistula can mean no dialysis access.

a.o: Dr. Inas felt and listened for the buzz over Mr. Sabri's fistula each day.
a.x: Checking the fistula's buzz was unnecessary for an inpatient.
a.w: A buzz shows the fistula is working.

a.o: Dr. Inas adjusted Mr. Sabri's antibiotic doses for his kidney failure.
a.x: The antibiotic dose doesn't matter in a man on dialysis.
a.w: Many antibiotics build up in kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked the dialysis unit to come and see Mr. Sabri on the ward.
a.x: His dialysis could wait until he went home from hospital.
a.w: Missing dialysis is dangerous.

t: Post-strep kidney problem called a urine infection
s:
Ali, 8, came in with his father because his urine had looked like cola for two days. His face looked puffy in the mornings. He had a sore throat two weeks ago. He had no burning or pain when passing urine.

Dr. Mahmoud found his blood pressure was 138/92, which is high for his age. His urine dipstick showed blood and protein but no nitrites.

He asked about rashes, joint pain and belly pain, which Ali did not have. He weighed him and found he had gained 2 kg since his last visit.

Ali's father is a taxi driver and said Ali had been passing less urine than usual. Ali was quiet and tired but playing with his father's phone.

Dr. Mahmoud diagnosed a urine infection, started antibiotics and booked a review in a week.
h: Dr. Mahmoud diagnosed a urine infection, started antibiotics and booked a review in a week

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud called Ali's cola urine and high BP a urine infection.
a.x: Ali needed same-day hospital care for kidney tests and his BP.
a.w: Cola urine, swelling and high blood pressure after a sore throat point to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which can cause kidney failure and fits.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud weighed Ali and compared it with his weight last month.
a.x: His weight was off topic for a boy with dark-colored urine.
a.w: Weight gain shows fluid build-up.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked Ali's mother about any rashes or joint pains lately.
a.x: Rashes and joint pains were off topic for a boy with dark urine.
a.w: They can point to other kidney diseases, like HSP.

a.o: Dr. Mahmoud asked how much urine Ali had been passing each day.
a.x: How much urine he passed was off topic for a boy with dark urine.
a.w: Less urine shows the kidneys are struggling.

t: Kidney injury without a bladder scan
s:
Mr. Kamel, 78, was admitted with confusion and belly pain. His creatinine had risen from 90 to 280. He takes oxybutynin for an overactive bladder, started a month ago. He has an enlarged prostate.

Dr. Ayman gave him IV fluids and stopped his ramipril. He checked his potassium, which was 5.6, and started a heart monitor.

He asked for a kidney ultrasound, which would be done the next day.

Mr. Kamel's wife said he had been going to the toilet often but passing only small amounts. His belly felt full above the pubic bone.

Dr. Ayman did not do a bladder scan or put in a catheter, writing "AKI, likely dehydration".
h: Dr. Ayman did not do a bladder scan or put in a catheter

a.o: Dr. Ayman missed urine retention as the cause of Mr. Kamel's injury.
a.x: He needed a bladder scan and a catheter, oxybutynin stopped.
a.w: A big prostate and an anticholinergic drug can stop the bladder emptying. Retention backs up into the kidneys and causes kidney injury and confusion.

a.o: Dr. Ayman stopped Mr. Kamel's ramipril while his kidney function was low.
a.x: His ramipril was fine to carry on at the same dose for now.
a.w: ACE inhibitors worsen kidney injury.

a.o: Dr. Ayman put Mr. Kamel on a heart monitor given his high potassium.
a.x: A heart monitor was unnecessary for a man with a kidney injury.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart rhythm problems.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked for an ultrasound scan of Mr. Kamel's kidneys.
a.x: Imaging was unnecessary for a man with a sudden kidney injury.
a.w: An ultrasound shows a blockage.

t: Rhabdomyolysis given slow fluids
s:
Mr. Raafat, 70, was found on the floor at home after lying there for a day after a fall. His legs were sore and his urine was dark brown. His CK was 48,000 and his creatinine 190. His potassium was 5.3.

Dr. Rehab checked his hips with an X-ray, which showed no fracture. She checked his heart tracing, which was normal.

She asked for a catheter to measure his urine every hour. She checked his skin for pressure sores, and found a red patch on his hip.

He lives alone and had pressed his alarm, but it had not worked. His neighbor found him.

She started IV fluids at 80 mL an hour, writing "elderly, avoid overload".
h: She started IV fluids at 80 mL an hour, writing "elderly, avoid overload"

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Raafat slow fluids for his rhabdomyolysis.
a.x: He needed rapid IV fluids, aiming for a high urine output.
a.w: Muscle breakdown floods the kidneys with myoglobin. Fast fluids flush it through and prevent kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Rehab X-rayed Mr. Raafat's hips after he was found on the floor.
a.x: The hip X-ray was off topic for a man with muscle breakdown.
a.w: A fall can break a hip.

a.o: Dr. Rehab put in a urinary catheter to measure Mr. Raafat's urine output.
a.x: A urinary catheter was unnecessary for a man who could still pee.
a.w: Hourly urine guides fluids.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mr. Raafat's skin for pressure sores after his long lie.
a.x: His skin was off topic for a man with muscle breakdown.
a.w: Long lies cause pressure sores.

t: Clarithromycin with tacrolimus
s:
Mrs. Samia, 45, had a kidney transplant three years ago from her brother. She takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and a low dose of prednisolone. Her kidney function has been stable, with a creatinine of 105. She came to the transplant clinic with a cough and fever for four days.

Dr. Nermine found crackles at the left base and an oxygen level of 95%. A chest X-ray showed a small patch of pneumonia. Her creatinine today was 110 and her last tacrolimus level was in range.

She checked that Mrs. Samia had taken every dose of her transplant medicines, and sent sputum and a viral swab, since transplant patients can catch unusual germs.

Mrs. Samia teaches primary school and said she catches everything from the children. She is allergic to penicillin, which gave her a rash as a child.

Dr. Nermine prescribed clarithromycin for a week, without changing the tacrolimus dose or planning a level check.
h: Dr. Nermine prescribed clarithromycin for a week, without changing the tacrolimus dose or planning a level check

a.o: Dr. Nermine gave Mrs. Samia clarithromycin on tacrolimus, with no level.
a.x: She needed a non-interacting antibiotic, such as doxycycline.
a.w: Clarithromycin blocks the breakdown of tacrolimus. Toxic levels can damage the new kidney and cause tremor and high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Nermine checked that Mrs. Samia never missed her transplant tablets.
a.x: Her transplant tablets were off topic in a simple chest infection.
a.w: Missed doses can cause rejection, and illness is a common time to miss them.

a.o: Dr. Nermine sent a viral swab from Mrs. Samia as well as a sputum sample.
a.x: A sputum sample alone is enough for a simple chest infection.
a.w: Transplant patients get viral and unusual infections that need different treatment.

a.o: Dr. Nermine avoided penicillin for Mrs. Samia given her history of rash.
a.x: A rash in childhood doesn't count as a real penicillin allergy.
a.w: A recorded penicillin allergy should be respected unless properly tested.

t: Polycystic kidneys and a sudden headache
s:
Mr. Waleed, 38, has polycystic kidney disease. His mother had the same condition and died of a brain bleed at 50. He came in with a sudden, severe headache that hit like a thunderclap while he was lifting weights at the gym. He said it was the worst headache of his life and he vomited once.

Dr. Hossam found his neck slightly stiff and his blood pressure 168/98. He was alert, with equal pupils and no weakness.

He gave him paracetamol, morphine and anti-sickness medicine. He asked about his usual headaches, and Mr. Waleed said he had migraines once or twice a year, which built up slowly with flashing lights.

His girlfriend said he had been under stress at work and had skipped meals. After an hour the headache had eased a little, and he wanted to go home to rest.

Dr. Hossam diagnosed a migraine brought on by exercise and sent him home without a CT scan.
h: Dr. Hossam diagnosed a migraine brought on by exercise and sent him home without a CT scan

a.o: Dr. Hossam sent Mr. Waleed home with a thunderclap headache, no CT.
a.x: He needed an urgent head CT, then an LP or CT angiogram.
a.w: Polycystic kidney disease raises the risk of brain aneurysms. A sudden worst-ever headache can be a subarachnoid hemorrhage, and pain relief does not rule it out.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked how Mr. Waleed's usual migraines start and how they feel.
a.x: His old migraines were off topic for this sudden new headache.
a.w: A headache that is different from usual is a warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Hossam checked Mr. Waleed's neck for stiffness during the exam.
a.x: The neck exam was unnecessary for a man with a bad headache.
a.w: A stiff neck can mean blood around the brain.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked about the sudden death of Mr. Waleed's mother.
a.x: His mother's death was off topic for his own new headache.
a.w: Brain aneurysms cluster in families with polycystic kidneys.

t: EPO started with low iron
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 60, has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 18. Her hemoglobin has fallen to 92 over six months, and she is tired and breathless on the stairs. Her ferritin is 45 and her transferrin saturation 12%.

Dr. Mervat checked her B12 and folate, which were normal, and asked about black stools and heavy bleeding, which she had none. Her stool test for hidden blood was negative.

She explained that healthy kidneys make a hormone that tells the bone marrow to make blood, and that her kidneys were not making enough. She checked her blood pressure, which was well controlled.

Mrs. Asmaa said she had been eating less because of nausea. Her daughter asked whether her mother needed a blood transfusion, and Dr. Mervat said she would rather avoid one if possible, to keep her safe for a future transplant.

Dr. Mervat started erythropoietin injections every week, without giving any iron.
h: Dr. Mervat started erythropoietin injections every week, without giving any iron

a.o: Dr. Mervat started Mrs. Asmaa on EPO without treating her low iron.
a.x: She needed IV iron to fill her stores before or with EPO.
a.w: EPO cannot make red cells without iron. Low iron is the most common reason EPO fails in kidney disease.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's B12 and folate levels as well as her iron.
a.x: Checking her B12 and folate levels was a waste of time.
a.w: Other causes of anemia should be ruled out first.

a.o: Dr. Mervat tried to avoid a blood transfusion for Mrs. Asmaa if she could.
a.x: A blood transfusion would have been quicker and better for her.
a.w: Transfusions can make antibodies that make a kidney transplant harder.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's blood pressure before starting EPO.
a.x: Her blood pressure was off topic before starting EPO.
a.w: EPO can raise blood pressure, so it must be controlled first.

t: Diabetic kidney disease without ramipril
s:
Mr. Ibrahim, 55, has had type 2 diabetes for ten years. His yearly urine test showed protein, with an albumin-creatinine ratio of 45, confirmed on a second sample. His eGFR was 62 and his blood pressure 136/84.

Dr. Ghada checked his HbA1c, which was 58, and his cholesterol, which was high, and started atorvastatin. She checked his feet and arranged his eye screening.

She advised him to stop smoking and to cut down on salt, and offered him a place on a stop-smoking course.

He works as a builder and said he was too busy to come to the clinic often. He asked if the protein meant he would need dialysis.

She told him the protein was "small" and did not start an ACE inhibitor, because "his blood pressure is fine".
h: did not start an ACE inhibitor, because "his blood pressure is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ghada held back an ACE inhibitor from Mr. Ibrahim with urine protein.
a.x: He needed an ACE inhibitor or ARB, plus an SGLT2 inhibitor.
a.w: These drugs protect the kidneys in diabetes with protein in the urine, whatever the blood pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada repeated Mr. Ibrahim's urine protein test to confirm the result.
a.x: One urine test is enough without any need to repeat it.
a.w: A second sample confirms that the protein is real.

a.o: Dr. Ghada started Mr. Ibrahim on a statin to protect his heart.
a.x: Statins harm the kidneys and should not be given to him.
a.w: Statins protect the heart, which is the main risk in kidney disease.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered Mr. Ibrahim a place on a stop-smoking course.
a.x: His smoking was off topic for a man with kidney disease.
a.w: Smoking speeds up kidney damage.

t: Bloody diarrhea in a child given antibiotics
s:
Laila, 5, came in with bloody diarrhea for three days after a family barbecue with undercooked burgers. Today she was pale, sleepy and had passed little urine since yesterday. Her stool test showed E. coli O157. Her platelets were 60, her hemoglobin 84 and her creatinine raised.

Dr. Dina checked her blood pressure, which was high, and asked for a blood film, which showed broken red cells.

She gave IV fluids carefully, with a fluid chart and daily weights, and called the children's kidney team, who arranged a transfer.

Laila's cousin, who was at the same barbecue, also had diarrhea. Her mother asked if the meat was to blame and whether they should tell anyone.

To fight the germ and stop the diarrhea, Dr. Dina started IV antibiotics and loperamide.
h: Dr. Dina started IV antibiotics and loperamide

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Laila antibiotics and loperamide for E. coli O157.
a.x: Laila needed no antibiotics or anti-diarrhea drugs at all.
a.w: Antibiotics and loperamide can increase toxin release and worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Dina called the children's kidney team about Laila early on.
a.x: The kidney team was not needed yet for a girl with diarrhea.
a.w: HUS often needs dialysis.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked for a blood film to look at Laila's red blood cells.
a.x: The blood film was unnecessary for a girl with bloody diarrhea.
a.w: Broken red cells confirm HUS.

a.o: Dr. Dina thought about Laila's cousin, who was ill after the same meal.
a.x: Her cousin was off topic for Laila's own illness and care.
a.w: A shared food source must be reported to public health.

t: Ramipril continued after a big creatinine rise
s:
Mr. Sami, 72, has high blood pressure, a past heart attack and narrowed arteries in his legs. He smoked for 40 years. He started ramipril two weeks ago, and his creatinine has risen from 100 to 165. His potassium is 5.2.

Dr. Hala checked his blood pressure, which had fallen from 168/96 to 128/76. She asked about dizziness, which he did not have, and about how much he was drinking.

When she listened over his belly, she heard a whooshing sound to the left of his belly button.

Mr. Sami said he felt better on the new tablet and his headaches had gone. His wife asked whether the kidney result was serious.

She continued the ramipril, saying "a rise is expected", and booked the next test in three months.
h: She continued the ramipril, saying "a rise is expected"

a.o: Dr. Hala kept Mr. Sami on ramipril after his creatinine rose 65%.
a.x: He needed ramipril stopped and a kidney artery scan.
a.w: A small rise is expected, but more than 30% suggests renal artery stenosis, and continuing can cause kidney failure.

a.o: Dr. Hala listened over Mr. Sami's belly for a whooshing sound.
a.x: Listening over his belly was off topic for a creatinine rise.
a.w: A whooshing sound suggests a narrowed artery.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked how much Mr. Sami had been drinking each day.
a.x: How much he was drinking was off topic for his kidney tests.
a.w: Dehydration can also raise creatinine on an ACE inhibitor.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Sami's potassium along with his creatinine.
a.x: His potassium was off topic for a man whose creatinine rose.
a.w: ACE inhibitors can raise potassium.

t: Spironolactone added without a potassium check
s:
Mr. Tamer, 74, has heart failure and kidney disease with an eGFR of 35. He takes ramipril, bisoprolol and furosemide. His heart doctor wrote suggesting spironolactone to help his heart. His last potassium, three months ago, was 5.0.

Dr. Ihab checked his blood pressure, which was 118/70, and his weight, which was steady. His ankles were a little swollen.

He asked about breathlessness at night and how many pillows he used; Mr. Tamer used two, as usual.

Mr. Tamer said he eats a lot of bananas and oranges because he was told they were good for the heart. He also uses a salt substitute.

Dr. Ihab started spironolactone 25 mg without checking his potassium or arranging a follow-up test.
h: Dr. Ihab started spironolactone 25 mg without checking his potassium or arranging a follow-up test

a.o: Dr. Ihab started Mr. Tamer's spironolactone with no potassium check.
a.x: He needed potassium and kidney tests before and after starting.
a.w: Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor and weak kidneys can cause dangerous high potassium.

a.o: Dr. Ihab followed the heart doctor's advice to add spironolactone.
a.x: Spironolactone is never used in anyone with kidney disease.
a.w: It helps heart failure if potassium is watched.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Tamer how many pillows he needs to sleep at night.
a.x: The number of pillows was off topic for a man with weak kidneys.
a.w: Needing more pillows means worse heart failure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Tamer's weight against his weight last time.
a.x: His weight was off topic for a man starting spironolactone.
a.w: Weight gain shows fluid build-up.

t: Missed dialysis sent home
s:
Mr. Fikry, 58, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week. He missed his last two sessions because he went to his village for a funeral. He came in feeling weak and a little breathless. His potassium was 6.8 and his heart tracing showed peaked T waves.

Dr. Nada gave him IV calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose and nebulized salbutamol. She put him on a monitor and gave him oxygen.

An hour later his potassium was 5.9. His chest X-ray showed some fluid in his lungs, and his weight was 4 kg above his usual dry weight.

He said he felt better and wanted to go home to rest. He promised to come to his next session in two days.

She sent him home and asked him to keep his next dialysis appointment, without calling the dialysis unit.
h: She sent him home and asked him to keep his next dialysis appointment, without calling the dialysis unit

a.o: Dr. Nada sent Mr. Fikry home after missed dialysis without arranging it.
a.x: Mr. Fikry needed urgent dialysis arranged for that same day.
a.w: Insulin and salbutamol only move potassium into cells for a few hours. Only dialysis removes it and the extra fluid.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fikry calcium gluconate for his changing heart tracing.
a.x: Calcium gluconate was unnecessary for a man who missed dialysis.
a.w: Calcium protects the heart.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Fikry's weight against his usual dry weight.
a.x: His weight was off topic for a man who had missed his dialysis.
a.w: Weight shows fluid gained.

a.o: Dr. Nada put Mr. Fikry on a heart monitor while he was in the department.
a.x: A heart monitor was unnecessary for a man who missed dialysis.
a.w: High potassium can cause heart rhythm problems.

t: Cloudy dialysis fluid treated with tablets
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 62, does peritoneal dialysis at home. She came in because her dialysis fluid had turned cloudy that morning, and she had a mild belly ache. She had no fever. Her exit site looked clean.

Dr. Fouad examined her belly, which was mildly tender all over. He asked about her technique, and she said she had rushed an exchange two days ago when her grandson was visiting.

He asked the dialysis nurse to check her exit site and to review her technique with her.

She lives with her husband and is very independent. She asked if she could keep doing her dialysis at home.

Dr. Fouad prescribed oral ciprofloxacin, without sending the fluid for a cell count and culture.
h: Dr. Fouad prescribed oral ciprofloxacin, without sending the fluid for a cell count and culture

a.o: Dr. Fouad treated Mrs. Nawal's cloudy dialysis fluid with tablets.
a.x: She needed the fluid tested, with antibiotics put into it.
a.w: Cloudy fluid in peritoneal dialysis is peritonitis until proven otherwise. Antibiotics into the fluid treat it best.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked Mrs. Nawal about her technique when changing her bags.
a.x: Her bag-changing technique was off topic for cloudy fluid.
a.w: A break in technique is a common cause.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked the dialysis nurse to retrain Mrs. Nawal at home.
a.x: Offering her retraining was insulting to a woman of her experience.
a.w: Retraining after a break in technique prevents more infections.

a.o: Dr. Fouad examined Mrs. Nawal's belly for tenderness during the visit.
a.x: Looking at the fluid was enough without any exam of her belly.
a.w: Tenderness supports peritonitis.

t: Blood in the urine treated as an infection
s:
Mr. Hassan, 66, came in because he had seen bright red blood in his urine three times in the last week. It did not hurt. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 45 years and worked in a dye factory.

Dr. Abeer checked his blood pressure and his belly, which were normal. His urine dipstick showed blood but no nitrites or white cells.

She sent his urine to the lab and checked his kidney function.

He said his wife had urine infections and he thought he had caught one.

He had no fever, no burning and no pain in his back. He takes aspirin after a mini-stroke and had lost a little weight, which he put down to eating less since retiring. He was keen not to make a fuss and said the blood had nearly stopped.

She prescribed antibiotics for a urine infection and did not refer him to urology.
h: She prescribed antibiotics for a urine infection and did not refer him to urology

a.o: Dr. Abeer treated Mr. Hassan's painless blood in the urine as an infection.
a.x: He needed urgent urology for a bladder camera and a scan.
a.w: Painless visible blood in the urine in a smoker over 45 can be bladder cancer. Dye work adds to the risk.

a.o: Dr. Abeer sent Mr. Hassan's urine to the lab for a full culture.
a.x: The dipstick was enough without sending the urine to a lab.
a.w: A lab test checks for infection and other causes.

a.o: Dr. Abeer checked Mr. Hassan's kidney function with a blood test that day.
a.x: His kidney function was off topic for blood in his urine.
a.w: Kidney disease can also cause blood in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Abeer asked Mr. Hassan about his work and any dyes he handles.
a.x: His job and work were off topic for blood in his urine.
a.w: Dye work raises the risk of bladder cancer.

t: Furosemide for a dry kidney injury
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 81, was admitted after a week of diarrhea and poor eating. Her creatinine had risen from 80 to 230. She had passed only 200 mL of urine in 12 hours. Her mouth was dry and her blood pressure 96/58.

Dr. Mai stopped her ramipril and her water tablet. She asked for a catheter and hourly urine measurements.

She checked her potassium, which was 5.1, and her chest, which was clear.

Her daughter said her mother had not been drinking much because she did not want to keep getting up.

She lives alone in a ground-floor flat and has mild memory problems. Her legs were not swollen and her chest X-ray showed no fluid. Her heart scan last year was normal. The nurse said she had drunk only a cup of tea since arriving.

To "get the kidneys going", Dr. Mai gave 80 mg of IV furosemide.
h: To "get the kidneys going", Dr. Mai gave 80 mg of IV furosemide

a.o: Dr. Mai gave furosemide to Mrs. Hanem, who was dry with kidney injury.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem needed IV fluids to correct her dehydration.
a.w: Furosemide removes more fluid and worsens kidney injury in a dry patient. It does not improve kidney recovery.

a.o: Dr. Mai stopped Mrs. Hanem's ramipril while her kidneys recovered.
a.x: Her ramipril was fine to carry on at the same dose as before.
a.w: ACE inhibitors worsen kidney injury.

a.o: Dr. Mai put in a urinary catheter to measure Mrs. Hanem's urine output.
a.x: A urinary catheter was unnecessary for a woman who was dry.
a.w: Hourly urine guides treatment.

a.o: Dr. Mai listened to Mrs. Hanem's chest as part of her fluid check.
a.x: Listening to her chest was unnecessary for a woman who was dry.
a.w: Clear lungs show she is not overloaded.

t: Kidney biopsy on clopidogrel
s:
Mr. Kareem, 50, has protein and blood in his urine and a falling eGFR. The kidney team planned a kidney biopsy the next morning. He takes clopidogrel after a heart stent two years ago, and atorvastatin.

Dr. Ayman checked his blood pressure, which was 132/80, his platelets and his clotting tests, which were normal.

He explained the biopsy and the risk of bleeding, and Mr. Kareem signed the consent form.

He asked whether he could eat breakfast before the biopsy. Dr. Ayman told him to fast from midnight.

Mr. Kareem works as a bus driver and wanted to get the biopsy done before his annual leave ended. His heart doctor had said his stent was stable and he had had no chest pain since. He had a nosebleed last month that took a long time to stop.

He did not stop the clopidogrel, writing "clotting normal".
h: He did not stop the clopidogrel, writing "clotting normal"

a.o: Dr. Ayman kept Mr. Kareem on clopidogrel before his kidney biopsy.
a.x: It should have stopped 7 days before, as agreed with cardiology.
a.w: Clopidogrel affects platelets, which normal clotting tests do not show. It raises the risk of serious bleeding after a kidney biopsy.

a.o: Dr. Ayman checked Mr. Kareem's blood pressure before the biopsy.
a.x: Checking his blood pressure was unnecessary before a biopsy.
a.w: High blood pressure raises biopsy bleeding risk.

a.o: Dr. Ayman explained the risk of bleeding to Mr. Kareem beforehand.
a.x: Explaining the bleeding risk was too frightening for him.
a.w: Patients must know the risks before consent.

a.o: Dr. Ayman told Mr. Kareem to fast from midnight before the biopsy.
a.x: Fasting was unnecessary for a needle biopsy of the kidney.
a.w: Fasting is needed for a procedure.

t: Febrile baby sent home with oral antibiotics
s:
Baby Yara, 7 weeks old, was brought in with a fever of 38.4°C and poor feeding for a day. She was a little sleepy but woke when handled. Her urine sample, caught clean, showed nitrites and white cells.

Dr. Rana checked her heart rate, which was 172, and her capillary refill, which was 3 seconds. She checked her soft spot, which was not bulging.

She sent the urine for culture and checked her blood sugar.

Her mother said Yara was her first baby and she was frightened. She asked if she could take her home.

Yara was born at term after a normal pregnancy and had been feeding well until yesterday. She had fewer wet nappies today. Her mother had given her no medicines. The department was very busy, and the children's ward had only one bed left.

Dr. Rana diagnosed a urine infection and sent Yara home with oral antibiotics.
h: Dr. Rana diagnosed a urine infection and sent Yara home with oral antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Baby Yara home with oral antibiotics for her fever.
a.x: Baby Yara needed admission, IV antibiotics and a sepsis check.
a.w: Babies under 3 months with a fever are high risk. A urine infection can spread to the blood or brain.

a.o: Dr. Rana felt the soft spot on top of Baby Yara's head during the exam.
a.x: The soft spot on her head was off topic for a baby with a fever.
a.w: A bulging soft spot can mean meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Rana sent Baby Yara's urine to the lab for culture before treatment.
a.x: The urine dipstick was enough without sending it for culture.
a.w: Culture guides treatment in babies.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked Baby Yara's blood sugar while she was in the department.
a.x: Her blood sugar was off topic for a baby with a fever like hers.
a.w: Sick babies can have low sugar.

t: Morphine for a dialysis patient
s:
Mr. Sabri, 70, has kidney failure and has dialysis three times a week. He was admitted with a broken hip after a fall. He was in a lot of pain.

Dr. Inas arranged surgery for the next day. She asked the dialysis unit to fit his session around the operation.

She checked his potassium, which was normal, and his blood count.

His wife said he was usually very alert and did crosswords every day.

Mr. Sabri lives with his wife in a flat with a lift and walks with a stick. He had dialysis the day before the fall. He takes a phosphate binder and a blood pressure tablet. His hip was shortened and turned out, and the X-ray showed a broken neck of femur. He was frightened of the operation.

She prescribed morphine 10 mg every four hours as needed.
h: She prescribed morphine 10 mg every four hours as needed

a.o: Dr. Inas gave regular morphine to Mr. Sabri, who has kidney failure.
a.x: He needed a safer painkiller, such as low-dose fentanyl.
a.w: Morphine's breakdown products build up in kidney failure and cause drowsiness, confusion and slow breathing.

a.o: Dr. Inas arranged Mr. Sabri's surgery quickly once he was stable.
a.x: His surgery could have waited until later in the week instead.
a.w: Early hip surgery improves recovery.

a.o: Dr. Inas planned Mr. Sabri's dialysis around the time of his surgery.
a.x: His dialysis could have been skipped around the time of surgery.
a.w: Missing dialysis is dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Inas checked Mr. Sabri's potassium level before his operation.
a.x: Checking his potassium was unnecessary before the operation.
a.w: High potassium is dangerous during surgery.

t: Naproxen for gout with weak kidneys
s:
Mr. Raouf, 69, woke up with a hot, red, swollen big toe that was too painful to touch with a bedsheet. He has had gout twice before. He has chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 28, high blood pressure and heart failure, and takes furosemide and ramipril.

Dr. Ghada examined the toe and found it very tender, with no break in the skin. He had no fever. His uric acid was high. She checked his last kidney tests and his potassium, which were stable.

She advised him to rest the foot, keep it cool with an ice pack wrapped in a towel, and keep the bedsheets off it with a frame. She told him to keep drinking water.

Mr. Raouf loves seafood and red meat and had been to a family feast two days ago. His wife asked whether he should stop his water tablet, which she had heard can cause gout.

Dr. Ghada prescribed naproxen 500 mg twice a day for a week, "the quickest way to settle gout".
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed naproxen 500 mg twice a day for a week

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave naproxen to Mr. Raouf despite his known weak kidneys.
a.x: He needed short-course prednisolone or low-dose colchicine.
a.w: NSAIDs can tip weak kidneys into failure and worsen heart failure, especially with ramipril and furosemide.

a.o: Dr. Ghada kept Mr. Raouf's furosemide going for his heart failure.
a.x: The water tablet should have stopped to help settle the gout.
a.w: His heart failure needs the diuretic; gout is treated in other ways.

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mr. Raouf to put an ice pack on his painful big toe.
a.x: Putting ice on the toe only makes an attack of gout worse.
a.w: Cooling the joint eases gout pain.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Raouf about the big family feast before the attack.
a.x: The food at the feast was off topic for an attack of gout.
a.w: Large meals of meat and seafood can trigger gout.

t: Dialysis line fever sent home
s:
Mrs. Inas, 58, has kidney failure and has dialysis through a tunneled line in her neck, while her fistula matures. She had shivers and a fever of 38.7°C during her dialysis session today, an hour after it started. Her blood pressure dropped to 98/60.

Dr. Fady examined the line, and the skin around it was a little red. Her chest was clear and her urine output tiny, as usual. She had no cough, no belly pain and no wounds.

He gave her paracetamol and a small IV fluid bolus, and her blood pressure came back to 118/72. Her shivers settled within an hour.

She lives with her husband, who drives her to dialysis. She said she felt much better and wanted to go home to cook for her grandchildren, who were visiting.

He sent her home with oral co-amoxiclav, without taking blood cultures from the line or a vein.
h: He sent her home with oral co-amoxiclav, without taking blood cultures from the line or a vein

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Mrs. Inas home on tablets, with no blood cultures.
a.x: She needed line and vein cultures, then IV vancomycin.
a.w: Shivers during dialysis with a tunneled line mean a line infection until proven otherwise, which can cause sepsis and endocarditis.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Inas a small fluid bolus when her pressure was low.
a.x: Fluids are always dangerous in patients who are on dialysis.
a.w: A small bolus treats low blood pressure safely.

a.o: Dr. Fady examined the skin around Mrs. Inas's dialysis line for redness.
a.x: The skin around the line was off topic for a woman with fever.
a.w: Redness can show where the infection starts.

a.o: Dr. Fady listened to Mrs. Inas's chest as part of looking for the fever.
a.x: Her chest was off topic for a woman on dialysis with a fever.
a.w: A chest infection is another common cause of fever.

t: Aspirin before a stroke scan
s:
Mr. Fathi, 67, came in by ambulance 50 minutes after his wife saw his face droop and his speech slur at breakfast. His right arm was weak. His sugar was 7.2 and his blood pressure 176/94. He takes metformin and amlodipine.

Dr. Nada called the stroke team at once and worked out his NIHSS score, which was 9. She checked his last-known-well time with his wife and wrote it down.

She asked the nurses to keep him nil by mouth until a swallow screen, and checked his blood count and clotting.

His wife said he was due to fly to Mecca next week and asked whether he would still be able to go. Mr. Fathi was frightened and kept trying to speak.

While waiting for the CT scanner, she gave him 300 mg of aspirin through a drip "to start treatment early".
h: she gave him 300 mg of aspirin through a drip "to start treatment early"

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Fathi aspirin before he had had any brain scan.
a.x: He needed an urgent CT first, with aspirin only after it.
a.w: One in five strokes is a bleed, and aspirin worsens it. Aspirin before scanning can also rule out thrombolysis.

a.o: Dr. Nada wrote down the exact time that Mr. Fathi was last seen well.
a.x: The time he was last well didn't matter for his treatment.
a.w: Clot-busting drugs depend on the time since onset.

a.o: Dr. Nada kept Mr. Fathi nil by mouth until his swallow was checked.
a.x: He could have eaten his breakfast while he waited for a scan.
a.w: Stroke can affect swallowing and food can go into the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Fathi's blood sugar soon after he arrived.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic for a man with a weak arm.
a.w: Low sugar can look exactly like a stroke.

t: Warning stroke sent home without aspirin
s:
Mrs. Samira, 71, came in because her left hand went weak and numb for 20 minutes yesterday, and she could not hold her cup. It went back to normal by itself. She has high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, which she was told about last year but chose not to treat.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found her strength and speech normal. Her pulse was irregular, at 88, and her blood pressure was 158/90.

He did a heart tracing, which confirmed atrial fibrillation. He asked about headaches and eye problems, which she did not have.

Mrs. Samira said she was too busy caring for her husband with dementia to go to the hospital. She wanted to wait and see if it happened again.

He booked her into the stroke clinic in six weeks and did not start any treatment.
h: He booked her into the stroke clinic in six weeks and did not start any treatment

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent Mrs. Samira away untreated after her recent TIA.
a.x: She needed aspirin and a stroke specialist within a day.
a.w: The risk of a full stroke is highest in the days after a TIA. AF makes the risk even higher.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a heart tracing on Mrs. Samira during the visit.
a.x: A heart tracing was unnecessary for a woman who felt better.
a.w: AF is a common cause of stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Samira about her caring duties for her husband.
a.x: Her home life and caring duties were off topic for her TIA.
a.w: Understanding barriers helps plan safe care.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Samira's strength again before she went home.
a.x: The exam was pointless once she had got completely better.
a.w: A normal exam helps confirm a TIA.

t: Fitting child left without a rescue drug
s:
Ahmed, 6, has epilepsy. He was brought in by ambulance having a seizure that started at home 8 minutes ago. His arms and legs were jerking and his lips were blue. His mother had not given his rescue medicine because she was too frightened.

Dr. Dina put him on his side, gave high-flow oxygen and checked his sugar, which was 5.4. She asked the nurse to time the seizure.

She put in a drip and took bloods, including his drug levels. She asked his mother about his usual medicines and allergies.

His mother said he had been ill with a cold and had missed his evening doses because he was vomiting.

Dr. Dina decided to wait another ten minutes "to see if it stops by itself" before giving any medicine.
h: Dr. Dina decided to wait another ten minutes "to see if it stops by itself"

a.o: Dr. Dina waited longer while Ahmed had been fitting for 8 minutes.
a.x: Ahmed needed IV lorazepam or buccal midazolam given at once.
a.w: A seizure over 5 minutes is unlikely to stop alone. The longer it lasts, the harder it is to stop and the higher the risk of brain damage.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Ahmed's blood sugar while he was still fitting.
a.x: His blood sugar was off topic in a child who was fitting.
a.w: Low sugar can cause fits.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked the nurse to time Ahmed's seizure from the start.
a.x: Timing the seizure was unnecessary while he was being treated.
a.w: The length of the seizure guides treatment.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked Ahmed's mother about any missed doses of his medicine.
a.x: Missed doses were off topic for a child who was fitting now.
a.w: Missed doses are a common cause of fits.

t: Valproate for a young woman without a plan
s:
Miss Reem, 19, had her first two seizures this year. Her EEG showed generalized epilepsy. She has myoclonic jerks in the mornings. She is a university student and has a boyfriend. She is not on contraception.

Dr. Mervat explained the diagnosis clearly and gave her advice on sleep, alcohol and showering instead of bathing.

She told her she could not drive until she had been seizure-free for a year, and to tell the licensing authority.

Miss Reem asked whether she could still have children one day. Dr. Mervat said most women with epilepsy have healthy babies.

She started sodium valproate, "the best drug for her type", without discussing pregnancy or contraception.
h: She started sodium valproate, "the best drug for her type", without discussing pregnancy or contraception

a.o: Dr. Mervat started valproate in Miss Reem without discussing pregnancy.
a.x: She needed another drug first, such as lamotrigine, not this.
a.w: Valproate in pregnancy causes birth defects in 1 in 10 babies and learning problems in up to 4 in 10.

a.o: Dr. Mervat told Miss Reem not to drive until her seizures were controlled.
a.x: Driving was off topic for a young woman with a new diagnosis.
a.w: Seizures while driving can kill.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised Miss Reem to take showers instead of baths for now.
a.x: That advice was unnecessary for a young woman with epilepsy.
a.w: People with epilepsy can drown in the bath during a seizure.

a.o: Dr. Mervat said most women with epilepsy go on to have healthy babies.
a.x: Saying that was only false comfort for a young woman like her.
a.w: With planning, most do.

t: Guillain-Barre watched with oxygen levels only
s:
Mr. Hossam, 35, was admitted with tingling in his feet and hands, then weakness climbing up his legs over three days. He had diarrhea two weeks ago. Today he could not stand. His reflexes were absent.

Dr. Ayman diagnosed Guillain-Barre syndrome and started IV immunoglobulin. He asked for a heart monitor because the illness can affect heart rhythm.

He gave blood thinner injections to prevent clots and asked the physiotherapist to see him.

Mr. Hossam's voice was a little weak and he coughed when drinking water. His wife asked if he would walk again.

Dr. Ayman asked the nurses to check his oxygen levels every four hours, saying "his sats are 98%, his breathing is fine".
h: asked the nurses to check his oxygen levels every four hours, saying "his sats are 98%, his breathing is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ayman relied on oxygen levels to watch Mr. Hossam's breathing.
a.x: He needed his FVC measured often, with ICU review.
a.w: Oxygen stays normal until breathing muscles fail suddenly. FVC falls first and warns of the need for a ventilator.

a.o: Dr. Ayman started Mr. Hossam on a course of IV immunoglobulin.
a.x: Immunoglobulin is useless for this kind of nerve weakness.
a.w: IVIG speeds recovery in GBS.

a.o: Dr. Ayman put Mr. Hossam on a heart monitor during his first days.
a.x: A heart monitor was unnecessary for a man with weak legs.
a.w: GBS can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mr. Hossam blood-thinning injections while in bed.
a.x: Blood thinners were unnecessary for a man resting in bed.
a.w: Immobile patients are at high risk of clots.

t: Gentamicin in myasthenia
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 52, has myasthenia gravis and takes pyridostigmine four times a day and a low dose of prednisolone. She was admitted with a kidney infection, with a fever of 38.8°C, shivers and pain in her right side. Her blood pressure was 112/70 and her pulse 104.

Dr. Fouad sent blood and urine cultures and gave IV fluids. He checked her kidney function, which was normal, and did an ultrasound, which showed no blockage.

He asked about her myasthenia, which had been stable for a year, with no drooping eyelids, double vision or trouble swallowing. He measured her breathing strength at the bedside, which was normal.

She works as a librarian and said she gets weak and slurred if her tablets are late. She asked the nurses to give them exactly on time, and Dr. Fouad wrote this on her chart.

He started IV gentamicin, writing "the best cover for kidney infections".
h: He started IV gentamicin, writing "the best cover for kidney infections"

a.o: Dr. Fouad gave gentamicin to Mrs. Nadia, who has myasthenia gravis.
a.x: Mrs. Nadia needed a safer antibiotic, such as ceftriaxone.
a.w: Gentamicin blocks the nerve-muscle junction and can cause a myasthenic crisis with breathing failure.

a.o: Dr. Fouad measured Mrs. Nadia's breathing strength at the bedside.
a.x: Her breathing was fine, so the test was a waste of time.
a.w: Infection can bring on a crisis, and breathing strength shows it early.

a.o: Dr. Fouad wrote the times of Mrs. Nadia's tablets clearly on her chart.
a.x: The timing of her tablets doesn't matter while she is in hospital.
a.w: Late pyridostigmine can cause weakness within hours.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked for an ultrasound of Mrs. Nadia's kidneys on the ward.
a.x: The kidney scan was off topic for a woman with a chest infection.
a.w: A blocked kidney with infection needs urgent drainage.

t: Facial weakness sparing the forehead
s:
Mr. Hany, 63, woke with the right side of his mouth drooping and dribbling when he drank tea. He could raise both eyebrows and wrinkle his forehead evenly. When asked, he said his right hand had felt clumsy doing up his buttons. He has high blood pressure and smokes 20 a day.

Dr. Abeer looked in his right ear for blisters of shingles and found none. His blood pressure was 178/96 and his sugar 6.1.

She asked about recent colds, ear pain and changes in taste, which he did not have. She noted when he was last seen well: at 11 the night before, when he went to bed.

His daughter said his speech sounded slightly slurred, but he insisted he felt fine and wanted to go back to his shop.

She diagnosed Bell's palsy, started prednisolone and eye drops, and sent him home.
h: She diagnosed Bell's palsy, started prednisolone and eye drops, and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Abeer called Mr. Hany's face droop Bell's palsy, forehead spared.
a.x: He needed stroke care, with an urgent brain scan and review.
a.w: Bell's palsy weakens the whole side of the face. Sparing the forehead, with a clumsy hand and slurred speech, points to a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Abeer looked in Mr. Hany's ear for any blisters during the exam.
a.x: His ear was off topic for a man whose face had started to droop.
a.w: Shingles of the facial nerve shows blisters in the ear.

a.o: Dr. Abeer noted the time when Mr. Hany was last seen to be well.
a.x: The time he was last well didn't matter for a droop of the face.
a.w: Stroke treatment depends on the time since onset.

a.o: Dr. Abeer listened to Mr. Hany's daughter about the change in his speech.
a.x: Only the patient's own view counts when taking the history.
a.w: Family often notice changes the patient misses.

t: Giant cell arteritis steroids delayed
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 74, came in with a new headache on her right temple for three weeks. Her scalp hurt when she combed her hair, and her jaw ached when she chewed bread. Yesterday her vision in the right eye went blurry for a few minutes. Her ESR was 88 and her CRP high.

Dr. Rehab felt a tender, thick, pulseless artery on her right temple. She checked her vision and eye movements, which were normal today.

She booked a temporal artery biopsy for the next week and an ultrasound of the temple arteries. She also asked about shoulder stiffness in the mornings, which Mrs. Fawzia had.

Mrs. Fawzia had lost 3 kg and felt tired. She lives alone and was frightened, asking whether she would go blind.

Dr. Rehab told her to wait for the biopsy before starting steroids, "so the result is clear".
h: Dr. Rehab told her to wait for the biopsy before starting steroids

a.o: Dr. Rehab held back steroids from Mrs. Fawzia until after her biopsy.
a.x: She needed high-dose prednisolone that same day, before biopsy.
a.w: With visual symptoms, giant cell arteritis can cause sudden, permanent blindness. The biopsy stays positive for weeks after steroids start.

a.o: Dr. Rehab felt Mrs. Fawzia's temples for tender, thickened arteries.
a.x: Feeling the temple arteries proves nothing either way at all.
a.w: A thick, tender, pulseless artery supports the diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked Mrs. Fawzia about any stiffness in her shoulders in the morning.
a.x: Her shoulders were off topic for a woman with a new headache.
a.w: Polymyalgia often comes with giant cell arteritis.

a.o: Dr. Rehab booked an ultrasound scan of the arteries in Mrs. Fawzia's temples.
a.x: An ultrasound scan of the arteries adds nothing to the diagnosis.
a.w: Ultrasound can show swollen artery walls quickly.

t: Morning headache with blurred discs
s:
Miss Lina, 24, came in with headaches every morning for a month. They were worse when she bent over or coughed, and she sometimes vomited on waking. She had put on 8 kg this year. She takes the combined pill and had started doxycycline for acne two months ago.

Dr. Ghada looked in her eyes with an ophthalmoscope and saw swollen optic discs on both sides. Her blood pressure was normal, and her arms and legs were strong.

She asked about her vision, and Miss Lina said it went gray for a few seconds when she stood up quickly. She also heard a whooshing sound in her ears at night.

Miss Lina is a law student and was stressed about exams. She asked for stronger painkillers so she could study.

Dr. Ghada diagnosed tension headaches, advised her on stress and posture, and prescribed co-codamol.
h: Dr. Ghada diagnosed tension headaches, advised her on stress and posture, and prescribed co-codamol

a.o: Dr. Ghada called Miss Lina's headaches tension type despite her discs.
a.x: Miss Lina needed an urgent same-day brain scan and eye review.
a.w: Swollen discs with morning headaches mean raised pressure in the skull, from a tumor, a clot in a brain vein, or idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

a.o: Dr. Ghada looked in the back of Miss Lina's eyes with her ophthalmoscope.
a.x: Looking in her eyes was unnecessary for a young woman's headaches.
a.w: Swollen discs are the key sign of raised pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Miss Lina about the whooshing sound she hears in her ears.
a.x: The noises in her ears were off topic for her headaches.
a.w: A pulsing sound is common with raised pressure in the skull.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Miss Lina about all of the medicines she has been taking.
a.x: Her acne tablets were off topic for a young woman's headaches.
a.w: Doxycycline and the pill can both play a part in raised pressure or vein clots.

t: Parkinson's tablets missed while nil by mouth
s:
Mr. Sami, 76, has had Parkinson's disease for nine years and takes co-careldopa four times a day at fixed times. He was admitted with a bowel blockage. The surgeons kept him nil by mouth and put a tube through his nose to drain his stomach.

Dr. Hala gave him IV fluids and checked his salts and kidney tests. She asked the surgeons to review him the same day, and they planned to wait 48 hours to see if the blockage cleared.

She asked the nurses for a falls risk check and a pressure mattress, as he was frail.

His wife said he gets very stiff, cannot swallow and becomes confused if he misses even one dose. She brought in his tablets and timetable.

Dr. Hala stopped all his tablets, writing "nil by mouth".
h: Dr. Hala stopped all his tablets, writing "nil by mouth"

a.o: Dr. Hala stopped Mr. Sami's Parkinson's tablets while nil by mouth.
a.x: He needed levodopa down the nose tube, or a skin patch.
a.w: Missing Parkinson's medicine can cause severe stiffness, swallowing problems, pneumonia and a dangerous reaction like neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the nurses for a pressure-relieving mattress for Mr. Sami.
a.x: The pressure mattress was unnecessary for a man of his size.
a.w: Frail, stiff patients get pressure sores quickly.

a.o: Dr. Hala let the surgeons wait 48 hours to see if the blockage settled.
a.x: Every bowel blockage needs an operation straight away.
a.w: Many adhesion blockages settle with drip and suck.

a.o: Dr. Hala looked at the tablet timetable that Mr. Sami's wife brought in.
a.x: A timetable from home was off topic while he was in hospital.
a.w: Parkinson's medicines must be given at the patient's own times.

t: Metoclopramide in Parkinson's disease
s:
Mrs. Hanem, 72, has Parkinson's disease and takes co-beneldopa. She was admitted after a fall with a broken wrist, which was set in plaster. After her pain medicines she felt very sick and vomited twice.

Dr. Mai checked her salts and sugar, which were normal, and listened to her belly, which was soft with normal sounds. She swapped her morphine for a smaller dose to ease the nausea.

She made sure Mrs. Hanem's Parkinson's tablets were given on time and asked the physiotherapist to check her walking before discharge.

Her son said his mother hates being sick and asked for "the strongest anti-sickness injection". Mrs. Hanem was trembling and anxious.

Dr. Mai prescribed metoclopramide 10 mg three times a day as needed.
h: Dr. Mai prescribed metoclopramide 10 mg three times a day as needed

a.o: Dr. Mai gave metoclopramide to Mrs. Hanem, who has Parkinson's.
a.x: Mrs. Hanem needed domperidone or ondansetron instead of that.
a.w: Metoclopramide blocks dopamine in the brain and can make Parkinson's much worse, with stiffness and falls.

a.o: Dr. Mai cut Mrs. Hanem's morphine dose when she became drowsy and sick.
a.x: Her morphine dose should have stayed exactly the same as before.
a.w: Opioids often cause nausea in older people.

a.o: Dr. Mai made sure Mrs. Hanem's Parkinson's tablets were given on time.
a.x: The timing of her tablets doesn't matter while in hospital.
a.w: Late doses cause stiffness and falls.

a.o: Dr. Mai asked the physiotherapist to check how Mrs. Hanem was walking.
a.x: Her walking was off topic for a woman with a broken wrist.
a.w: Falls in Parkinson's are common, and a plaster changes balance.

t: Glucose before thiamine in a heavy drinker
s:
Mr. Medhat, 55, was brought in by the police after being found confused in the street. He smelled of alcohol. He was unsteady and could not walk in a straight line, and his eyes flickered when he looked to the side. His sugar was 2.9.

Dr. Rehab checked his airway and breathing, which were fine, and looked for head injuries, finding only a graze. She asked for a CT scan of his head.

She sent blood tests, including his liver function, salts and alcohol level, and put him on a monitor.

His brother arrived and said Mr. Medhat drinks a bottle of spirits a day and hardly eats. He had been like this since his wife died last year.

To treat the low sugar, Dr. Rehab gave him a glucose drip first, and planned to give thiamine "once he's stable".
h: Dr. Rehab gave him a glucose drip first, and planned to give thiamine "once he's stable"

a.o: Dr. Rehab gave Mr. Medhat a glucose drip before giving any thiamine.
a.x: He needed IV thiamine straight away, before giving glucose.
a.w: Glucose without thiamine can bring on or worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy, causing permanent memory loss.

a.o: Dr. Rehab asked for a CT scan of Mr. Medhat's head after his fall.
a.x: The head scan was unnecessary in a man who drinks heavily.
a.w: Drinkers often fall and can have a hidden brain bleed.

a.o: Dr. Rehab looked closely at Mr. Medhat's eye movements during the exam.
a.x: His eye movements were off topic for a man who drinks heavily.
a.w: Flickering eyes, confusion and unsteadiness point to Wernicke's.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mr. Medhat's salts, including his magnesium.
a.x: His salts were off topic for a confused man who drinks heavily.
a.w: Low sodium and magnesium are common in heavy drinkers.
