t: First seizure and told he can drive
s:
Mr. Tarek, 32, came in after a fit at work yesterday. His colleagues saw him stiffen and jerk for about a minute, and he bit his tongue. He was confused for 20 minutes after. He had been working night shifts and sleeping badly.

Dr. Ihab examined him and found nothing abnormal. His blood tests, including sugar and salts, were normal. He referred him to the first seizure clinic within two weeks.

He advised him not to swim alone, to shower instead of bath, and to avoid heights at work until he was seen.

Mr. Tarek works as a delivery driver and said he would lose his job if he could not drive. He asked whether one seizure really counted.

Dr. Ihab told him he could carry on driving "because it was probably caused by tiredness".
h: Dr. Ihab told him he could carry on driving "because it was probably caused by tiredness"

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Tarek he could drive on after his first seizure.
a.x: He should stop driving and tell the licensing authority.
a.w: A seizure at the wheel can kill the driver and others. Sleep loss can trigger seizures but doesn't remove the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab referred Mr. Tarek to a specialist first seizure clinic.
a.x: One seizure on its own doesn't need a specialist to see it.
a.w: A first seizure needs specialist review and tests.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told Mr. Tarek to take showers instead of baths for now.
a.x: That advice was unnecessary after one seizure on its own.
a.w: People can drown in a bath during a seizure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mr. Tarek about how much sleep he had been getting.
a.x: His sleep was off topic for a man who has had one seizure.
a.w: Lack of sleep can trigger seizures.

t: Head injury on warfarin sent home
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 80, tripped on a rug at home and hit her head on a table. She did not pass out. She has a small bump above her left eye and a mild headache. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation, and her INR last week was 2.6.

Dr. Hamed found her alert, with a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 and no weakness. Her pupils were equal. He cleaned the cut and closed it with glue.

He checked her eyesight and her neck, which were fine, and asked about the rug. He asked the falls team to visit her home.

Her daughter said her mother lives alone but she could stay with her tonight. Mrs. Nawal wanted to go home and was cross about the fuss.

Dr. Hamed sent her home with head injury advice, without a CT scan, because "her GCS is 15".
h: Dr. Hamed sent her home with head injury advice, without a CT scan, because "her GCS is 15"

a.o: Dr. Hamed sent Mrs. Nawal home on warfarin after a head injury.
a.x: She needed a head CT within eight hours, with an INR check.
a.w: People on blood thinners can have a slow brain bleed even if they seem well at first.

a.o: Dr. Hamed asked the falls team to visit Mrs. Nawal at home soon.
a.x: The falls team was off topic for a woman with a cut on her head.
a.w: Preventing the next fall matters.

a.o: Dr. Hamed closed the cut on Mrs. Nawal's forehead with skin glue.
a.x: Skin glue is not safe to use on the face or the forehead.
a.w: Glue is fine for small face cuts.

a.o: Dr. Hamed checked Mrs. Nawal's neck for pain after her fall.
a.x: Her neck was off topic for a woman with a cut on her head.
a.w: Head injuries can come with neck injuries.

t: Migraine with aura on the combined pill
s:
Miss Sara, 23, came in with headaches. She described zigzag lines in her vision for 20 minutes, followed by a throbbing headache on one side with nausea. This happens twice a month. She has taken the combined pill for three years.

Dr. Ghada examined her and found nothing abnormal. She checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her eyes.

She prescribed sumatriptan and an anti-sickness tablet, and advised her to keep a headache diary and avoid skipping meals.

Miss Sara said she liked the pill because her periods were lighter and her skin was better. She did not want to change it.

Dr. Ghada continued the combined pill, saying "the migraines aren't caused by it".
h: Dr. Ghada continued the combined pill, saying "the migraines aren't caused by it"

a.o: Dr. Ghada kept Miss Sara on the combined pill despite aura migraine.
a.x: She needed a method without estrogen, such as a coil.
a.w: Estrogen with migraine with aura raises the risk of stroke.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed sumatriptan for Miss Sara to take during attacks.
a.x: Triptans are dangerous in young women and should be avoided.
a.w: Triptans are standard migraine treatment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Miss Sara to keep a headache diary for two months.
a.x: Headache diaries are useless for a young woman with migraine.
a.w: A diary helps find triggers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Miss Sara not to skip meals during her busy days.
a.x: Skipping meals doesn't matter for a young woman with migraine.
a.w: Hunger is a common migraine trigger.

t: More codeine for daily headaches
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 41, came in with daily headaches for four months. She had had migraines for years, but now she had a dull headache almost every day. She takes co-codamol most days and ibuprofen when it is bad, about 20 days a month.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found nothing abnormal. Her blood pressure and eyes were normal.

He asked about stress, sleep and caffeine. She drinks five cups of coffee a day and sleeps badly.

Mrs. Rasha is a nurse on night shifts and said the headaches were stopping her working. She asked for something stronger.

Dr. Ihab increased her co-codamol to the higher strength and told her to take it whenever she needed.
h: Dr. Ihab increased her co-codamol to the higher strength and told her to take it whenever she needed

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Rasha stronger co-codamol for her daily headaches.
a.x: She needed help to stop painkillers, plus prevention.
a.w: Painkillers on 10 to 15 days a month or more can cause daily headaches. More painkillers make it worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Rasha how much coffee and tea she drinks each day.
a.x: Caffeine was off topic for a woman with daily headaches.
a.w: Too much caffeine can cause headaches.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Rasha's eyes as part of looking into her headaches.
a.x: Her eyes were off topic for a woman with daily headaches.
a.w: Swollen discs would mean raised pressure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Rasha about how well she has been sleeping.
a.x: Her sleep was off topic for a woman with daily headaches.
a.w: Poor sleep worsens headaches.

t: Confusion after a fall called dementia
s:
Mr. Kamal, 82, has mild dementia and lives in a care home. He fell three weeks ago and hit his head. Since then he has become more confused and sleepy, and his left leg is weaker. He takes aspirin and clopidogrel.

Dr. Mervat checked his urine and chest, which were clear. His blood tests were normal apart from a mild anemia.

She asked the care home staff, who said he used to walk to the dining room alone but now needs two people.

His son said his father had been "slipping away" and asked whether this was just the dementia getting worse.

Dr. Mervat said it was likely "progression of dementia" and did not arrange a scan.
h: Dr. Mervat said it was likely "progression of dementia" and did not arrange a scan

a.o: Dr. Mervat blamed Mr. Kamal's new confusion on his dementia.
a.x: Mr. Kamal needed a CT scan of his head soon after the fall.
a.w: A fall weeks before, new weakness and confusion on blood thinners point to a chronic subdural hematoma, which can be drained.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mr. Kamal's urine and chest for any infection.
a.x: His urine and chest were off topic for a man after a fall.
a.w: Infections are common causes of confusion.

a.o: Dr. Mervat asked the care home staff how Mr. Kamal usually was.
a.x: Asking the care home staff was unnecessary for his confusion.
a.w: Staff know his usual abilities.

a.o: Dr. Mervat noticed Mr. Kamal's anemia on his blood count results.
a.x: His anemia was off topic for an older man who is confused.
a.w: Blood thinners can cause bleeding.

t: Tight carotid narrowing not referred
s:
Mr. Raouf, 66, had a TIA two weeks ago, with weakness in his right hand and trouble finding words for 30 minutes. A scan of his neck arteries showed 80% narrowing of his left carotid artery.

Dr. Fady started aspirin and clopidogrel, a high-dose statin, and treated his blood pressure. He advised him to stop smoking.

He told him not to drive for a month and checked his sugar, which was normal.

Mr. Raouf said he was afraid of operations and asked whether tablets would be enough.

He is a retired army officer and walks two miles every morning. His heart tracing showed a normal rhythm. He had had his hernia repaired under general anesthetic years ago without problems. His wife said she would rather he had whatever gave him the best chance of avoiding a big stroke.

Dr. Fady agreed tablets were enough and did not refer him to a vascular surgeon.
h: Dr. Fady agreed tablets were enough and did not refer him to a vascular surgeon

a.o: Dr. Fady didn't refer Mr. Raouf for surgery on his carotid narrowing.
a.x: He needed a vascular surgeon to see him within 2 weeks.
a.w: Surgery on a tight, symptomatic carotid narrowing greatly lowers the risk of a major stroke.

a.o: Dr. Fady started Mr. Raouf on a statin after his warning stroke.
a.x: Statins were unnecessary for a man after a warning stroke.
a.w: Statins lower stroke risk.

a.o: Dr. Fady told Mr. Raouf not to drive for one month after his TIA.
a.x: Telling him not to drive was unnecessary after a short TIA.
a.w: Driving rules apply after a TIA.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised Mr. Raouf to stop smoking as soon as he could.
a.x: His smoking was off topic for a man after a warning stroke.
a.w: Smoking raises stroke risk.

t: Stroke patient fed without a swallow test
s:
Mrs. Amal, 75, was admitted with a stroke affecting her left side. She was drowsy but rousable. Her speech was slurred and she was dribbling. A CT showed a clot, not a bleed.

Dr. Ayman started aspirin through a nasogastric tube and asked the stroke nurses to check her blood pressure and sugar.

He asked the physiotherapist to see her and arranged a pressure mattress.

Her daughter brought her favorite soup and asked to feed her mother.

Mrs. Amal lives with her husband, who has heart failure, and she is usually his main carer. She was a keen cook and had made the same lentil soup for her family for fifty years. When the nurse gave her a sip of water earlier, she coughed and her voice sounded wet and gurgly afterwards.

Dr. Ayman said she could have the soup, without a swallow screen.
h: Dr. Ayman said she could have the soup, without a swallow screen

a.o: Dr. Ayman let Mrs. Amal eat before any swallow test.
a.x: She needed to stay nil by mouth until a swallow screen.
a.w: Stroke can affect swallowing, and food or drink can go into the lungs, causing pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mrs. Amal's aspirin through a tube in her nose.
a.x: Her aspirin should have waited until she could swallow again.
a.w: Aspirin is given early once a bleed is ruled out, by tube or suppository if needed.

a.o: Dr. Ayman arranged a pressure-relieving mattress for Mrs. Amal.
a.x: The pressure mattress could have waited a week or so for her.
a.w: Weak, drowsy stroke patients get pressure sores quickly.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked the physiotherapist to see Mrs. Amal early on.
a.x: Therapy should have waited until she was much stronger.
a.w: Early, gentle therapy helps stroke recovery.

t: Encephalitis treated without aciclovir
s:
Mrs. Nesma, 48, came in with fever, headache and strange behavior for two days. She was confused and had a fit in the ambulance. Her CT scan was normal. Her lumbar puncture showed raised white cells, mainly lymphocytes.

Dr. Dina gave her IV ceftriaxone and a seizure medicine. She asked for an MRI and an EEG.

She asked for the spinal fluid to be tested for viruses with PCR.

Her husband said she had been talking nonsense and smelling things that weren't there.

She works as an accountant and had no recent travel. She has no allergies and takes no regular medicines. Her kidney function was normal. Her blood pressure was 132/80 and her neck was only mildly stiff. The MRI had a waiting list until the next morning.

Dr. Dina did not start aciclovir, writing "await viral PCR".
h: Dr. Dina did not start aciclovir, writing "await viral PCR"

a.o: Dr. Dina held back aciclovir from Mrs. Nesma until the PCR result.
a.x: Mrs. Nesma needed IV aciclovir to be started at once.
a.w: Fever, confusion, fits and smell changes suggest herpes encephalitis. Every hour without aciclovir raises the risk of death and brain damage.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked for an MRI scan of Mrs. Nesma's brain on the first day.
a.x: The MRI scan was unnecessary for a woman with a fever.
a.w: MRI can show changes from encephalitis.

a.o: Dr. Dina gave Mrs. Nesma a seizure medicine after her first fit.
a.x: A seizure medicine was unnecessary after a single fit.
a.w: Seizures must be controlled.

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Mrs. Nesma's spinal fluid for a viral PCR test.
a.x: The PCR test on her spinal fluid was unnecessary.
a.w: PCR confirms the virus.

t: Brain bleed without nimodipine
s:
Mr. Waleed, 45, was admitted with a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a burst brain aneurysm. The aneurysm was coiled today. He is awake and talking.

Dr. Hossam asked for neurological checks every hour and kept his blood pressure steady.

He gave him IV fluids to keep him well hydrated and checked his sodium.

His wife asked whether he would have more bleeding.

Mr. Waleed is a bank manager and had a sudden thunderclap headache while playing tennis. He smokes and has high blood pressure, which he had not been treating. His blood pressure now was 138/82. His mother had died young of a stroke. He was alert and had no weakness, though his headache was still bad.

Dr. Hossam did not prescribe nimodipine, writing "aneurysm secured".
h: Dr. Hossam did not prescribe nimodipine, writing "aneurysm secured"

a.o: Dr. Hossam gave no nimodipine after Mr. Waleed's brain bleed.
a.x: Mr. Waleed needed nimodipine by mouth for 21 days.
a.w: Nimodipine reduces brain damage from narrowing of the arteries after a bleed.

a.o: Dr. Hossam asked for hourly neurological checks on Mr. Waleed.
a.x: Once the aneurysm is coiled, the checks can stop.
a.w: A drop in alertness can mean artery spasm or fluid build-up.

a.o: Dr. Hossam kept Mr. Waleed well hydrated with fluids on the ward.
a.x: Fluids should have been cut to protect his brain.
a.w: Dehydration worsens artery narrowing after a bleed.

a.o: Dr. Hossam checked Mr. Waleed's sodium level every day.
a.x: His sodium level was off topic after a brain bleed.
a.w: Low sodium is common after a brain bleed.

t: Antipsychotic first for agitation in dementia
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 85, has Alzheimer's disease and was admitted with a urine infection. At night she became agitated, calling out and trying to get out of bed.

Dr. Rana treated the infection and checked her pain, which seemed to be from constipation. She gave her a laxative.

She asked the nurses to keep the lights low and to have a familiar person nearby.

Her daughter said her mother calms down with music and familiar photos.

Mrs. Fawzia was a retired music teacher and still hummed the songs she used to teach. At home she sleeps well with her own blanket and a night light. She had a small stroke two years ago and takes aspirin. The night nurses were busy and asked for something to calm her.

Dr. Rana prescribed regular haloperidol at night "to keep her settled".
h: Dr. Rana prescribed regular haloperidol at night "to keep her settled"

a.o: Dr. Rana started haloperidol for Mrs. Fawzia's agitation.
a.x: She needed causes treated first, with antipsychotics last.
a.w: Antipsychotics in dementia raise the risk of stroke, falls and death.

a.o: Dr. Rana treated Mrs. Fawzia's constipation during her stay.
a.x: Her constipation was off topic for a woman who is agitated.
a.w: Pain and constipation often cause agitation in dementia.

a.o: Dr. Rana asked for someone familiar to sit with Mrs. Fawzia.
a.x: Visitors only make her agitation worse than it was before.
a.w: Familiar people calm patients with dementia.

a.o: Dr. Rana treated the urine infection found in Mrs. Fawzia.
a.x: Her urine infection was not linked to her behavior at all.
a.w: Infection often causes sudden confusion in dementia.

t: Phenytoin pushed without a heart monitor
s:
Mr. Samy, 61, was admitted after a run of seizures. He had two doses of lorazepam in the ambulance and was now drowsy but not fitting. He has heart disease and takes bisoprolol. His sugar and salts were normal.

Dr. Ayman decided to load him with IV phenytoin to stop more seizures. He worked out the dose by his weight, 82 kg, and checked that he had no allergy.

He checked a heart tracing before starting, which showed a slow but normal rhythm of 56. He asked the nurses to check his breathing and oxygen every 15 minutes.

The ward was short of monitors, and the only one was in use for another patient. Mr. Samy's son asked whether his father would have more fits.

Dr. Ayman gave the phenytoin by a quick push over five minutes, without a heart monitor, "to get it in before the next fit".
h: Dr. Ayman gave the phenytoin by a quick push over five minutes, without a heart monitor

a.o: Dr. Ayman gave Mr. Samy IV phenytoin fast, with no heart monitor.
a.x: It needed giving slowly, with heart and BP monitoring.
a.w: Fast IV phenytoin can cause low blood pressure, slow heart rhythms and cardiac arrest, especially with heart disease and a beta blocker.

a.o: Dr. Ayman worked out Mr. Samy's phenytoin dose from his body weight.
a.x: A fixed dose of phenytoin is safer for every adult patient.
a.w: Phenytoin loading doses are worked out by weight.

a.o: Dr. Ayman did a heart tracing on Mr. Samy before starting the phenytoin.
a.x: The heart tracing was a waste of time while he was fitting.
a.w: A baseline tracing shows heart block that makes phenytoin dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Ayman asked the nurses for breathing checks every 15 minutes.
a.x: Breathing checks were not needed once the fits had stopped.
a.w: Lorazepam and fits can both slow breathing.

t: Lumbar puncture on rivaroxaban
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 57, was admitted with confusion and a low fever for a day. Her CT head was normal. The team planned a lumbar puncture to check for meningitis or encephalitis. She takes rivaroxaban for atrial fibrillation, last taken this morning.

Dr. Mervat had already started IV ceftriaxone and aciclovir so treatment would not be delayed. She checked her platelets, which were normal, and her kidney function, which was mildly reduced.

She explained the procedure to Mrs. Asmaa's husband, as Mrs. Asmaa was too confused to consent, and wrote the decision down as being in her best interests.

Her husband said she had a heart stent five years ago but no recent clots. He asked whether the test was painful.

Dr. Mervat did the lumbar puncture that afternoon, six hours after the rivaroxaban dose, writing "clotting tests normal".
h: Dr. Mervat did the lumbar puncture that afternoon, six hours after the rivaroxaban dose

a.o: Dr. Mervat did Mrs. Asmaa's LP six hours after her rivaroxaban.
a.x: The LP should have waited about 48 hours after her last dose.
a.w: A bleed around the spinal cord after a lumbar puncture on a blood thinner can cause paralysis. Normal clotting tests do not show rivaroxaban's effect.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started antibiotics and aciclovir before the lumbar puncture.
a.x: Treatment should have waited for the spinal fluid results.
a.w: Treatment should never be delayed for a lumbar puncture.

a.o: Dr. Mervat acted in Mrs. Asmaa's best interests while she was confused.
a.x: She should have waited until Mrs. Asmaa could give consent.
a.w: When a patient lacks capacity, urgent tests can be done in their best interests.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Asmaa's kidney function before the procedure.
a.x: Her kidney function was off topic before a lumbar puncture.
a.w: Rivaroxaban lasts longer when the kidneys are weak.

t: Spinal injury patient laid flat with a pounding headache
s:
Mr. Karim, 29, has a spinal cord injury at the level of his upper chest after a car crash two years ago. He was in hospital for a pressure sore. This afternoon he suddenly had a pounding headache, a blocked nose and sweating above his chest. His blood pressure was 210/120 and his pulse 52.

Dr. Hala recognized that his usual blood pressure was about 100/60. She checked his catheter bag, which was empty, and saw that the tube was kinked under his leg.

She asked the nurse to loosen his tight leg straps and checked his skin for any new pressure area.

Mr. Karim said this had happened once before when his bladder was full. He was frightened and his face was flushed.

Dr. Hala laid him flat to rest and gave him a pain-relief tablet for the headache, saying she would come back after the round.
h: Dr. Hala laid him flat to rest and gave him a pain-relief tablet for the headache

a.o: Dr. Hala laid Mr. Karim flat and left his very high blood pressure.
a.x: He needed sitting up, with his catheter unkinked at once.
a.w: This is autonomic dysreflexia. The blood pressure can cause a stroke or fits within minutes unless the trigger, often a blocked bladder, is removed.

a.o: Dr. Hala compared Mr. Karim's blood pressure with his usual reading.
a.x: His usual blood pressure reading was off topic at that time.
a.w: People with high spinal injuries usually have low blood pressure, so 210 is a huge rise.

a.o: Dr. Hala asked the nurse to loosen the straps on Mr. Karim's legs.
a.x: The straps on his legs were off topic for a pounding headache.
a.w: Tight clothing below the injury can trigger dysreflexia.

a.o: Dr. Hala checked Mr. Karim's catheter for any kink or blockage.
a.x: His catheter was off topic for a man with a pounding headache.
a.w: A blocked bladder is the most common trigger.

t: Twisted ovary sent for a routine scan
s:
Miss Rahma, 24, came in with sudden, severe pain low on her right side that started three hours ago while dancing. She has vomited four times. She knows she has a 6 cm cyst on her right ovary from a scan last month.

Dr. Soha checked her pregnancy test, which was negative, and her temperature, which was normal. Her belly was very tender on the right low down.

She checked her urine, which was clear, and gave her IV morphine and an anti-sickness drug.

Miss Rahma said the pain came in waves and was the worst she had ever had. She is engaged and asked whether she could still have children. The ultrasound department was closed until morning.

Dr. Soha booked a routine ultrasound for the next morning and admitted her for pain relief.
h: booked a routine ultrasound for the next morning and admitted her for pain relief

a.o: Dr. Soha left Miss Rahma's likely ovarian torsion until morning.
a.x: She needed urgent gynecology review and keyhole surgery.
a.w: Sudden pain with vomiting and a known cyst suggests a twisted ovary. Delay can kill the ovary.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked a pregnancy test for Miss Rahma on arrival.
a.x: A pregnancy test was off topic for a girl with sudden pain.
a.w: Ectopic pregnancy must be ruled out.

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Miss Rahma IV morphine for her severe pain.
a.x: Morphine hides the signs and should not have been given.
a.w: Pain relief is right and doesn't hide the diagnosis.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Miss Rahma's urine for any sign of infection.
a.x: Checking her urine was unnecessary for pain on one side.
a.w: A kidney stone can cause this pain.

t: High blood pressure in pregnancy sent home
s:
Mrs. Yasmin, 32, is 35 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came to the antenatal clinic with a headache for two days and flashing lights in her eyes. Her feet and face had swollen in the last week. Her blood pressure was 162/110 and her urine showed 2+ protein.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat, which was normal, and felt her belly, which was tender just under the ribs on the right. Her reflexes were brisk.

She sent blood tests for her liver, kidneys and platelets, and gave her paracetamol for the headache.

Mrs. Yasmin is a pharmacist and had a busy week at work. Her husband was away, and she asked whether she could go home and rest instead of staying.

Dr. Soha started labetalol tablets and sent her home, asking her to come back in two days for a blood pressure check.
h: Dr. Soha started labetalol tablets and sent her home, asking her to come back in two days

a.o: Dr. Soha sent Mrs. Yasmin home with severe pre-eclampsia.
a.x: She needed admission, BP control and magnesium sulfate.
a.w: A blood pressure of 160/110 with headache, visual signs, right upper belly pain and protein means severe pre-eclampsia, which can cause fits, strokes and liver rupture.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat while Mrs. Yasmin was there.
a.x: The baby's heartbeat was off topic for the mother's blood pressure.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can affect the baby's growth and well-being.

a.o: Dr. Soha started Mrs. Yasmin on labetalol for her high blood pressure.
a.x: Blood pressure should never be lowered during a pregnancy.
a.w: Labetalol is the first choice for high blood pressure in pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Soha sent liver blood tests for Mrs. Yasmin during the visit.
a.x: Liver tests were off topic for a woman with high blood pressure.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can damage the liver and lower platelets.

t: Fit in pregnancy treated with diazepam only
s:
Mrs. Heba, 28, is 37 weeks pregnant. She had a fit in the antenatal ward. Her blood pressure was 168/112 and her urine had 3+ protein. She had complained of a headache all morning.

Dr. Soha turned her onto her left side, gave oxygen and called the senior obstetrician and anesthetist. The fit stopped after two minutes.

She gave labetalol through a drip to lower her blood pressure and checked the baby's heartbeat, which was slow during the fit but recovered.

Mrs. Heba's mother was waiting outside and was terrified. She asked whether her daughter had epilepsy.

Dr. Soha gave IV diazepam to stop more fits, and did not start magnesium sulfate.
h: Dr. Soha gave IV diazepam to stop more fits, and did not start magnesium sulfate

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Heba diazepam for her eclamptic fit, no magnesium.
a.x: She needed IV magnesium sulfate, a loading dose then a drip.
a.w: Magnesium is the drug that prevents and treats eclamptic fits. It works better than diazepam or phenytoin.

a.o: Dr. Soha turned Mrs. Heba onto her left side during and after the fit.
a.x: She should have been laid flat on her back during the fit.
a.w: Lying on the left side stops the womb pressing on the big vein.

a.o: Dr. Soha lowered Mrs. Heba's very high blood pressure after the fit.
a.x: Her blood pressure is not urgent at all after a fit like that.
a.w: Very high blood pressure can cause a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Soha called the senior obstetrician to come at once for Mrs. Heba.
a.x: The junior doctor could have managed the fit alone just fine.
a.w: Eclampsia needs a team.

t: Postpartum bleed while waiting for blood
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 30, delivered her third baby an hour ago. She suddenly started bleeding heavily, and the midwife estimated 1,000 mL of blood loss. Her pulse was 118 and her blood pressure 98/60. Her uterus felt soft and boggy above her belly button.

Dr. Rana called for help and put in two large drips. She sent blood for crossmatch and a blood count.

She checked the placenta, which was complete, and looked for tears, finding only a small graze.

Mrs. Nadia's husband was holding the baby and asked why there was so much blood. He was pale himself.

Dr. Rana started IV fluids and waited for the blood to arrive, without rubbing the uterus or giving any drug to make it contract.
h: without rubbing the uterus or giving any drug to make it contract

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't rub Mrs. Nadia's uterus or give drugs to firm it.
a.x: She needed uterine massage and oxytocin, then other drugs.
a.w: A soft uterus is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. Making it contract stops the bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rana checked that Mrs. Nadia's placenta had come out complete.
a.x: The placenta was off topic for a woman who was bleeding heavily.
a.w: A piece left inside can cause bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rana put in two large drips while Mrs. Nadia was bleeding.
a.x: One small drip is enough for a woman bleeding after birth.
a.w: Heavy bleeding needs fast fluids and blood.

a.o: Dr. Rana looked for any tears in the birth canal as a cause.
a.x: Tears in the birth canal were off topic for the bleeding.
a.w: Tears are another cause of bleeding after birth.

t: Rhesus-negative bleed without anti-D
s:
Mrs. Rana, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant with her second baby. She came in with light bleeding after falling on the stairs. She has no pain. Her blood group is O negative, and her husband is A positive. The baby's heartbeat was normal on the scan.

Dr. Ihab examined her and found no tenderness. The scan showed the placenta was high and the baby was well.

He checked the size of the bleed and explained that light bleeding after a fall is often minor. He advised her to rest for a day.

Mrs. Rana said she had anti-D injections in her first pregnancy and did not like needles. She asked whether she needed one this time.

He told her the bleed was small and sent her home without anti-D.
h: He told her the bleed was small and sent her home without anti-D

a.o: Dr. Ihab sent Mrs. Rana home with no anti-D after her bleed.
a.x: She needed anti-D within 72 hours, with a Kleihauer test.
a.w: Any bleed or fall after 12 weeks in a rhesus-negative mother can let the baby's blood cross. Antibodies can harm this and future babies.

a.o: Dr. Ihab did a scan to check where Mrs. Rana's placenta was lying.
a.x: The scan was unnecessary for a woman with a small bleed.
a.w: A low placenta can cause bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Rana's tummy for any tenderness during the visit.
a.x: Tenderness was off topic for a woman with a small bleed.
a.w: Pain can mean the placenta is separating.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Rana about how her first pregnancy went.
a.x: Her first pregnancy was off topic for this bleed in pregnancy.
a.w: She needs anti-D in each pregnancy.

t: Internal exam with a low placenta
s:
Mrs. Amal, 33, is 32 weeks pregnant with her third baby. She came in with painless bright red bleeding that soaked a pad. Her 20-week scan said the placenta was low-lying, but she missed her follow-up scan. Her blood pressure was 118/74.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heartbeat, which was normal, and felt her belly, which was soft and not tender. She put in a drip and sent blood for crossmatch.

She gave steroid injections to help the baby's lungs in case of an early birth.

Mrs. Amal had two cesareans before. Her husband asked whether the baby would be all right.

To see whether the cervix was opening, Dr. Soha did an internal exam with her fingers before the scan.
h: Dr. Soha did an internal exam with her fingers before the scan

a.o: Dr. Soha did an internal exam on Mrs. Amal before any scan was done.
a.x: She needed an ultrasound first, with no finger exam at all.
a.w: A finger exam can tear a low placenta and cause a massive bleed.

a.o: Dr. Soha gave Mrs. Amal steroid injections for the baby's lungs.
a.x: Steroid injections were unnecessary at this stage of pregnancy.
a.w: Steroids help the baby's lungs if born early.

a.o: Dr. Soha sent Mrs. Amal's blood to the lab for a crossmatch.
a.x: A crossmatch was unnecessary for a woman with a small bleed.
a.w: Heavy bleeding may need transfusion.

a.o: Dr. Soha asked Mrs. Amal about any cesareans in her past pregnancies.
a.x: Her past cesareans were off topic for a bleed in pregnancy.
a.w: Past cesareans raise the risk of a placenta growing into the scar.

t: Group B strep in labor without antibiotics
s:
Mrs. Sara, 29, is in labor at 39 weeks with her first baby. Her waters broke four hours ago and the fluid was clear. A swab taken at 36 weeks, because her sister's baby had been very ill with an infection, showed group B streptococcus. She has no allergies.

Dr. Ihab checked her temperature, which was 37.1°C, and the baby's heart tracing, which was normal. He examined her and found her cervix 4 cm open.

He offered her pain relief, and she chose an epidural. He also checked her blood pressure and asked the midwife to keep a fluid chart.

Mrs. Sara had planned a water birth and was disappointed about the epidural. Her husband asked whether the swab result meant the baby would be sick.

Dr. Ihab did not start IV antibiotics, writing "no fever, waters clear, baby well".
h: Dr. Ihab did not start IV antibiotics, writing "no fever, waters clear, baby well"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Mrs. Sara no antibiotics in labor for her group B strep.
a.x: She needed IV benzylpenicillin every four hours in labor.
a.w: Group B strep can cause sepsis and meningitis in newborns. Antibiotics in labor greatly lower the risk, with or without fever.

a.o: Dr. Ihab took Mrs. Sara's temperature regularly throughout her labor.
a.x: Temperature checks in labor were only a waste of time.
a.w: A fever in labor can mean infection in the womb.

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mrs. Sara choose an epidural for her pain relief.
a.x: An epidural spreads the infection and should be avoided.
a.w: Pain relief is her choice and is safe with group B strep.

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept watching the baby's heart tracing throughout labor.
a.x: The tracing was not needed once it had been normal at first.
a.w: Changes in the tracing can be the first sign of infection.

t: Hyperemesis sent home with ketones
s:
Mrs. Lobna, 24, is 9 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She has been vomiting about ten times a day for a week and can't keep even water down. She has lost 3 kg. Her urine showed 3+ ketones, her pulse was 108 and her mouth was dry.

Dr. Rasha checked her salts, which showed a low potassium of 3.1, and her thyroid tests, which were slightly overactive, as often happens in early pregnancy.

She arranged a scan, which showed a single baby with a normal heartbeat and no twins.

Mrs. Lobna works as a dental nurse and had been too sick to go to work. She felt dizzy when she stood up and asked whether the vomiting would harm the baby.

Dr. Rasha gave her anti-sickness tablets and sent her home, advising "small, dry meals".
h: Dr. Rasha gave her anti-sickness tablets and sent her home

a.o: Dr. Rasha sent Mrs. Lobna home with severe vomiting and ketones.
a.x: She needed admission for IV fluids and anti-sickness drugs.
a.w: Hyperemesis with weight loss, ketones and low potassium can cause kidney injury, Wernicke's encephalopathy and clots.

a.o: Dr. Rasha arranged a pregnancy scan for Mrs. Lobna to check the dates.
a.x: The scan was off topic for a woman who is vomiting so much.
a.w: Twins or a molar pregnancy can cause severe vomiting.

a.o: Dr. Rasha did not treat Mrs. Lobna's slightly overactive thyroid test.
a.x: The overactive thyroid needed tablets started at once.
a.w: Pregnancy hormones often raise thyroid tests briefly in early pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Lobna's potassium along with her other salts.
a.x: Her salts were off topic for a woman who is vomiting a lot.
a.w: Vomiting lowers potassium.

t: Low-dose folic acid for a woman with epilepsy
s:
Mrs. Dina, 30, came to plan her first pregnancy. She has epilepsy, well controlled on lamotrigine, and has not had a fit for three years. Her BMI is 33. She does not smoke or drink.

Dr. Rasha checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her rubella immunity, which was good. She sent a blood count and thyroid test.

She talked with her neurologist, who agreed to keep the lamotrigine and to check her levels during pregnancy, as they often fall.

Mrs. Dina works as a graphic designer and had read about pregnancy online. She asked about safe foods, and Dr. Rasha told her to avoid liver and unpasteurized cheese.

Dr. Rasha advised her to take the usual 400 microgram folic acid tablet from the pharmacy, starting now.
h: Dr. Rasha advised her to take the usual 400 microgram folic acid tablet from the pharmacy

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mrs. Dina the usual low dose of folic acid.
a.x: She needed 5 mg of folic acid daily, from before conception.
a.w: Epilepsy drugs and a BMI over 30 both raise the risk of spine defects, so the high dose is needed.

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mrs. Dina on her lamotrigine while trying for a baby.
a.x: All epilepsy drugs must be stopped before a pregnancy starts.
a.w: Lamotrigine is one of the safer epilepsy drugs in pregnancy, and fits are dangerous.

a.o: Dr. Rasha planned lamotrigine level checks during Mrs. Dina's pregnancy.
a.x: Lamotrigine levels don't change at all during a pregnancy.
a.w: Pregnancy speeds up the breakdown of lamotrigine.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Mrs. Dina to avoid eating liver while she is pregnant.
a.x: Liver is a healthy food to eat while a woman is pregnant.
a.w: Liver is very high in vitamin A, which can harm the baby.

t: Sugar test not offered to a high-risk mother
s:
Mrs. Sahar, 34, is 16 weeks pregnant with her third baby. Her BMI is 36. Her mother and sister have type 2 diabetes. Her last baby weighed 4.6 kg at birth.

Dr. Mervat checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her urine, which had no protein. She started 5 mg folic acid because of her weight.

She booked her routine scans and gave her healthy eating advice.

Mrs. Sahar works as a cashier and said she was always thirsty in her last pregnancy. She asked if she should worry about her sugar.

Her first two babies were born by cesarean, and she was told the second baby was "very big". She drinks a lot of fizzy drinks at work and has gained 6 kg already in this pregnancy.

Dr. Mervat said her urine showed no sugar, so she would not need a sugar test.
h: Dr. Mervat said her urine showed no sugar, so she would not need a sugar test

a.o: Dr. Mervat didn't offer Mrs. Sahar a sugar test in her pregnancy.
a.x: She needed a glucose tolerance test, early for her history.
a.w: Obesity, family diabetes and a big last baby raise the risk of pregnancy diabetes. Urine sugar tests miss it.

a.o: Dr. Mervat started Mrs. Sahar on 5 mg of folic acid a day.
a.x: The usual 400 micrograms of folic acid was enough for her.
a.w: A BMI over 30 needs the higher dose.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Sahar's urine for protein at the visit.
a.x: Protein in her urine was off topic at a routine visit.
a.w: Protein can mean pre-eclampsia.

a.o: Dr. Mervat gave Mrs. Sahar advice about healthy eating in pregnancy.
a.x: Giving her advice about healthy eating was rude to her.
a.w: Diet helps prevent too much weight gain.

t: Reduced baby movements told normal
s:
Mrs. Yara, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came in because the baby had been moving much less since yesterday. Usually the baby kicks a lot after dinner and when she lies down at night. Her pregnancy had been healthy so far.

Dr. Soha checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her urine, which was clear. She felt her belly, which was soft, and measured the bump, which matched her dates.

She listened with a handheld Doppler for a minute and heard a heartbeat of 140.

Mrs. Yara is a teacher and said she had been busy with exams at school and might not have noticed. She felt silly for coming in and apologized for wasting time.

Dr. Soha reassured her that the heartbeat was normal and sent her home without a CTG.
h: Dr. Soha reassured her that the heartbeat was normal and sent her home without a CTG

a.o: Dr. Soha sent Mrs. Yara home after reduced movements with no CTG.
a.x: She needed a CTG for at least 20 minutes, with a growth scan.
a.w: Reduced movements can be the first sign a baby is in trouble. A one-minute heartbeat check does not show the baby is well.

a.o: Dr. Soha measured the size of Mrs. Yara's bump with a tape measure.
a.x: The size of her bump was off topic for reduced movements.
a.w: A small bump can mean the baby is not growing well.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Yara's blood pressure during her visit.
a.x: Her blood pressure was off topic for reduced baby movements.
a.w: Pre-eclampsia can affect the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha told Mrs. Yara she was right to come in about the movements.
a.x: She should not have come in to the unit for something like that.
a.w: Women should always come in with reduced movements.

t: Bleeding after sex blamed on a normal smear
s:
Mrs. Hala, 38, came in with bleeding after sex for two months. She also had a watery, sometimes blood-stained discharge between periods. Her last smear test a year ago was normal. She has three children and smokes 10 cigarettes a day.

Dr. Ghada asked about pain, which she did not have, and sent swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhea. She checked a pregnancy test, which was negative.

She asked about her periods, which were regular, and her contraception, which was condoms. She advised her to stop smoking.

Mrs. Hala was embarrassed and said her husband was worried. She asked whether it could be cancer, because her aunt had died of it.

Dr. Ghada said cancer was unlikely because the smear was normal, and did not examine her cervix.
h: Dr. Ghada said cancer was unlikely because the smear was normal, and did not examine her cervix

a.o: Dr. Ghada relied on a normal smear for Mrs. Hala's bleeding.
a.x: Her cervix needed a look with a speculum, referred if odd.
a.w: A normal smear does not rule out cervical cancer. Bleeding after sex always needs the cervix to be seen.

a.o: Dr. Ghada sent swabs from Mrs. Hala to look for any infection.
a.x: Swabs were unnecessary for a woman with bleeding after sex.
a.w: Chlamydia can cause bleeding after sex.

a.o: Dr. Ghada advised Mrs. Hala to stop smoking as soon as she could.
a.x: Her smoking was off topic for a woman with bleeding after sex.
a.w: Smoking raises the risk of cervical cancer.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked a pregnancy test for Mrs. Hala during the visit.
a.x: A pregnancy test was off topic for bleeding after sex.
a.w: Pregnancy can cause bleeding.

t: Bleeding after menopause blamed on HRT
s:
Mrs. Nawal, 58, came in with vaginal bleeding for a week. She went through the menopause six years ago. She started continuous combined HRT tablets a year ago and had had no bleeding until now. Her BMI is 36 and she has type 2 diabetes.

Dr. Ihab checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and asked about her breasts. She had no lumps and her mammogram last year was clear.

He asked whether she had missed any doses or started other medicines, and she had not.

Mrs. Nawal said she felt much better on the HRT, with no more hot flushes or night sweats, and did not want to stop it.

He said the HRT caused the bleeding and told her to carry on, without arranging a scan.
h: He said the HRT caused the bleeding and told her to carry on, without arranging a scan

a.o: Dr. Ihab blamed Mrs. Nawal's new bleeding on HRT, with no scan.
a.x: She needed an urgent scan of the womb lining.
a.w: New bleeding after the menopause, even on HRT, can be womb cancer. Obesity and diabetes raise the risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked whether Mrs. Nawal had missed any doses of her HRT.
a.x: Missed doses of HRT don't matter for bleeding of this kind.
a.w: Missed doses can cause bleeding on HRT.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked when Mrs. Nawal last had her mammogram done.
a.x: Her breasts were off topic for bleeding after the menopause.
a.w: HRT slightly raises breast cancer risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab noted that Mrs. Nawal had no bleeding for the first year.
a.x: The timing of the bleeding was off topic for her HRT.
a.w: New bleeding after a settled spell on HRT needs checking.

t: Breech at 37 weeks booked for cesarean
s:
Mrs. Amira, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with her second baby. Her first baby was born normally three years ago. A scan showed the baby was breech, bottom first, with plenty of fluid around it. The baby was growing well and the placenta was high.

Dr. Soha explained what breech means and checked her blood pressure, which was normal. She checked her blood group, which was positive.

She asked about Mrs. Amira's wishes for the birth and her first labor, which was quick and easy.

Mrs. Amira said she wanted a normal birth if at all possible, because she has a toddler at home and wanted a fast recovery.

Dr. Soha booked a cesarean for 39 weeks, without offering an attempt to turn the baby.
h: Dr. Soha booked a cesarean for 39 weeks, without offering an attempt to turn the baby

a.o: Dr. Soha didn't offer to try turning Mrs. Amira's breech baby.
a.x: She should have been offered external cephalic version.
a.w: Turning the baby works in about half of women, more after a previous birth, and can avoid a cesarean.

a.o: Dr. Soha asked Mrs. Amira about her wishes for the birth.
a.x: The doctor should decide the type of birth all on her own.
a.w: Women should share in birth decisions.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked the position of Mrs. Amira's placenta on the scan.
a.x: The placenta was off topic for a baby lying in a breech position.
a.w: A low placenta rules out turning the baby.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Amira's blood group before planning the birth.
a.x: Her blood group was off topic for a baby lying breech.
a.w: Rhesus-negative women need anti-D after a turning attempt.

t: Shoulder dystocia with fundal pressure
s:
Mrs. Heba, 34, has gestational diabetes and was in labor with a baby estimated at 4.3 kg. The head was delivered, but then pulled back against her perineum. The next contraction did not deliver the shoulders.

Dr. Rana called for help, including the senior obstetrician and the newborn team. She noted the time the head was born.

She asked Mrs. Heba to stop pushing and laid the bed flat. She told her calmly what was happening.

Mrs. Heba's husband was frightened and asked why the baby was stuck. The midwife held Mrs. Heba's hand.

To push the baby out, Dr. Rana asked the midwife to press hard on the top of Mrs. Heba's belly.
h: Dr. Rana asked the midwife to press hard on the top of Mrs. Heba's belly

a.o: Dr. Rana used fundal pressure for Mrs. Heba's shoulder dystocia.
a.x: She needed McRoberts' position and pressure above the pubis.
a.w: Pressing on the top of the womb pushes the shoulder harder against the bone and can tear the womb or damage the baby's nerves.

a.o: Dr. Rana called for help as soon as Mrs. Heba's baby got stuck.
a.x: She should have managed the stuck shoulder all on her own there.
a.w: Shoulder dystocia needs a team.

a.o: Dr. Rana noted the exact time that the baby's head was born.
a.x: The time of the head's birth was off topic for this problem.
a.w: Time matters for the baby's oxygen.

a.o: Dr. Rana laid the bed flat as she began to free the baby's shoulder.
a.x: The bed's position doesn't matter at all for a stuck shoulder.
a.w: Flat is needed for McRoberts' position.

t: Postnatal psychosis sent home
s:
Mrs. Rasha, 29, had her first baby five days ago. Her husband brought her back because she had not slept for three nights, was talking very fast and said the baby was "not hers". She had bipolar disorder as a teenager but stopped treatment years ago.

Dr. Fady checked her for infection, and her temperature, urine and blood tests were normal. He checked her thyroid.

He asked about thoughts of harming herself or the baby. She said she heard voices telling her the baby was evil.

Her husband was exhausted and frightened. Her mother offered to stay with them at home.

Dr. Fady diagnosed "baby blues", advised rest and sent her home with her mother.
h: Dr. Fady diagnosed "baby blues", advised rest and sent her home with her mother

a.o: Dr. Fady called Mrs. Rasha's symptoms baby blues and sent her home.
a.x: She needed urgent psychiatric review and admission.
a.w: Hearing voices, no sleep and odd beliefs about the baby after birth, with past bipolar disorder, mean postpartum psychosis, an emergency that can lead to suicide or harm to the baby.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Rasha for any infection as a cause of confusion.
a.x: Infection was off topic for a new mother who was so unwell.
a.w: Infection can cause confusion after birth.

a.o: Dr. Fady gently asked Mrs. Rasha about any thoughts of harming the baby.
a.x: Asking about harming the baby was a cruel question to ask her.
a.w: Asking about harm is vital for safety.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Rasha's thyroid as part of her blood tests.
a.x: Her thyroid was off topic for a new mother with these symptoms.
a.w: Thyroid problems after birth can affect mood.

t: Methotrexate for an ectopic with a heartbeat
s:
Mrs. Nermine, 31, came in with pain on her right side at 7 weeks of pregnancy. A scan showed an ectopic pregnancy in her right tube, 4 cm across, with a heartbeat. Her hCG was 8,200. She was stable, with a blood pressure of 118/76.

Dr. Soha explained the diagnosis gently. She checked her blood count, kidney and liver tests, which were normal.

She asked about her plans for future pregnancies, and Mrs. Nermine said she very much wanted children.

Mrs. Nermine was frightened of surgery and asked whether there was a tablet or injection instead.

Dr. Soha gave her methotrexate and planned to check her hCG on days 4 and 7.
h: Dr. Soha gave her methotrexate and planned to check her hCG on days 4 and 7

a.o: Dr. Soha gave methotrexate for an ectopic with a heartbeat.
a.x: She needed keyhole surgery to remove the ectopic pregnancy.
a.w: Methotrexate fails often when there is a heartbeat, the hCG is over 5,000 or the mass is large. A burst tube can bleed fatally.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Nermine's liver and kidney tests on admission.
a.x: Liver and kidney tests were unnecessary for an ectopic like this.
a.w: Methotrexate can harm the liver and kidneys.

a.o: Dr. Soha talked with Mrs. Nermine about her future pregnancies.
a.x: Future pregnancies were off topic during an emergency like this.
a.w: Plans affect the type of surgery.

a.o: Dr. Soha explained Mrs. Nermine's diagnosis to her gently.
a.x: Being kind only wastes valuable time in an emergency.
a.w: Losing a pregnancy is distressing, and gentle news helps.

t: Magnesium drip without reflex checks
s:
Mrs. Asmaa, 26, is on a magnesium sulfate drip after severe pre-eclampsia. She delivered by cesarean six hours ago. Her blood pressure was 148/94. Her urine output had fallen to 15 mL an hour for the last three hours.

Dr. Rehab checked her blood tests, which showed a rising creatinine. She asked for her fluids to be measured carefully.

She checked her wound, which was clean, and her uterus, which was firm.

Mrs. Asmaa said she felt heavy and sleepy, and her speech was a little slurred. Her breathing rate was 11.

She is a primary school teacher and this was her first baby, a girl now in the newborn unit for warmth and feeding help. Her husband had gone to see the baby. The night midwife had written that she seemed more drowsy than an hour ago but put it down to tiredness after surgery.

Dr. Rehab continued the magnesium at the same rate, without checking her reflexes or her magnesium level.
h: Dr. Rehab continued the magnesium at the same rate, without checking her reflexes or her magnesium level

a.o: Dr. Rehab kept Mrs. Asmaa's magnesium running without any checks.
a.x: She needed reflex and blood level checks, with calcium ready.
a.w: Magnesium builds up when the kidneys slow down. Sleepiness, slurred speech and slow breathing are signs of toxicity.

a.o: Dr. Rehab measured all of Mrs. Asmaa's fluids in and out carefully.
a.x: Fluid charts were unnecessary once the baby had been delivered.
a.w: Low urine shows kidney problems, which make magnesium build up.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Asmaa's uterus was firm after the delivery.
a.x: Her uterus was off topic for a woman on a magnesium drip.
a.w: A firm uterus shows she is not bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Asmaa's creatinine while she was on magnesium.
a.x: Her kidney tests were off topic for a woman on a magnesium drip.
a.w: Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys.

t: Oxytocin increased after a previous cesarean
s:
Mrs. Samia, 33, had a cesarean three years ago. She is in labor at 40 weeks, planning a vaginal birth. Her labor was slow, so oxytocin was started.

Dr. Ihab checked the baby's heart tracing, which had started to show late dips. He checked her cervix, which had not changed for three hours.

He asked about her pain. She had a sharp, constant pain over her old scar, even between contractions.

Her husband said she had been coping well until now. The midwife said her contractions had become weaker.

Her first cesarean was for a breech baby, and the scar healed well. She had read a lot about vaginal birth after cesarean and was keen to try. Her pulse had risen to 112 in the last half hour, and the midwife noticed a little fresh bleeding.

Dr. Ihab increased the oxytocin "to get things moving".
h: Dr. Ihab increased the oxytocin "to get things moving"

a.o: Dr. Ihab raised Mrs. Samia's oxytocin despite signs of a torn womb.
a.x: She needed oxytocin stopped and an urgent cesarean.
a.w: Constant scar pain, weaker contractions and a worsening heart tracing after a past cesarean point to uterine rupture, which can kill mother and baby.

a.o: Dr. Ihab looked closely at the baby's heart tracing during labor.
a.x: The baby's heart tracing was off topic for her new pain.
a.w: Tracing changes show the baby is in trouble.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked Mrs. Samia about any new pain between her contractions.
a.x: Her new pain was off topic for a woman in a long labor.
a.w: Scar pain is a warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked how far Mrs. Samia's cervix had opened in labor.
a.x: Checking her cervix was unnecessary for a woman in labor.
a.w: Slow progress is a warning sign.

t: Cord prolapse left lying flat
s:
Mrs. Lina, 30, is in labor at 38 weeks with her second baby. Her waters broke suddenly. The midwife saw a loop of cord at the entrance of the vagina. The baby's heart rate dropped to 80.

Dr. Rana called for help and asked the team to prepare for an emergency cesarean.

She told Mrs. Lina calmly what was happening and asked the midwife to stop the oxytocin.

Mrs. Lina's husband asked whether the baby would be all right.

Her first baby was born quickly and easily. The baby's head had been high in the pelvis at her last check, and there was a lot of fluid around the baby. The theater team said they needed ten minutes to be ready.

While waiting, she left Mrs. Lina lying flat on her back and did not lift the baby's head off the cord.
h: she left Mrs. Lina lying flat on her back and did not lift the baby's head off the cord

a.o: Dr. Rana didn't take the pressure off the cord while they waited.
a.x: She needed knees-to-chest, with the baby's head pushed up.
a.w: The baby's head presses on the cord and cuts off oxygen. Lifting it buys time.

a.o: Dr. Rana called for help at once when she felt the cord.
a.x: She could have handled the prolapsed cord all on her own.
a.w: Cord prolapse needs a whole team fast.

a.o: Dr. Rana stopped Mrs. Lina's oxytocin drip as soon as she felt the cord.
a.x: Oxytocin speeds the birth and should have carried on as before.
a.w: Contractions press the baby onto the cord.

a.o: Dr. Rana got the team ready for an emergency cesarean for Mrs. Lina.
a.x: A normal birth should have been tried before a cesarean.
a.w: With the cervix not fully open, a fast cesarean is safest.

t: Preterm labor without steroids
s:
Mrs. Reem, 27, is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. She came in with tightenings every five minutes for three hours and a little blood-stained mucus. Her cervix was 3 cm open. Her waters had not broken, and she had no fever.

Dr. Soha checked the baby's heart tracing, which was normal, and confirmed the baby was head down. She started nifedipine to slow the contractions and arranged a bed in a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit.

She started magnesium sulfate to protect the baby's brain, as birth before 32 weeks looked likely. She sent a swab for group B strep and checked her urine for infection.

Mrs. Reem is a nurse and asked many questions about what the baby would face. Her husband was driving back from another city and would arrive in three hours.

Dr. Soha did not give steroid injections, writing "contractions may settle with nifedipine".
h: Dr. Soha did not give steroid injections, writing "contractions may settle with nifedipine"

a.o: Dr. Soha held back steroids from Mrs. Reem in early labor at 30 weeks.
a.x: She needed two steroid injections, given 12 to 24 hours apart.
a.w: Steroids before an early birth help the baby's lungs and lower the risk of death, brain bleeds and bowel problems. They work best when given early.

a.o: Dr. Soha started magnesium sulfate for Mrs. Reem to protect the baby.
a.x: Magnesium is only used to stop fits in women with pre-eclampsia.
a.w: Magnesium before 32 weeks protects the baby's brain from cerebral palsy.

a.o: Dr. Soha moved Mrs. Reem to a hospital with a newborn intensive care unit.
a.x: Moving her to another hospital was too risky while in labor.
a.w: A very early baby does best when born where intensive care is ready.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Reem's urine for infection as a cause of labor.
a.x: Her urine was off topic for a woman already in early labor.
a.w: Infection can trigger early labor.

t: Fever after a cesarean given tablets
s:
Mrs. Amal, 30, had an emergency cesarean four days ago after a long labor. She was sent home yesterday but came back with a fever of 38.9°C, shivers and lower belly pain. Her pulse was 122 and her blood pressure 98/60. Her vaginal loss smelled bad.

Dr. Rehab examined her and found her womb tender. Her wound was clean and dry. Her breasts were soft, with no red patches. Her calves were soft and not swollen.

She took blood cultures and a vaginal swab and measured her lactate, which was 3.4. She asked about breastfeeding, which was going well.

Mrs. Amal's mother was looking after the baby and asked whether her daughter could breastfeed while on antibiotics.

Dr. Rehab started oral co-amoxiclav and sent her home, with a review in two days.
h: Dr. Rehab started oral co-amoxiclav and sent her home, with a review in two days

a.o: Dr. Rehab sent Mrs. Amal home on tablets with sepsis after surgery.
a.x: She needed admission for IV antibiotics within an hour.
a.w: A fast pulse, low blood pressure and a high lactate mean sepsis from infection of the womb, which can kill quickly after birth.

a.o: Dr. Rehab checked Mrs. Amal's calves for any swelling or tenderness.
a.x: Her calves were off topic for a woman with a fever after surgery.
a.w: Clots in the legs are common after a cesarean.

a.o: Dr. Rehab looked at Mrs. Amal's breasts as a cause of her fever.
a.x: Her breasts were off topic for a woman with a fever after surgery.
a.w: Mastitis is another cause of fever after birth.

a.o: Dr. Rehab measured Mrs. Amal's lactate along with her other bloods.
a.x: Measuring her lactate was unnecessary for a fever after surgery.
a.w: A high lactate shows how severe sepsis is.

t: Mastitis and told to stop breastfeeding
s:
Mrs. Hana, 28, had her baby three weeks ago. She came in with a red, hot, painful patch on her left breast for a day, a fever of 38.2°C and aches all over. She had no lump. Her baby had been feeding less often because he was sleeping longer at night.

Dr. Ghada examined her and found a red wedge on the upper part of the breast, with no swelling or fluid under the skin. Her nipple had a small crack.

She prescribed flucloxacillin for ten days and paracetamol. She advised warm packs before feeds and asked the health visitor to check the baby's latch.

Mrs. Hana was in pain and tearful, and said her mother-in-law thought her milk was "bad". She asked whether the antibiotics would harm the baby.

Dr. Ghada told her to stop feeding from the left breast until the infection cleared, and to give formula instead.
h: Dr. Ghada told her to stop feeding from the left breast until the infection cleared

a.o: Dr. Ghada told Mrs. Hana to stop feeding from her infected breast.
a.x: She should have kept feeding from both, sore side first.
a.w: Emptying the breast helps mastitis clear. Stopping can lead to an abscess, and the milk is safe for the baby.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked the health visitor to check how the baby latches on.
a.x: The baby's latch was off topic for a mother with an infection.
a.w: A poor latch causes cracked nipples and mastitis.

a.o: Dr. Ghada prescribed flucloxacillin when Mrs. Hana did not improve.
a.x: Antibiotics pass into the milk and will harm the baby.
a.w: Flucloxacillin is safe in breastfeeding.

a.o: Dr. Ghada suggested warm packs on the breast before each feed.
a.x: Heat on the breast only makes the infection worse than before.
a.w: Warmth helps milk flow.

t: Morning-after pill on day five
s:
Miss Salma, 22, came in four and a half days after unprotected sex, when a condom split. She is not using other contraception. Her period is regular and she is mid-cycle. She has no medical problems and takes no medicines.

Dr. Ihab took a careful history and checked that she was not already pregnant from earlier sex. Her pregnancy test was negative.

He talked about future contraception and offered her chlamydia and gonorrhea tests, which she accepted.

Miss Salma is a university student and was anxious. She asked which option worked best and said she was willing to have a coil if needed.

He prescribed levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, saying "it works for up to five days".
h: He prescribed levonorgestrel 1.5 mg, saying "it works for up to five days"

a.o: Dr. Ihab gave Miss Salma levonorgestrel at day four and a half.
a.x: She should have been offered a copper coil, or ulipristal now.
a.w: Levonorgestrel is licensed only up to 72 hours and works poorly after that. A copper coil works up to five days.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked for an earlier pregnancy with a quick urine test.
a.x: A pregnancy test was unnecessary before emergency contraception.
a.w: Emergency contraception doesn't work on an existing pregnancy.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered Miss Salma tests for sexual infections as well.
a.x: Infection tests were off topic for emergency contraception.
a.w: Unprotected sex carries a risk of infection.

a.o: Dr. Ihab talked with Miss Salma about contraception for the future.
a.x: Talking about future contraception was preachy at that time.
a.w: Planning ahead prevents more emergencies.

t: Molar pregnancy without hCG follow-up
s:
Mrs. Nermine, 35, had heavy bleeding at 10 weeks of pregnancy. A scan showed a "snowstorm" pattern, and her hCG was 180,000. She had a suction evacuation, and the lab confirmed a complete molar pregnancy.

Dr. Soha explained the diagnosis and checked her blood group, which was positive. She checked her thyroid, which was a little overactive, and her blood pressure.

She advised her to avoid getting pregnant for now and discussed contraception, starting the combined pill.

Mrs. Nermine was sad and asked whether she could try again soon. She said she lived far from the hospital.

Dr. Soha told her the evacuation had cured it and discharged her, without registering her for hCG follow-up.
h: Dr. Soha told her the evacuation had cured it and discharged her, without registering her for hCG follow-up

a.o: Dr. Soha discharged Mrs. Nermine without any hCG follow-up booked.
a.x: She needed a specialist center for her hCG checks until normal.
a.w: A molar pregnancy can turn into a cancer, choriocarcinoma. Rising hCG is the warning sign.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Nermine's thyroid along with her other bloods.
a.x: Her thyroid was off topic for a woman after a molar pregnancy.
a.w: High hCG can overstimulate the thyroid.

a.o: Dr. Soha advised Mrs. Nermine to avoid getting pregnant for now.
a.x: That advice was unnecessary for a woman after a molar pregnancy.
a.w: A new pregnancy would hide a rising hCG.

a.o: Dr. Soha checked Mrs. Nermine's blood group before her procedure.
a.x: Her blood group was off topic for a woman with a molar pregnancy.
a.w: Rhesus-negative women may need anti-D.

t: Painful red eye given dilating drops
s:
Mrs. Fawzia, 68, came in with severe pain in her right eye and a headache since watching TV in a dark room last night. She had vomited twice. She saw halos around lights and her vision was blurred. She is long-sighted and wears thick glasses.

Dr. Nada found her right eye red, with a hazy cornea and a mid-sized pupil that did not react to light. The eye felt hard as stone through the lid.

She gave her anti-sickness medicine and morphine for the pain, and asked her to lie flat on her back.

Mrs. Fawzia's son said his mother had never had eye problems before, apart from her glasses. He asked whether she was having a stroke.

To get a better look at the back of the eye, Dr. Nada put dilating drops in both eyes and planned for the eye team to see her in the morning.
h: Dr. Nada put dilating drops in both eyes and planned for the eye team to see her in the morning

a.o: Dr. Nada put dilating drops in Mrs. Fawzia's eye with glaucoma.
a.x: She needed pressure-lowering drops and an urgent eye review.
a.w: Dilating the pupil closes the drainage angle further. Acute angle closure can blind the eye within hours.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mrs. Fawzia anti-sickness medicine for her vomiting.
a.x: Her vomiting was off topic for a woman with a painful red eye.
a.w: High eye pressure causes vomiting.

a.o: Dr. Nada gently felt the hardness of the eye through the closed lid.
a.x: Feeling the eye through the lid was useless for her diagnosis.
a.w: A rock-hard eye shows very high pressure.

a.o: Dr. Nada noted that Mrs. Fawzia is long-sighted and wears glasses.
a.x: Her glasses were off topic for a woman with a painful red eye.
a.w: Long-sighted eyes have narrow angles.

t: Floaters and a shadow told to wait
s:
Mr. Hesham, 58, came in with a shower of new floaters in his left eye since yesterday, like a swarm of flies. This morning he noticed a gray shadow coming in from the top of his vision. He is very short-sighted and had cataract surgery on that eye last year.

Dr. Ghada checked his vision, which was 6/9 in the left eye, and his pupils, which reacted normally. She could not see the back of his eye well without dilating drops.

She asked about flashes of light, and he had seen them in the corner of his eye last night. She asked about any blow to the head, and there was none.

Mr. Hesham is a tailor and was worried about losing work. He said the floaters were annoying but did not hurt.

Dr. Ghada told him floaters are common with age and booked him into the routine eye clinic in six weeks.
h: Dr. Ghada told him floaters are common with age and booked him into the routine eye clinic in six weeks

a.o: Dr. Ghada booked Mr. Hesham's floaters and shadow for six weeks' time.
a.x: Mr. Hesham needed the eye emergency service the same day.
a.w: New floaters, flashes and a curtain-like shadow mean a retinal tear or detachment. Repair before the center is affected saves sight.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Hesham about any flashes of light in that eye.
a.x: Flashes of light were off topic for a man with new floaters.
a.w: Flashes mean the retina is being pulled.

a.o: Dr. Ghada noted that Mr. Hesham is very short-sighted and wears glasses.
a.x: His glasses were off topic for a man with floaters in one eye.
a.w: Short sight and past cataract surgery raise the risk of detachment.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mr. Hesham's pupils with a light during the exam.
a.x: His pupils were off topic for a man with floaters in one eye.
a.w: An abnormal pupil reaction can show a large detachment.

t: Sudden blindness in one eye sent to clinic
s:
Mr. Raouf, 72, suddenly lost almost all the sight in his right eye an hour ago, while reading the newspaper. It did not hurt. He has high blood pressure and atrial fibrillation and stopped his blood thinner a month ago because of bruising.

Dr. Fouad found he could only see hand movements with the right eye. The right pupil reacted poorly to light. Through the ophthalmoscope, the retina looked pale with a cherry-red spot in the center.

He checked his blood pressure, 168/94, and sent an ESR and CRP to rule out giant cell arteritis. Mr. Raouf had no headache or jaw pain.

His wife said this was the second time; three days ago his vision went dark for five minutes and came back. Mr. Raouf was frightened and asked if it would come back.

Dr. Fouad referred him to the eye clinic for the next morning and sent him home.
h: Dr. Fouad referred him to the eye clinic for the next morning and sent him home

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent Mr. Raouf home with a retinal artery occlusion.
a.x: He needed same-day eye and stroke review, as it is a stroke.
a.w: A blocked retinal artery is an eye stroke. He is at high risk of a brain stroke, especially with untreated atrial fibrillation.

a.o: Dr. Fouad sent blood for an ESR and CRP as part of his assessment.
a.x: Those blood tests were off topic for sudden loss of vision.
a.w: Giant cell arteritis can block the eye artery too.

a.o: Dr. Fouad asked Mr. Raouf about any headache or pain when chewing.
a.x: Headache and jaw pain were off topic for his loss of vision.
a.w: Those point to giant cell arteritis.

a.o: Dr. Fouad took Mr. Raouf's earlier dark spell in that eye seriously.
a.x: The earlier dark spell had passed and so it didn't matter now.
a.w: A brief loss of vision is a warning sign of a stroke.

t: Chemical splash examined before washing
s:
Mr. Atef, 40, splashed oven cleaner into his left eye while cleaning his restaurant kitchen ten minutes ago. He could not open the eye because of the pain. The bottle said it contained sodium hydroxide, an alkali.

Dr. Nada asked for the bottle and checked the label. She checked his right eye, which was fine.

She gave him anesthetic eye drops to ease the pain so he could open his eye.

His colleague had driven him in and said Mr. Atef had rinsed his eye for a few seconds under the tap.

Before washing the eye, Dr. Nada sent him to wait for the slit lamp to check the damage and his vision.
h: Before washing the eye, Dr. Nada sent him to wait for the slit lamp to check the damage and his vision

a.o: Dr. Nada delayed washing Mr. Atef's alkali-burned eye to examine it.
a.x: He needed his eye washed at once, before any exam at all.
a.w: Alkali burns keep damaging the eye every second. Washing comes first, even before checking vision.

a.o: Dr. Nada asked for the bottle of the cleaning product that splashed him.
a.x: The label on the bottle didn't matter for his treatment.
a.w: Alkali burns are worse than acid burns.

a.o: Dr. Nada gave Mr. Atef anesthetic drops so he could open his eye.
a.x: Anesthetic drops were unnecessary for an eye splash like this.
a.w: Numbing drops let the eye be opened and washed.

a.o: Dr. Nada checked Mr. Atef's other eye for any splash as well.
a.x: The other eye was off topic for a splash to only one eye.
a.w: Splashes often hit both eyes.

t: Contact lens ulcer patched
s:
Miss Rana, 23, came in with a painful red right eye for a day. She wears soft contact lenses, which she sometimes sleeps in. The eye was watering, she could not bear bright light, and her vision was blurred. She had removed the lens.

Dr. Inas stained the eye with fluorescein and saw a small white spot on the cornea with a stain around it. She checked her vision, which was reduced.

She advised her not to wear contact lenses until the eye was healed and to bring her lenses and case for testing.

Miss Rana works as a receptionist and said she sometimes rinsed her lenses with tap water.

Dr. Inas put on an eye patch and chloramphenicol ointment, and booked her into the eye clinic in a week.
h: Dr. Inas put on an eye patch and chloramphenicol ointment, and booked her into the eye clinic in a week

a.o: Dr. Inas patched Miss Rana's eye and booked her clinic in a week.
a.x: She needed same-day eye review and hourly antibiotics.
a.w: A white spot on the cornea in a lens wearer is a corneal ulcer, often from Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba. Patching can make it worse, and it can scar within days.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked Miss Rana to bring in her contact lenses and their case.
a.x: Her lenses and case were off topic for a painful red eye.
a.w: The lens case can grow the germ.

a.o: Dr. Inas told Miss Rana to stop wearing her contact lenses for now.
a.x: Her lenses were fine to keep wearing while the eye healed.
a.w: Lenses must stop while infected.

a.o: Dr. Inas asked Miss Rana whether she rinses her lenses in tap water.
a.x: Tap water was off topic for a woman with a painful red eye.
a.w: Tap water can carry Acanthamoeba.

t: Steroid drops for a branching ulcer
s:
Mr. Sami, 45, came in with a red, watery, gritty left eye for four days. He had a cold sore last week. His vision was a little blurred. He does not wear contact lenses.

Dr. Ghada stained his eye with fluorescein and saw a branching, tree-shaped ulcer on the cornea.

She checked his vision and asked about previous eye problems, and he had a similar one two years ago.

Mr. Sami is a teacher and wanted to be fit for school the next week. He asked for something to make the redness go away quickly.

He has mild asthma and uses an inhaler. The eye was not painful enough to stop him sleeping, and the pupil reacted normally. His wife had read that steroid drops calm red eyes fast and asked for them.

Dr. Ghada prescribed prednisolone eye drops four times a day to settle the inflammation.
h: Dr. Ghada prescribed prednisolone eye drops four times a day to settle the inflammation

a.o: Dr. Ghada gave steroid drops for Mr. Sami's herpes eye ulcer.
a.x: He needed antivirals and an eye review, with no steroids.
a.w: A branching ulcer is herpes simplex. Steroid drops make it spread and can perforate the cornea.

a.o: Dr. Ghada stained Mr. Sami's eye with dye to look at the ulcer.
a.x: Staining the eye was unnecessary for a simple red eye.
a.w: The stain shows the ulcer shape.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Sami whether he gets cold sores on his lips.
a.x: Cold sores on his lips were off topic for his red eye.
a.w: The same virus causes cold sores and eye ulcers.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mr. Sami about any past eye problems or infections.
a.x: His past eye problems were off topic for this new red eye.
a.w: Herpes eye ulcers often come back.

t: Swollen eyelid in a child treated with tablets
s:
Yusuf, 7, came in with a swollen, red right eyelid for two days after a cold. Today the eye was bulging a little, it hurt to move, and he said he saw double. He had a fever of 38.9°C and was miserable.

Dr. Dina gently opened the lid and found the eye red, with reduced movement looking up and out. She checked his vision with a chart, which was a little reduced, and his pupils, which reacted normally.

She sent blood tests and asked about his vaccines, which were up to date. She gave him paracetamol and ibuprofen for the fever.

His mother said he had blocked sinuses all week. She works night shifts and asked whether they could go home and come back tomorrow if he was worse.

Dr. Dina diagnosed a lid infection and sent him home with oral co-amoxiclav, with a review in two days.
h: Dr. Dina diagnosed a lid infection and sent him home with oral co-amoxiclav

a.o: Dr. Dina sent Yusuf home on tablets with signs of orbital cellulitis.
a.x: Yusuf needed admission, IV antibiotics and an urgent CT.
a.w: Painful eye movement, double vision, bulging and reduced vision mean infection behind the eye. It can cause blindness, brain abscess or meningitis.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Yusuf's vision with a picture chart in the department today.
a.x: A vision chart is unreliable in a child of Yusuf's age.
a.w: Reduced vision is a red flag for orbital infection.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked Yusuf's mother about his recent sinus infection.
a.x: His sinuses were off topic for a child with a swollen eyelid.
a.w: Orbital cellulitis often spreads from the sinuses.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked Yusuf's pupils with a light as part of her exam.
a.x: His pupils were off topic for a child with a swollen eyelid.
a.w: A poor pupil reaction can show pressure on the optic nerve.

t: Diabetes eye screening skipped
s:
Mr. Hamdy, 52, has had type 2 diabetes for eight years. He came for his yearly review. His HbA1c was 74 and his blood pressure 148/92. He said his vision was perfect and he only needed reading glasses.

Dr. Ihab checked his feet, which had good feeling and pulses, and his kidney tests, which showed a little protein. He started ramipril for his blood pressure and kidneys.

He talked about diet and offered a place on a diabetes education course, which Mr. Hamdy accepted.

Mr. Hamdy said he had missed his last two eye screening appointments because they made his eyes blurry for hours after the drops, and he had to work.

Dr. Ihab agreed that eye screening could stop "since his eyesight is fine".
h: Dr. Ihab agreed that eye screening could stop "since his eyesight is fine"

a.o: Dr. Ihab let Mr. Hamdy stop eye screening as his eyesight was fine.
a.x: He should have been helped back into yearly eye screening.
a.w: Diabetic eye disease causes no symptoms until it is advanced. Screening finds it early, when laser or injections can save sight.

a.o: Dr. Ihab started Mr. Hamdy on ramipril for protein in his urine.
a.x: Ramipril was off topic for a man skipping his eye screening.
a.w: ACE inhibitors protect the kidneys in diabetes with protein in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Ihab offered Mr. Hamdy a place on a course about his diabetes.
a.x: Diabetes courses are a waste of time for a man like Mr. Hamdy.
a.w: Education helps people control their sugar.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Hamdy's feet as part of his yearly diabetes review.
a.x: His feet were off topic at a visit about eye screening.
a.w: Diabetes damages nerves and blood flow in the feet.

t: Hydroxychloroquine without eye checks
s:
Mrs. Samia, 50, has lupus and has taken hydroxychloroquine 400 mg a day for seven years. She weighs 54 kg. Her lupus has been quiet, with only mild joint pain. Her kidney function has slowly fallen to an eGFR of 55.

Dr. Mervat checked her blood count, urine and complement levels, which were stable. She checked her blood pressure, which was normal.

She advised her to use sun cream and a hat, as sunlight can trigger lupus flares, and checked that she was up to date with her flu vaccine.

Mrs. Samia said she had noticed some trouble reading small print, but thought it was her age. She had never had an eye test since starting the tablets.

Dr. Mervat continued the same dose and told her to see an optician for reading glasses.
h: Dr. Mervat continued the same dose and told her to see an optician for reading glasses

a.o: Dr. Mervat ignored the eye risk of Mrs. Samia's hydroxychloroquine.
a.x: She needed retinal screening, with her dose reviewed as well.
a.w: After five years, hydroxychloroquine can damage the retina, especially with high doses and poor kidney function. The damage is permanent.

a.o: Dr. Mervat advised Mrs. Samia to wear sun cream when she is outside.
a.x: Sun cream was off topic for a woman with lupus on tablets.
a.w: Sunlight can trigger lupus flares.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Samia's complement levels with her bloods.
a.x: Complement tests were unnecessary for a woman with stable lupus.
a.w: Complement levels help show lupus activity.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked whether Mrs. Samia had had her flu vaccine.
a.x: Vaccines were off topic for a woman with stable lupus on tablets.
a.w: People on immune medicines need flu protection.

t: Eye injury with pressure on the eye
s:
Mr. Ali, 30, was hit in the left eye by a piece of glass when a window broke at work. His vision was very blurred. Dr. Fady saw a cut through the cornea, with dark tissue poking out and a peaked pupil.

He checked the vision in both eyes, and asked about his last meal and his tetanus status, which was up to date.

He gave him an anti-sickness injection, as vomiting could raise the eye pressure, and pain relief.
