a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Mohsen's kidney tests along with his sugars.
a.x: His kidney tests were off topic for a man with high sugars.
a.w: Poor kidneys make insulin last longer.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for Mr. Mohsen's sugar to be checked before meals.
a.x: Checking his sugar before every meal was far too often for him.
a.w: Checks show if the new dose is safe.

t: Feeding started without checking the tube position
s:
Mr. Hamed, 71, had a stroke three days ago and cannot swallow safely. The speech therapist advised feeding through a nose tube. He is drowsy but rousable.

Dr. Hany asked the nurse to put in a fine-bore nasogastric tube. The nurse put it in and Mr. Hamed coughed a little during the procedure.

Dr. Hany checked his blood tests before feeding, including phosphate, which was normal, and asked the dietitian to plan his feeds.

The nurse tried to draw back fluid to test it, but nothing came. The X-ray department was busy and said a film would take two hours. Mr. Hamed had not eaten for three days.

Dr. Hany told the nurse to start the feed anyway, since "the tube went in easily".
h: told the nurse to start the feed anyway, since "the tube went in easily"

a.o: Dr. Hany started the feed without confirming where the tube was.
a.x: He should have waited for a pH test or an X-ray before any feed.
a.w: A tube in the lung is easy to miss, and feed in the lung can cause deadly pneumonia.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Hamed's phosphate level before any feeding.
a.x: Phosphate was off topic for a man about to start tube feeds.
a.w: Feeding after starvation can drop phosphate dangerously.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked the dietitian to plan Mr. Hamed's tube feeds.
a.x: The dietitian was unnecessary for a simple standard feed like this.
a.w: Feeds must match his needs.

a.o: Dr. Hany followed the speech therapist's advice not to feed by mouth.
a.x: He should have let Mr. Hamed try soft food by mouth first.
a.w: Unsafe swallowing can cause choking and pneumonia.

t: Operation side not marked
s:
Mr. Sabry, 62, was booked for a right knee replacement. His left knee is also arthritic but less painful. His consent form says "right total knee replacement".

Dr. Tarek checked his name band, his blood tests and his ECG, which were fine. He confirmed his allergies with him.

He asked Mr. Sabry which knee was being operated on, and Mr. Sabry pointed to the right one.

The ward was busy and theatre was waiting. Dr. Tarek did not have a skin marker with him. Both knees looked the same, and the X-rays were on the computer in theatre.

Dr. Tarek sent him to theatre without marking the operation site, writing "side confirmed verbally".
h: sent him to theatre without marking the operation site

a.o: Dr. Tarek didn't mark the side of Mr. Sabry's knee before theatre.
a.x: He should have marked the right knee with an arrow on the ward.
a.w: Wrong-side surgery is a "never event". Marking, with consent and checklist, is a simple way to stop it.

a.o: Dr. Tarek asked Mr. Sabry himself which knee was being operated on.
a.x: Asking him was unnecessary, as the consent form said which side.
a.w: Asking the patient is part of checking the side.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Sabry's allergies before he went to theatre.
a.x: His allergies were off topic for a planned knee replacement.
a.w: Allergies matter for drugs used in theatre.

a.o: Dr. Tarek checked Mr. Sabry's ECG and blood tests before surgery.
a.x: The ECG was unnecessary for a fit man having a knee operation.
a.w: It is part of checking fitness for an anesthetic.

t: Swab count skipped at the end of surgery
s:
Mrs. Nadia, 45, had an open operation to remove her womb. It was long, with heavy bleeding, and many swabs were used to soak up blood. The scrub nurse had changed halfway through.

Dr. Mervat stopped the bleeding and checked the bladder and bowel, which were not injured. The anesthetist gave two units of blood.

Dr. Mervat checked the drain and the wound edges before closing.

At the end, the new scrub nurse said she was not sure of the count from before her shift. The theatre was running late and the next patient was waiting.

Dr. Mervat closed the belly without waiting for a full swab and instrument count, saying "I'm sure we have everything".
h: closed the belly without waiting for a full swab and instrument count

a.o: Dr. Mervat closed Mrs. Nadia's belly without a full swab count.
a.x: She should have waited for a correct swab and instrument count.
a.w: A swab left inside causes infection, pain and more surgery. Long, bloody operations with staff changes carry the highest risk.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked Mrs. Nadia's bladder and bowel for any injury.
a.x: Checking her bladder and bowel only made a long operation longer.
a.w: These can be injured during a womb operation.

a.o: The anesthetist gave Mrs. Nadia two units of blood during surgery.
a.x: Blood was not needed, as fluids alone would have been enough.
a.w: She had heavy bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Mervat checked the drain and wound edges before closing.
a.x: The drain was off topic once the bleeding had been stopped.
a.w: A working drain shows if bleeding continues.

t: Paracetamol given twice in two forms
s:
Mrs. Dalia, 77, weighs 45 kg and is on the ward after a fall with a broken wrist. She is frail and eats little. She was prescribed co-codamol 30/500, two tablets four times a day, for pain.

Dr. Rasha checked her wrist, which was in a cast, and her fingers, which were warm and moved well. She checked her kidney and liver tests, which were normal.

She also prescribed a laxative to prevent constipation from the codeine.

Mrs. Dalia said she still had pain at night. The nurse asked if she could have something extra. Mrs. Dalia had already had four doses of co-codamol that day.

Dr. Rasha added paracetamol 1 g four times a day on top of the co-codamol.
h: added paracetamol 1 g four times a day on top of the co-codamol

a.o: Dr. Rasha added paracetamol 1 g on top of Mrs. Dalia's co-codamol.
a.x: She needed a different extra painkiller, not more paracetamol.
a.w: Co-codamol already has paracetamol. This doubles the dose to 8 g a day, which can destroy the liver.

a.o: Dr. Rasha prescribed Mrs. Dalia a laxative to go with her codeine.
a.x: A laxative was unnecessary for a woman who eats so little.
a.w: Codeine causes constipation.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked that Mrs. Dalia's fingers were warm and moving.
a.x: Her fingers were off topic for a woman whose wrist was in a cast.
a.w: A tight cast can cut off blood to the hand.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Dalia's liver tests along with her kidneys.
a.x: Her liver tests were unnecessary after a simple fall like hers.
a.w: Paracetamol is broken down in the liver.

t: Phone order for a drug not read back
s:
Mr. Atef, 69, is on the ward with heart failure. At night the nurse phoned Dr. Karim because his blood pressure had dropped to 92/58 and he felt dizzy. He takes furosemide, ramipril and bisoprolol.

Dr. Karim asked for his pulse, which was 64, his urine output and his latest kidney tests, which showed his creatinine had risen.

He asked the nurse to lie him flat for a while and to check his blood pressure every hour.

Dr. Karim was in the ER with a sick patient and could not come to the ward. The line was noisy. He told the nurse to hold the ramipril and lower the bisoprolol to "one point two five" milligrams.

Dr. Karim gave the orders over the phone and hung up, without asking the nurse to read them back.
h: gave the orders over the phone and hung up, without asking the nurse to read them back

a.o: Dr. Karim gave phone orders without asking for a read-back.
a.x: He should have had the nurse read the drug names and doses back.
a.w: "One point two five" and "twelve point five" sound alike on a noisy line. Read-back catches mistakes before they reach the patient.

a.o: Dr. Karim told the nurse to hold Mr. Atef's ramipril for the night.
a.x: His ramipril should have carried on to protect his weak heart.
a.w: Low blood pressure and rising creatinine are reasons to pause it.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked for Mr. Atef's blood pressure to be checked hourly.
a.x: Hourly blood pressure checks were far too much for one dizzy spell.
a.w: His blood pressure needs close watching.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked the nurse about Mr. Atef's urine output.
a.x: His urine was off topic for a man whose blood pressure had dropped.
a.w: Low urine can mean the kidneys are struggling.

t: Blood tubes labeled at the desk
s:
Dr. Rasha was asked to take group and save samples from two patients in the same bay. Both are due for surgery the next morning. One is Mr. Ahmed Hassan and the other is Mr. Ahmed Hussein.

She checked each patient's name band and asked them their full name and date of birth. She took the blood from each patient in turn.

She washed her hands between patients and used a new tray for each.

The bay was busy and she carried both sets of tubes back to the nurses' desk. She planned to print the labels there, as the printer was there.

Dr. Rasha labeled both sets of tubes at the desk, after leaving the patients' bedsides.
h: Dr. Rasha labeled both sets of tubes at the desk, after leaving the patients' bedsides

a.o: Dr. Rasha labeled the blood tubes at the desk, not the bedside.
a.x: She should have labeled each tube right at the bedside.
a.w: Labeling away from the patient, especially with similar names, can mix up samples and lead to the wrong blood being given.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked each man for his full name and date of birth.
a.x: Asking their dates of birth was unnecessary with name bands on.
a.w: Two identifiers stop patient mix-ups.

a.o: Dr. Rasha used a new tray for each patient she took blood from.
a.x: A new tray for each patient only wasted equipment.
a.w: It keeps each patient's samples separate.

a.o: Dr. Rasha washed her hands between the two patients in the bay.
a.x: Washing between patients wasted time on a busy ward like that.
a.w: Hand washing stops germs spreading.

t: Needlestick injury not reported
s:
Dr. Karim took blood from Mr. Ehab, 35, who injects drugs. Mr. Ehab was agitated and moved suddenly. The used needle went into Dr. Karim's finger through his glove.

Dr. Karim let the wound bleed freely and washed it under running water with soap. He did not scrub or suck it.

He finished looking after Mr. Ehab, who was being treated for an abscess. He disposed of the needle safely in the sharps bin.

Dr. Karim was halfway through a busy shift and did not want to leave the department short. Mr. Ehab's HIV and hepatitis status was not known. He did not want to make a fuss.

Dr. Karim put on a plaster and carried on, without reporting the injury or contacting occupational health.
h: carried on, without reporting the injury or contacting occupational health

a.o: Dr. Karim carried on working without reporting his needlestick.
a.x: He should have reported it at once for a risk check.
a.w: HIV prevention medicine works best within an hour or two. Hepatitis B and C need follow-up testing too.

a.o: Dr. Karim let his finger bleed freely and washed it with soap.
a.x: He should have squeezed the wound hard to push the germs out.
a.w: Gentle bleeding and washing is the right first aid.

a.o: Dr. Karim put the used needle straight into the sharps bin.
a.x: He should have recapped the needle first.
a.w: Recapping causes more needlestick injuries.

a.o: Dr. Karim didn't suck the wound on his finger after the injury.
a.x: Sucking the wound would have cleared the germs from his finger.
a.w: Sucking doesn't help and may spread infection.

t: Hands not washed between patients with diarrhea
s:
Dr. Fady was on the ward round. Mrs. Abla, 80, in bed 4, has diarrhea, and her stool test came back positive for C. difficile. She is in a side room.

Dr. Fady put on gloves and an apron before going in. He examined her belly and checked her fluid balance.

He started oral vancomycin and stopped her omeprazole, which can make the infection worse.

As he came out, he took off his gloves and apron. The alcohol gel dispenser was by the door. Mr. Ali in bed 5, who had just had hip surgery, was next on the round.

Dr. Fady rubbed his hands with alcohol gel and went straight to examine Mr. Ali.
h: Dr. Fady rubbed his hands with alcohol gel and went straight to examine Mr. Ali

a.o: Dr. Fady cleaned his hands with only alcohol gel after Mrs. Abla.
a.x: He should have washed his hands with soap and water.
a.w: Alcohol gel doesn't kill C. difficile spores. Soap and water remove them.

a.o: Dr. Fady stopped Mrs. Abla's omeprazole when he started treatment.
a.x: Her omeprazole should have carried on to protect her stomach.
a.w: Stomach acid drugs raise the risk of C. difficile.

a.o: Dr. Fady put on an apron as well as gloves before going in to her.
a.x: Gloves alone were enough; the apron wasted time.
a.w: Aprons stop spores spreading on clothes.

a.o: Dr. Fady started Mrs. Abla on oral vancomycin for her infection.
a.x: IV vancomycin would have worked much better than the tablets.
a.w: Only oral vancomycin reaches the gut.

t: Sleeping tablet for a confused older woman
s:
Mrs. Thuraya, 88, was admitted with a urine infection. She has become confused at night, trying to climb out of bed and calling out. She uses a walking frame and fell at home last month.

Dr. Rasha checked her for pain, a full bladder and constipation, and found none. Her antibiotics had been started and her blood tests were improving.

She asked the nurses to keep the lights low, place her near the nurses' desk and make sure her glasses and hearing aid were in.

At 2 am the nurse called because Mrs. Thuraya was still awake and restless. Her daughter could not come in at night.

Dr. Rasha prescribed zopiclone 7.5 mg to help her sleep.
h: Dr. Rasha prescribed zopiclone 7.5 mg to help her sleep

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mrs. Thuraya zopiclone to help her sleep.
a.x: She should have avoided sleeping tablets altogether.
a.w: Sleeping tablets in older people with delirium raise the risk of falls and hip fractures and make confusion worse.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Thuraya for a full bladder and constipation.
a.x: A full bladder was off topic for a woman confused at night.
a.w: Urine retention can cause restlessness.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for Mrs. Thuraya's bed to be near the nurses' desk.
a.x: Moving her near the desk disturbed other patients.
a.w: Staff can watch her more closely.

a.o: Dr. Rasha made sure Mrs. Thuraya's glasses were in.
a.x: Her glasses and hearing aid didn't matter at night in bed.
a.w: Poor sight and hearing make delirium worse.

t: Syringe left without a label
s:
Mr. Amr, 50, is in intensive care with sepsis. He needs several medicines through his central line. Dr. Hany was called to give a bolus dose of a drug to raise his blood pressure.

Dr. Hany checked the drug and its dose with a nurse. He washed his hands and cleaned the line hub before connecting.

He drew up metaraminol into a 10 ml syringe. A second syringe of saline for flushing lay next to it on the same tray.

Mr. Amr's blood pressure was 78/40 and the nurse urged him to be quick. The labels were in a drawer across the room.

Dr. Hany drew up the drug and the flush without labeling either syringe, and put both on the tray.
h: drew up the drug and the flush without labeling either syringe

a.o: Dr. Hany left both of Mr. Amr's syringes on the tray without labels.
a.x: He should have labeled each syringe as soon as he drew it up.
a.w: Clear liquids look the same. Unlabeled syringes are mixed up easily, giving the wrong drug or dose.

a.o: Dr. Hany cleaned the line hub before connecting the syringe to it.
a.x: Cleaning the hub wasted time when his pressure was so low.
a.w: Line infections are a big risk in intensive care.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked the drug and its dose with a nurse before giving it.
a.x: A second check was unnecessary for a drug he knew well.
a.w: A second check catches drug errors.

a.o: Dr. Hany gave Mr. Amr a drug to raise his blood pressure quickly.
a.x: Fluids alone would have been enough to raise his blood pressure.
a.w: Very low blood pressure in sepsis can need drugs.

t: Full-dose clot prevention in kidney failure
s:
Mrs. Hekmat, 76, weighs 48 kg and was admitted with pneumonia. She has chronic kidney disease, and her eGFR is 18. She will be in bed for a few days.

Dr. Fady did a clot risk assessment and found she was at high risk of clots and low risk of bleeding.

He checked her blood count, which showed normal platelets, and her clotting tests, which were normal.

He prescribed calf compression devices while she was in bed and checked that she had no leg ulcers.

Mrs. Hekmat said she had bruised easily since starting aspirin for her heart. Her daughter asked whether the injections would hurt. The pharmacist was off the ward that day and the drug chart had not yet been checked.

Dr. Fady prescribed enoxaparin 40 mg daily, the standard dose, without adjusting for her kidneys.
h: prescribed enoxaparin 40 mg daily, the standard dose, without adjusting for her kidneys

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mrs. Hekmat full-dose enoxaparin with an eGFR of 18.
a.x: He should have lowered the dose to 20 mg a day.
a.w: Enoxaparin builds up when kidney function is very low, raising bleeding risk, especially in a small older woman.

a.o: Dr. Fady did a clot risk assessment for Mrs. Hekmat on admission.
a.x: A clot risk assessment was unnecessary for a short stay.
a.w: It decides who needs clot prevention.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Hekmat's platelets before starting the injections.
a.x: Her platelets were off topic for pneumonia.
a.w: Low platelets raise bleeding risk with heparin.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Hekmat's legs for ulcers before compression.
a.x: Leg ulcers were off topic for the calf compression devices.
a.w: Compression can harm skin with ulcers.

t: Morphine switched to oxycodone at the same dose
s:
Mr. Badr, 66, has lung cancer that has spread to his bones. He takes modified-release morphine 60 mg twice a day, which controls his pain well. He has had hallucinations on morphine and asked to change.

Dr. Rasha checked his kidney tests, which had worsened a little, and decided oxycodone would be a better choice.

She prescribed a laxative, as he was constipated, and an as-needed dose for breakthrough pain.

Mr. Badr was tired and drowsy at times. His wife was worried he was sleeping too much. He had not been told about the risk of drowsiness with a new opioid.

Dr. Rasha switched him to modified-release oxycodone 60 mg twice a day, the same number as his morphine.
h: switched him to modified-release oxycodone 60 mg twice a day, the same number as his morphine

a.o: Dr. Rasha switched Mr. Badr to oxycodone at the same 60 mg dose.
a.x: She should have given about half: 30 mg twice a day.
a.w: Oxycodone is about twice as strong as morphine. The same number of milligrams is a big overdose that can stop his breathing.

a.o: Dr. Rasha prescribed Mr. Badr a laxative for his constipation.
a.x: A laxative wasn't needed once the morphine was stopped.
a.w: Opioids nearly always cause constipation.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Badr's kidney tests before changing his opioid.
a.x: His kidneys were off topic for cancer pain.
a.w: Poor kidneys cause morphine to build up and cause hallucinations.

a.o: Dr. Rasha gave Mr. Badr an as-needed dose for breakthrough pain as well.
a.x: A breakthrough dose on top was too much for a drowsy man.
a.w: Cancer pain often flares between doses.

t: Bedbound patient not turned
s:
Mr. Shawki, 82, had a stroke a week ago. He cannot move his left side and spends most of the day in bed. He is thin, and he has been incontinent of urine.

Dr. Ihab checked his swallowing plan and his fluids, which were going well. He started physiotherapy and asked the dietitian to review his poor appetite.

He checked his skin and found the area over his tailbone was red and did not fade when pressed.

The ward was short of nurses that week. Mr. Shawki was lying on a standard mattress. His son asked if anything could be done for the red skin.

Dr. Ihab wrote "skin intact" and did not arrange a pressure mattress or regular turning.
h: wrote "skin intact" and did not arrange a pressure mattress or regular turning

a.o: Dr. Ihab saw Mr. Shawki's red tailbone but arranged no pressure care.
a.x: He needed a pressure mattress and turning every 2 to 4 hours.
a.w: Redness that doesn't fade is an early pressure sore. Without turning, it can break down into a deep wound.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked the dietitian to review Mr. Shawki's poor appetite.
a.x: His diet was off topic for a man recovering from a stroke.
a.w: Poor nutrition makes pressure sores worse.

a.o: Dr. Ihab started physiotherapy for Mr. Shawki a week after his stroke.
a.x: Physiotherapy should have waited until he was much stronger.
a.w: Early movement helps recovery.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Shawki's fluids along with his swallowing plan.
a.x: His fluids were off topic once his swallowing plan was in place.
a.w: Dehydration makes skin more fragile.

t: Family pressing the pain pump button
s:
Mr. Lotfy, 67, had a big bowel operation yesterday. He has a morphine pain pump that gives a small dose each time he presses the button, with a five-minute lockout. He is sleepy after the anesthetic.

Dr. Karim checked his pain score, which was 3 out of 10, and his wound, which was clean. He prescribed regular paracetamol and an anti-sickness drug.

He checked that naloxone was prescribed in case of too much morphine, and asked for hourly breathing rate checks.

Mr. Lotfy's wife said she had been pressing the button for him while he slept, "so he would not wake up in pain". His breathing rate was 10 a minute.

Dr. Karim praised her for helping and told her to keep pressing the button whenever he seemed uncomfortable.
h: told her to keep pressing the button whenever he seemed uncomfortable

a.o: Dr. Karim told Mr. Lotfy's wife to keep pressing his morphine button.
a.x: He should have told her kindly that only Mr. Lotfy may press it.
a.w: The pump is safe because a sleepy patient stops pressing. When others press it, morphine can build up and stop his breathing.

a.o: Dr. Karim prescribed regular paracetamol for Mr. Lotfy after surgery.
a.x: Paracetamol wasn't needed with a morphine pump running.
a.w: Paracetamol lowers the morphine needed.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked that naloxone was prescribed for Mr. Lotfy.
a.x: Prescribing naloxone was far too cautious for a small pump dose.
a.w: Naloxone reverses too much morphine.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked for Mr. Lotfy's breathing rate to be checked hourly.
a.x: Hourly breathing checks were unnecessary for a man so sleepy.
a.w: A slow breathing rate is an early sign of too much morphine.

t: Sick patient sent to the scanner alone
s:
Mr. Farid, 58, came in after a car crash. He has a head injury and his GCS dropped from 14 to 11 in the last hour. His breathing is noisy and his oxygen is 92% on a mask. His blood pressure is 100/60.

Dr. Karim gave him oxygen and put in two drip lines. He kept his neck still in a collar. He called the anesthetist to review his airway.

He booked an urgent CT scan of his head and neck. The scanner was at the other end of the hospital.

The ER was very busy and short of staff. The anesthetist was still ten minutes away. A porter was free to take him.

Dr. Karim sent Mr. Farid to the CT scanner with only the porter, without a doctor, a monitor or airway equipment.
h: sent Mr. Farid to the CT scanner with only the porter, without a doctor, a monitor or airway equipment

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Farid off to the scanner with only a porter.
a.x: He should have gone with an airway doctor, a monitor and kit.
a.w: A falling GCS and noisy breathing mean he could stop breathing on the way. Transfers are a risky time.

a.o: Dr. Karim kept Mr. Farid's neck still in a collar after the crash.
a.x: The collar was unnecessary for a man who could still talk.
a.w: A neck injury hasn't been ruled out.

a.o: Dr. Karim called the anesthetist to review Mr. Farid's airway.
a.x: Calling the anesthetist was too early, before the CT result.
a.w: His airway may need protecting soon.

a.o: Dr. Karim put two drip lines into Mr. Farid on arrival in the ER.
a.x: One drip line would have been enough for a blood pressure of 100.
a.w: He may need fluids or blood fast.

t: Wrong patient's X-ray read
s:
Two men named Mohamed Ali are on the same ward. One, 34, came in with pneumonia. The other, 71, is waiting for hip surgery. Dr. Rasha was asked to review the chest X-ray of the younger man.

She examined him and heard crackles on the right. His oxygen was 93% on air and his temperature 38.6°C.

She opened the X-ray on the computer by typing the name "Mohamed Ali". The film showed a large heart and no pneumonia.

She did not check the date of birth or hospital number on the image. The older man has heart failure. The younger man asked why his antibiotics were being stopped.

Dr. Rasha wrote "chest X-ray clear, no pneumonia" and stopped the younger man's antibiotics.
h: wrote "chest X-ray clear, no pneumonia" and stopped the younger man's antibiotics

a.o: Dr. Rasha read the older Mr. Ali's X-ray for the younger man.
a.x: She should have checked two identifiers on the image.
a.w: Patients with the same name are easily mixed up. Treatment based on the wrong result can harm both.

a.o: Dr. Rasha examined the younger Mr. Ali's chest and heard crackles.
a.x: Examining his chest was unnecessary with an X-ray to look at.
a.w: Examination should match the X-ray.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked the younger Mr. Ali's oxygen level on air.
a.x: His oxygen level was off topic for an X-ray.
a.w: Low oxygen shows how ill he is.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked the younger Mr. Ali's temperature on her review.
a.x: His temperature was off topic for a man with a clear X-ray.
a.w: Fever supports an infection.

t: Oral medicine drawn up in an IV syringe
s:
Mr. Nashaat, 60, has a feeding tube after a stroke. He takes his medicines as liquids through the tube. He also has an IV line in his arm for antibiotics.

Dr. Hany checked his drug chart and changed his tablets to liquid forms with the pharmacist. He checked his IV line site, which was clean.

He asked the nurse to flush the feeding tube with water before and after each medicine.

The ward had run out of purple oral syringes. The nurse asked if she could use a normal IV syringe instead. Both the feeding tube and the IV line were taped near each other on his chest.

Dr. Hany told her it was fine to use the IV syringes for the liquid medicines.
h: told her it was fine to use the IV syringes for the liquid medicines

a.o: Dr. Hany let Mr. Nashaat's oral medicines be drawn up in IV syringes.
a.x: He should have found purple oral syringes from another ward.
a.w: Oral liquid in an IV syringe can be pushed into a vein by mistake, which can be deadly.

a.o: Dr. Hany asked for Mr. Nashaat's feeding tube to be flushed with water.
a.x: The water flushes were unnecessary with liquid medicines.
a.w: Flushing stops the tube blocking.

a.o: Dr. Hany changed Mr. Nashaat's tablets to liquids with the pharmacist.
a.x: Asking the pharmacist was unnecessary for simple liquids.
a.w: Some tablets can't be crushed or changed to liquid.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Mr. Nashaat's IV line site, which was clean.
a.x: The IV site was off topic for medicines given down the tube.
a.w: An infected line can cause sepsis.

t: MRI booked without a metal check
s:
Mrs. Inayat, 70, was admitted with dizziness and slurred speech. Dr. Fady thought she might have had a small stroke at the back of the brain.

He examined her and found she was unsteady on her feet. Her CT scan was normal, which can happen with this type of stroke.

He started aspirin and checked her sugar and blood pressure, which were normal.

Mrs. Inayat was a little muddled and her daughter was not there. There was a scar under her left collarbone. Her notes from another hospital had not arrived.

Dr. Fady booked an urgent MRI scan of her brain and sent her down, without a metal safety check.
h: booked an urgent MRI scan of her brain and sent her down, without a metal safety check

a.o: Dr. Fady sent Mrs. Inayat for an MRI without a metal safety check.
a.x: He should have checked her for a pacemaker before the MRI.
a.w: The scar may be a pacemaker. MRI magnets can stop a pacemaker working or heat metal inside the body.

a.o: Dr. Fady started Mrs. Inayat on aspirin after her normal CT scan.
a.x: Aspirin was unsafe until the MRI had ruled out any bleeding.
a.w: Her CT ruled out bleeding.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Inayat's sugar and blood pressure on arrival.
a.x: Her sugar was off topic for a woman with slurred speech.
a.w: Low sugar can look like a stroke.

a.o: Dr. Fady booked an urgent MRI even though her CT scan was normal.
a.x: The normal CT scan was enough, so the MRI was not needed.
a.w: CT often misses strokes at the back of the brain.

t: Spinal chemotherapy given with the IV drug in the same tray
s:
Omar, 19, has leukemia and came to the day unit for chemotherapy. Today he needs methotrexate into the spine by lumbar puncture, and vincristine into a vein.

Dr. Hany checked his blood count, which was safe for treatment, and his consent form. He positioned him for the lumbar puncture and cleaned the skin.

He asked the nurse to bring the syringes. Both drugs arrived together in one tray from pharmacy, and the vincristine was not in a small IV bag.

The unit was running late. There was no second check of the drug name against the route. Omar was anxious and wanted it done quickly.

Dr. Hany picked up a syringe from the shared tray and began to inject it into the spine, without checking the label aloud with a second person.
h: picked up a syringe from the shared tray and began to inject it into the spine, without checking the label aloud with a second person

a.o: Dr. Hany took a syringe from the shared tray with no second check.
a.x: Two people should have checked the spinal drug aloud first.
a.w: Vincristine given into the spine is almost always fatal. Separate delivery and double checks prevent this never event.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Omar's blood count before his chemotherapy that day.
a.x: His blood count was off topic for a planned treatment.
a.w: Low counts can make chemotherapy unsafe.

a.o: Dr. Hany checked Omar's consent form before the lumbar puncture.
a.x: Consent was already given, so checking it again wasted time.
a.w: Consent should be confirmed before each treatment.

a.o: Dr. Hany cleaned Omar's skin before starting the lumbar puncture.
a.x: Cleaning the skin was unnecessary for a quick needle.
a.w: A spinal infection is dangerous.

t: High warning score not escalated
s:
Mrs. Raga, 66, had a hip replacement two days ago. At 3 am her early warning score rose to 7. Her pulse was 118, her breathing rate 26, her blood pressure 92/60 and her temperature 38.9°C. She was newly confused.

The nurse called Dr. Rasha, who came to see her. She took blood cultures and a lactate, which was 3.6.

She checked her wound, which was red and leaking, and her calves, which were soft. She listened to her chest, which was clear.

Dr. Rasha was the only doctor covering four wards that night. The senior doctor was asleep in the on-call room. She did not want to wake him.

Dr. Rasha wrote "review in the morning", and gave paracetamol, without starting antibiotics or calling a senior.
h: wrote "review in the morning", and gave paracetamol, without starting antibiotics or calling a senior

a.o: Dr. Rasha left Mrs. Raga until morning with a warning score of 7.
a.x: She should have started the sepsis plan and called her senior.
a.w: A score of 7 with a high lactate means sepsis that can kill within hours. Waking a senior is expected.

a.o: Dr. Rasha took blood cultures from Mrs. Raga before anything else.
a.x: Blood cultures could have waited until the morning team came.
a.w: Cultures should be taken before antibiotics.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Raga's calves, which were soft, at 3 am.
a.x: Her calves were off topic for a woman with a fever and confusion.
a.w: A clot can cause a fast pulse after hip surgery.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Raga's lactate along with her blood cultures.
a.x: The lactate was unnecessary, as her warning score said enough.
a.w: A high lactate shows how severe sepsis is.

t: Liquid medicine written in ml, not mg
s:
Yassin, 4, weighs 16 kg and is on the ward with a chest infection. He needs paracetamol for fever. The ward stocks paracetamol syrup at 120 mg in 5 ml.

Dr. Dina weighed him on the ward and worked out his dose at 15 mg/kg, which is 240 mg.

She checked his temperature, which was 38.8°C, and his fluid intake, which was good.

His mother said they use a stronger syrup at home, 250 mg in 5 ml. The drug chart had separate boxes for mg and ml, and the nurse asked her to write clearly.

Dr. Dina wrote "paracetamol 10 ml four times a day" on the chart, without a dose in mg.
h: wrote "paracetamol 10 ml four times a day" on the chart, without a dose in mg

a.o: Dr. Dina wrote Yassin's paracetamol dose in ml, not in mg.
a.x: She should have written the dose in mg, as 240 mg each time.
a.w: A dose in ml depends on the strength. 10 ml of the stronger syrup is 500 mg, twice his dose.

a.o: Dr. Dina weighed Yassin before working out his dose.
a.x: Weighing him was unnecessary, as his age was enough.
a.w: Children's doses are worked out by weight.

a.o: Dr. Dina checked how much Yassin had been drinking with his fever.
a.x: His fluid intake was off topic for a boy with a chest infection.
a.w: A feverish child can get dry.

a.o: Dr. Dina asked Yassin's mother about the stronger syrup used at home.
a.x: The syrup they use at home was off topic in hospital.
a.w: Strengths differ, which changes the volume.

t: Heparin drip with no clotting checks
s:
Mr. Raouf, 62, has a clot in his lung and also kidney failure. He was started on a heparin drip because it can be stopped quickly if he bleeds and is safer with poor kidneys.

Dr. Fady checked his blood count and his clotting tests before starting, which were normal. He prescribed the drip by the hospital's weight-based chart.

He asked the nurses to watch for any bleeding, such as from his gums or in his urine.

The night shift was busy. The hospital chart says the clotting test, APTT, must be checked six hours after starting and after each change. Mr. Raouf was due a dialysis session the next day.

Dr. Fady wrote "continue heparin drip at the same rate" and did not order any APTT checks.
h: wrote "continue heparin drip at the same rate" and did not order any APTT checks

a.o: Dr. Fady kept Mr. Raouf's heparin drip going with no APTT checks.
a.x: He should have ordered an APTT six hours after the start.
a.w: Heparin drips need regular checks. Too much causes bleeding, too little lets the clot grow.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Raouf's platelets and clotting before starting.
a.x: Checking his platelets first was unnecessary for heparin.
a.w: Heparin can drop the platelets.

a.o: Dr. Fady chose a heparin drip for Mr. Raouf rather than tablets.
a.x: Tablets would have been better than a drip for his clot.
a.w: Heparin is safer in kidney failure and can be stopped fast.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked the nurses to watch Mr. Raouf for any bleeding.
a.x: The nurses had other jobs than watching his gums and urine.
a.w: Bleeding is the main risk of heparin.

t: One insulin pen used for two patients
s:
Two patients on a ward bay, Mr. Saber and Mr. Lotfy, both take the same rapid-acting insulin with meals. Mr. Lotfy's pen had run out and pharmacy was closed.

Dr. Rasha checked both patients' sugar charts and doses. She asked the nurse to check Mr. Lotfy's sugar before lunch, which was 13.

She explained to Mr. Lotfy that his own pen would come from pharmacy in the morning.

The nurse asked what to do in the meantime. Mr. Saber's pen was half full. The nurse said she would change the needle each time.

Dr. Rasha told the nurse to use Mr. Saber's pen for Mr. Lotfy too, with a new needle.
h: told the nurse to use Mr. Saber's pen for Mr. Lotfy too, with a new needle

a.o: Dr. Rasha let Mr. Saber's insulin pen be used for Mr. Lotfy too.
a.x: She should have got Mr. Lotfy his own pen, or a vial and syringe.
a.w: Blood can flow back into the pen, so sharing spreads HIV and hepatitis even with a new needle.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked for Mr. Lotfy's sugar to be checked before lunch.
a.x: Checking his sugar before lunch was unnecessary that day.
a.w: The dose depends on his sugar.

a.o: Dr. Rasha told Mr. Lotfy his own pen would come in the morning.
a.x: He didn't need to know about the pen coming from pharmacy.
a.w: Patients should know about changes to their care.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked both men's sugar charts and insulin doses herself.
a.x: Checking one man's chart was enough, as the insulin was the same.
a.w: Each patient's dose is different.

t: Pending potassium left out of handover
s:
Dr. Rasha was finishing a long day shift. Mr. Hosny, 72, on her ward, had a potassium of 6.4 this afternoon. She gave him calcium, insulin and dextrose, and his ECG settled.

She stopped his ramipril and spironolactone and sent a repeat potassium, due back at 10 pm. She wrote this clearly in his notes.

She checked his kidney tests, which had worsened, and asked the nurses to keep him on a heart monitor.

At handover, the night doctor, Dr. Sameh, had 120 patients to cover. The handover was rushed because the ER was calling. Dr. Rasha handed over four other patients by name.

Dr. Rasha left without mentioning Mr. Hosny or his pending potassium result in the handover.
h: left without mentioning Mr. Hosny or his pending potassium result in the handover

a.o: Dr. Rasha left Mr. Hosny's 10 pm potassium out of her handover.
a.x: She should have told the night doctor about the result.
a.w: Notes are not a handover. A night doctor with 120 patients won't find a result no one told him about.

a.o: Dr. Rasha stopped Mr. Hosny's ramipril and spironolactone that day.
a.x: His ramipril should have carried on to protect his kidneys.
a.w: Ramipril raises potassium.

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mr. Hosny on a heart monitor overnight.
a.x: The monitor was unnecessary once the ECG settled down.
a.w: High potassium can cause deadly rhythms.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Hosny's kidney tests along with his potassium.
a.x: His kidneys were off topic for a high potassium level.
a.w: Worse kidneys explain the high potassium.

t: Lung shadow on an X-ray not followed up
s:
Mr. Sobhy, 64, came into the ER after a fall with pain in his right ribs. He smokes 30 a day. A chest X-ray showed no broken ribs, but the radiologist's report said "2 cm nodule in the left upper lobe, CT advised".

Dr. Karim examined his chest and gave him pain relief and breathing exercises. He checked his oxygen, which was normal.

He told him to stop smoking and gave him a leaflet about rib injuries.

The report arrived on the computer after Dr. Karim had read the X-ray himself. Mr. Sobhy was keen to go home. His GP was not told about the scan.

Dr. Karim sent him home without reading the full report or arranging a CT or telling his GP.
h: sent him home without reading the full report or arranging a CT or telling his GP

a.o: Dr. Karim missed the lung nodule in Mr. Sobhy's X-ray report.
a.x: He should have read the report and arranged the CT.
a.w: A new nodule in a heavy smoker may be lung cancer. Findings outside the main question must still be acted on.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Sobhy breathing exercises for his sore ribs.
a.x: Breathing exercises weren't needed with no broken ribs.
a.w: Deep breaths prevent chest infection after rib injuries.

a.o: Dr. Karim told Mr. Sobhy to stop smoking before he went home.
a.x: Stop-smoking advice was off topic after a fall.
a.w: Every contact is a chance to help someone stop.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Sobhy's oxygen level.
a.x: His oxygen was off topic for a man with pain in his ribs.
a.w: Rib injuries can affect breathing.

t: Stopped warfarin left on the discharge list
s:
Mrs. Ehsan, 80, was admitted with a bleed from her stomach while on warfarin for atrial fibrillation. She was given blood and her bleeding stopped after a scope.

The team, with the heart doctors, decided to stop her warfarin for now, and to review it in clinic in a month. Dr. Fady started omeprazole.

He checked her blood count before discharge, which was stable, and booked her follow-up in the heart clinic.

The discharge letter was copied from her admission medicine list. Mrs. Ehsan's husband fills her pill box at home and said he would follow the letter.

Dr. Fady sent the discharge letter with warfarin still on the medicine list and no note that it had been stopped.
h: sent the discharge letter with warfarin still on the medicine list and no note that it had been stopped

a.o: Dr. Fady left Mrs. Ehsan's stopped warfarin on her discharge list.
a.x: He should have listed warfarin as stopped, and said why.
a.w: The discharge letter guides the family and GP. A wrong list means she may restart warfarin and bleed again.

a.o: Dr. Fady started Mrs. Ehsan on omeprazole after her stomach bleed.
a.x: Omeprazole was unnecessary once the scope had stopped it.
a.w: It helps heal a stomach bleed.

a.o: Dr. Fady booked Mrs. Ehsan's follow-up in the heart clinic.
a.x: The heart clinic was off topic for a stomach bleed.
a.w: The clot risk from AF must be reviewed.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mrs. Ehsan's blood count before she went home.
a.x: Her blood count was unnecessary once the bleeding stopped.
a.w: A stable count shows the bleeding stopped.

t: Home insulin missed on admission
s:
Mr. Saad, 45, has type 1 diabetes and was admitted with a broken ankle after a fall. He takes long-acting insulin at night and rapid insulin with meals. He was brought in by ambulance and did not have his pens.

Dr. Rasha wrote up his pain relief and his clot prevention. She checked his sugar, which was 9.

She asked the orthopedic team to see his ankle and checked his blood tests, which were normal.

Mr. Saad was drowsy from morphine and did not mention his insulin. His wife was on her way with his medicine bag. The drug chart had a space for usual medicines.

Dr. Rasha wrote "no regular medicines" on his drug chart, without asking his wife or checking his GP record.
h: wrote "no regular medicines" on his drug chart, without asking his wife or checking his GP record

a.o: Dr. Rasha wrote "no regular medicines" for Mr. Saad unchecked.
a.x: She should have checked his home medicines with his wife.
a.w: People with type 1 diabetes need insulin every day. Without it, they can get ketoacidosis within hours.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Saad's sugar when he arrived on the ward.
a.x: His sugar was off topic for a man with a broken ankle.
a.w: His diabetes needed checking.

a.o: Dr. Rasha wrote up clot prevention for Mr. Saad.
a.x: Clot prevention was unnecessary for a 45-year-old man.
a.w: A broken ankle and bed rest raise the risk of clots.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked the orthopedic team to see Mr. Saad's broken ankle.
a.x: She could have managed his ankle alone without the bone team.
a.w: Fractures need the bone team.

t: Chest pain left in the waiting room
s:
Mr. Mahmoud, 59, came into the ER at 9 pm with central chest pain for an hour, spreading to his left arm. He has diabetes and smokes. He was sweaty and pale.

The triage nurse took his blood pressure, which was 150/90, and his pulse, which was 96. She gave him a triage category.

Dr. Karim was told about him by the nurse while he was stitching a wound in another room. He asked the nurse to take blood tests.

The ER waiting room was full and the heart monitor beds were all taken. The ECG machine was in use. The wait to be seen was two hours.

Dr. Karim told the nurse to send Mr. Mahmoud back to the waiting room until a bed was free, without an ECG.
h: told the nurse to send Mr. Mahmoud back to the waiting room until a bed was free, without an ECG

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Mahmoud back to the waiting room with no ECG.
a.x: He needed an ECG within 10 minutes and a monitored bed.
a.w: Chest pain with sweating in a diabetic smoker may be a heart attack. A blocked artery needs opening within minutes to hours.

a.o: The nurse checked Mr. Mahmoud's blood pressure and pulse at triage.
a.x: Checking his blood pressure only wasted time at triage.
a.w: Blood pressure helps choose treatment.

a.o: Dr. Karim asked the nurse to take blood tests from Mr. Mahmoud.
a.x: Blood tests should have waited for a bed.
a.w: Troponin helps diagnose a heart attack.

a.o: The nurse gave Mr. Mahmoud a triage category when he arrived.
a.x: Triage was unnecessary for a man who walked in himself.
a.w: Triage decides who is seen first.

t: Surgical referral with no observations
s:
Mrs. Fadia, 54, came into the ER with pain in her right upper belly for two days. She has known gallstones. Her temperature is 38.9°C, her pulse 120 and her blood pressure 88/54. Her bilirubin is 80.

Dr. Karim started IV fluids and antibiotics, and sent blood cultures and a lactate, which was 4.2.

He arranged an ultrasound, which showed stones and a wide bile duct.

He phoned the surgical registrar, who was in theatre and asked him to be quick. The surgical team had five other referrals waiting.

Dr. Karim said only "lady with gallstones and tummy pain, can you see her when you're free", without giving her observations, results or how unwell she was.
h: said only "lady with gallstones and tummy pain, can you see her when you're free"

a.o: Dr. Karim gave a vague referral, with no observations or results.
a.x: He should have used SBAR, with her vital signs and results.
a.w: Without key facts, a busy surgeon will rank her low. She needs an urgent bile duct drainage.

a.o: Dr. Karim arranged an ultrasound of Mrs. Fadia's belly in the ER.
a.x: The ultrasound could have waited for the surgeons to decide.
a.w: It showed the blocked bile duct.

a.o: Dr. Karim started antibiotics before the surgeons had seen her.
a.x: He should have waited for the surgeons before antibiotics.
a.w: Sepsis needs antibiotics within an hour.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mrs. Fadia's lactate with her blood cultures.
a.x: Her lactate was off topic for a woman with gallstones.
a.w: A high lactate shows severe sepsis.

t: Blood culture result after discharge not checked
s:
Mr. Kamal, 60, was admitted with a fever after a dental extraction. He has a heart murmur he was told about years ago. He felt better after one day of IV antibiotics and was keen to go home.

Dr. Fady took two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics and switched him to oral amoxicillin to finish at home.

He listened to his heart and noted a soft murmur. He checked his urine, which was clear.

The blood cultures were still pending when Mr. Kamal left on a Friday afternoon. Dr. Fady was rotating to a new job on Monday. No one was named to check the results.

Dr. Fady discharged him without arranging for anyone to check the blood cultures or an echo.
h: discharged him without arranging for anyone to check the blood cultures or an echo

a.o: Dr. Fady left no one to check Mr. Kamal's pending blood cultures.
a.x: He should have handed the result to a named doctor.
a.w: Fever after dental work with a murmur may be endocarditis. A positive culture after discharge must be acted on.

a.o: Dr. Fady took two sets of blood cultures before any antibiotics.
a.x: Taking cultures first delayed his antibiotics.
a.w: Antibiotics first can make cultures falsely negative.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Kamal's urine, which was clear, on the ward.
a.x: His urine was off topic for a fever after dental work.
a.w: A urine infection can cause fever.

a.o: Dr. Fady listened to Mr. Kamal's heart and noted a soft murmur.
a.x: His heart was off topic for a man with a tooth taken out.
a.w: A murmur raises the risk of endocarditis.

t: Frail woman sent home with no care checks
s:
Mrs. Khadiga, 87, lives alone in a second-floor flat with no lift. She was admitted with a urine infection and confusion, which has now cleared. She walks with a frame and fell twice in hospital.

Dr. Rasha finished her antibiotics and checked her blood tests, which were normal. She stopped her sleeping tablet.

She checked she could manage her tablets and wrote a clear discharge letter to her GP.

Mrs. Khadiga's son lives in another city. The physio and occupational therapist had not seen her yet because they were busy. The ward needed beds.

Dr. Rasha sent her home by taxi the same day, without a physio, occupational therapy or care assessment.
h: sent her home by taxi the same day, without a physio, occupational therapy or care assessment

a.o: Dr. Rasha sent Mrs. Khadiga home without any care assessment.
a.x: She needed physio, OT and a care package checked first.
a.w: A frail woman who fell twice, living alone up stairs, is likely to fall again and come back.

a.o: Dr. Rasha stopped Mrs. Khadiga's sleeping tablet before discharge.
a.x: She needed her sleeping tablet to settle at home alone.
a.w: Sleeping tablets raise falls in older people.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Khadiga could manage her tablets.
a.x: Checking her tablets was unnecessary before she went home.
a.w: Mistakes with tablets at home are common.

a.o: Dr. Rasha wrote a clear discharge letter to her GP.
a.x: Writing a long letter to her GP was a waste of time.
a.w: Her GP needs to know what happened.

t: Confused man moved wards at 2 am
s:
Mr. Mounir, 84, has dementia and was admitted with pneumonia. He was settled in a quiet bay near the nurses' desk on the medical ward. His confusion was getting better.

Dr. Ihab reviewed him at midnight. His oxygen was good, and he was eating and drinking.

He checked his antibiotics and his fluid balance, and asked the nurse to keep his glasses and hearing aid close.

At 2 am the bed manager asked to move a stable patient to free up the bed for an ER admission. The ward manager suggested Mr. Mounir. His daughter had asked that he not be moved.

Dr. Ihab agreed and Mr. Mounir was moved to a surgical ward at 2 am.
h: Dr. Ihab agreed and Mr. Mounir was moved to a surgical ward at 2 am

a.o: Dr. Ihab agreed to move Mr. Mounir, who has dementia, at 2 am.
a.x: He should have moved a patient without confusion instead.
a.w: Moving people with dementia, especially at night, worsens delirium, raises falls and makes care less safe.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked the nurse to keep Mr. Mounir's glasses close by.
a.x: His glasses didn't matter for a man asleep at night.
a.w: Seeing and hearing well helps prevent delirium.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Mounir's fluid balance on his midnight review.
a.x: His fluid balance was off topic for a man with pneumonia.
a.w: Dehydration can cause confusion.

a.o: Dr. Ihab reviewed Mr. Mounir on the ward at midnight.
a.x: A review at midnight was too late to be of any real use.
a.w: A review shows if he is stable.

t: Patient on another ward missed on the round
s:
Mrs. Inshirah, 70, was admitted under the medical team with a chest infection. There were no medical beds, so she was placed on the orthopedic ward.

On Monday, Dr. Fady did the ward round on the medical ward and saw all 24 patients there. He wrote clear plans and checked each patient's blood tests.

He made sure the medical patients' discharge letters were ready.

Mrs. Inshirah's name was not on the ward's whiteboard. The orthopedic nurses thought the medical team would come. Her fever had come back on Sunday.

Dr. Fady finished the round without checking the list of patients on other wards, and Mrs. Inshirah was not seen that day.
h: finished the round without checking the list of patients on other wards

a.o: Dr. Fady missed Mrs. Inshirah, who was on the orthopedic ward.
a.x: He should have checked his team's full list and seen her.
a.w: Patients on other wards are often missed and can get worse unseen. Her fever had come back.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked each patient's blood tests on the round.
a.x: Checking every blood test was unnecessary on a round.
a.w: Results guide each plan.

a.o: Dr. Fady made sure the discharge letters were ready on the round.
a.x: The discharge letters could have waited until the afternoon.
a.w: Ready letters help people go home on time.

a.o: Dr. Fady wrote clear plans for every patient on the medical ward.
a.x: Writing a full plan for each patient was unnecessary.
a.w: Clear plans help the nurses and the next doctor.

t: Note written without date, time or name
s:
Mr. Barakat, 69, has heart failure and was seen by Dr. Ihab in the evening because of new breathlessness. His oxygen had dropped to 90% and he had crackles in both lungs.

Dr. Ihab gave him IV furosemide and oxygen, and asked for a chest X-ray and a daily weight.

He asked the nurses to call him if his oxygen fell below 88% and to keep a fluid chart.

The next morning, Mr. Barakat got worse. The day team found a note in his file but could not tell when it was written or who wrote it, so they could not call to ask what was given.

Dr. Ihab wrote his note without the date, the time, his name or his bleep number.
h: Dr. Ihab wrote his note without the date, the time, his name or his bleep number

a.o: Dr. Ihab wrote Mr. Barakat's note without date, time or name.
a.x: He should have added the date, time, his name and his bleep.
a.w: Notes guide the next team. Without these details, no one knows when treatment was given or who to ask.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked for a daily weight for Mr. Barakat.
a.x: A daily weight was off topic for a man short of breath.
a.w: Weight shows fluid build-up in heart failure.

a.o: Dr. Ihab told the nurses to call him if oxygen fell below 88%.
a.x: A call-back level was unnecessary with nurses watching him.
a.w: It tells nurses when to call for help.

a.o: Dr. Ihab asked for a chest X-ray for Mr. Barakat that evening.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary with crackles in both lungs.
a.w: It shows fluid in the lungs.

t: GP never told about a new heart drug
s:
Mr. Taher, 66, was admitted with fast atrial fibrillation. He was started on apixaban to prevent strokes and bisoprolol to slow his heart. His kidney tests were normal.

Dr. Fady explained the new medicines to Mr. Taher and gave him a leaflet and a blood thinner alert card.

He arranged a heart scan in four weeks and told him to see his GP in two weeks for a blood pressure and heart rate check.

The ward was very busy. The discharge letter was written but left in Mr. Taher's notes. His GP still had his old medicine list.

Mr. Taher also takes clarithromycin now and then for chest infections, prescribed by his GP. He said he would book his GP visit when he got his next chest infection.

Dr. Fady did not send the discharge letter to the GP.
h: Dr. Fady did not send the discharge letter to the GP

a.o: Dr. Fady left Mr. Taher's discharge letter in his notes, unsent.
a.x: He should have sent the letter to the GP that day.
a.w: The GP needs to know about new drugs like a blood thinner to continue them safely and avoid harmful mixes.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave Mr. Taher a blood thinner alert card and a leaflet.
a.x: The alert card was unnecessary with a leaflet.
a.w: It warns other doctors he is on a blood thinner.

a.o: Dr. Fady arranged a heart scan for Mr. Taher in four weeks' time.
a.x: The heart scan was off topic for a man with a fast pulse.
a.w: It checks the heart's structure in new AF.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Taher's kidney tests before the apixaban.
a.x: His kidney tests were off topic for starting apixaban.
a.w: Apixaban dose depends on the kidneys.

t: Older man discharged home alone at midnight
s:
Mr. Hamdi, 83, was admitted with dizziness, which settled after his blood pressure tablets were reduced. He lives alone and uses a stick. He is slightly deaf.

Dr. Rasha checked his blood pressure lying and standing, which was now steady, and his ECG, which was normal.

She wrote a clear plan for his GP to check his blood pressure in a week.

It was 11:30 pm and a bed was needed for an ER patient. Mr. Hamdi's family could not collect him until the morning. It was cold and raining.

Mr. Hamdi had not eaten since lunch and his heating at home had been off for three days. He said he did not mind going, as he did not want to be a burden. The ward had a discharge lounge that opened at 8 am.

Dr. Rasha discharged him home alone by taxi at midnight.
h: discharged him home alone by taxi at midnight

a.o: Dr. Rasha sent Mr. Hamdi home alone by taxi at midnight.
a.x: He should have stayed until morning or until family came.
a.w: Night discharges of older people raise the risk of falls, confusion and readmission, with no one to help at home.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Hamdi's blood pressure lying and standing.
a.x: Checking it standing was unnecessary for a man in bed.
a.w: A drop on standing causes dizziness.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mr. Hamdi's ECG, which was normal.
a.x: His ECG was off topic for a man with dizziness from tablets.
a.w: Heart rhythm problems can cause dizziness.

a.o: Dr. Rasha asked the GP to check Mr. Hamdi's blood pressure in a week.
a.x: A GP blood pressure check was unnecessary once it was steady.
a.w: His tablets were just changed.

t: IV fluids left running for three days unchecked
s:
Mrs. Nabila, 79, weighs 50 kg and was admitted with vomiting, now settled. She has heart failure. On day one, she was started on IV fluids at 125 ml an hour.

Dr. Ihab saw her on day three. She was eating and drinking well. He listened to her heart and checked her medicines.

He checked her blood pressure, which was normal, and her urine output, which was good.

The fluid prescription had been rewritten by different doctors each night without a review. Her ankles were swollen and she was more breathless. Her weight was up 3 kg. No fluid chart had been kept.

Dr. Ihab rewrote the same IV fluids for another day, without stopping them or checking her fluid balance.
h: rewrote the same IV fluids for another day, without stopping them or checking her fluid balance

a.o: Dr. Ihab rewrote Mrs. Nabila's IV fluids without any review.
a.x: He should have stopped the IV fluids, as she was drinking.
a.w: IV fluids should be reviewed every day. Too much fluid in a small woman with heart failure causes fluid on the lungs.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Nabila's urine output on day three.
a.x: Her urine output was off topic for a woman now drinking well.
a.w: Urine shows if she is well hydrated.

a.o: Dr. Ihab listened to Mrs. Nabila's heart on his day three review.
a.x: Her heart was off topic for a woman admitted with vomiting.
a.w: Her heart failure makes fluid risky.

a.o: Dr. Ihab went through Mrs. Nabila's medicines on day three.
a.x: Her medicines were unnecessary to check on day three.
a.w: Some medicines need changing when fluids change.

t: Unused drip line left in for five days
s:
Mr. Ramzy, 58, was admitted with a skin infection on his leg. He had IV antibiotics through a cannula in his arm for two days, then switched to tablets.

Dr. Fady checked his leg each day, and the redness was going down. He drew round the edge with a pen.

He checked his blood tests, which were improving, and his sugar, which was normal.

Three days later, the cannula was still in his arm, unused. The site was red and sore. No one had written when it was put in.

Mr. Ramzy said the arm had been throbbing since the night before and he had felt hot. He was due to go home in a day or two. The nurse asked whether the cannula was still needed.

Dr. Fady wrote "keep cannula in case" and left it in place.
h: wrote "keep cannula in case" and left it in place

a.o: Dr. Fady left Mr. Ramzy's unused cannula in, "just in case".
a.x: He should have removed the cannula and checked the site.
a.w: Unused lines cause infections that can spread to the blood. They should be checked daily and removed when not needed.

a.o: Dr. Fady drew round the edge of the redness on Mr. Ramzy's leg.
a.x: Drawing round the redness was unnecessary and messy.
a.w: It shows if the infection is spreading.

a.o: Dr. Fady checked Mr. Ramzy's sugar along with his blood tests.
a.x: His sugar was off topic for a man with a leg infection.
a.w: Diabetes raises skin infection risk.

a.o: Dr. Fady switched Mr. Ramzy from IV antibiotics to tablets.
a.x: His IV antibiotics should have carried on until discharge.
a.w: Improving infections can switch to tablets.

t: Urine catheter kept with no reason
s:
Mrs. Zahra, 75, had a urine catheter put in when she came in very unwell with sepsis, to measure her urine output. She is now much better, walking to the toilet with help and drinking well.

Dr. Rasha reviewed her on day five. Her blood tests were back to normal. She switched her antibiotics to tablets.

She checked her walking with the physio and planned her discharge for two days later.

The catheter was still in. Mrs. Zahra said it was uncomfortable and asked when it would come out. No one had written why it was still needed.

The nurses said it was easier to measure her urine with the catheter in. Mrs. Zahra had a urine infection with a catheter two years ago. Her daughter asked if she could start walking more on the ward.

Dr. Rasha wrote "leave catheter in until discharge for convenience".
h: wrote "leave catheter in until discharge for convenience"

a.o: Dr. Rasha kept Mrs. Zahra's catheter in just for convenience.
a.x: She should have taken the catheter out, as it wasn't needed.
a.w: Every day a catheter stays in raises the risk of urine infection. It also slows getting back on her feet.

a.o: Dr. Rasha switched Mrs. Zahra's antibiotics from IV to tablets.
a.x: Her IV antibiotics should have carried on for longer.
a.w: She was well enough for tablets.

a.o: Dr. Rasha checked Mrs. Zahra's walking with the physio on day five.
a.x: Her walking was off topic for a woman recovering from sepsis.
a.w: Safe walking is needed before discharge.

a.o: Dr. Rasha planned Mrs. Zahra's discharge for two days later.
a.x: Planning her discharge on day five was much too early.
a.w: Planning ahead helps a safe discharge.

t: IV antibiotics never reviewed
s:
Mr. Akram, 52, was admitted with a chest infection five days ago and started on IV co-amoxiclav. He now has no fever, is eating well and his CRP has fallen from 180 to 30.

Dr. Ihab saw him on the ward round. His oxygen was normal on air, and his chest sounded better.

He checked his blood culture results, which were negative, and his kidney tests, which were normal.

Mr. Akram asked when he could go home. He works as a driver and was worried about his job. The drip had already been changed twice because of sore veins.

Dr. Ihab wrote "continue IV antibiotics" with no plan to switch to tablets or a stop date.
h: wrote "continue IV antibiotics" with no plan to switch to tablets or a stop date

a.o: Dr. Ihab kept Mr. Akram on IV antibiotics with no plan to stop.
a.x: He should have switched him to tablets, with a stop date.
a.w: Antibiotics should be reviewed at 48 to 72 hours. Long IV courses keep people in hospital and raise line infections and resistance.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Akram's blood culture results on the round.
a.x: His blood cultures were off topic once his fever had gone.
a.w: Results guide the right antibiotic.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Akram's kidney tests on the ward round.
a.x: His kidney tests were unnecessary for a chest infection.
a.w: Antibiotic doses may depend on kidney function.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mr. Akram's oxygen level on air on day five.
a.x: His oxygen on air was off topic now his chest sounded better.
a.w: Normal oxygen supports going home.

t: Phone advice to a GP not written down
s:
Dr. Fady, the medical registrar, was called by a GP about Mrs. Soad, 68. She had a potassium of 6.1 on a routine blood test and was on ramipril and spironolactone. She felt well.

Dr. Fady asked about her ECG, which the GP had done and was normal, and her kidney tests, which were stable.

He advised stopping the spironolactone, repeating the blood test the next day, and sending her in if it was over 6.5.

The GP asked if Dr. Fady would note the advice in case anything changed. Mrs. Soad was later admitted at night with a potassium of 7.2, and the night team had no record of the call.

Dr. Fady gave his advice over the phone and did not write it down or record who called.
h: did not write it down or record who called

a.o: Dr. Fady gave advice about Mrs. Soad by phone with no record.
a.x: He should have written down the call, the advice and the GP.
a.w: Phone advice is part of care. Without a record, the next team can't know what was planned, and there is no proof of what was said.

a.o: Dr. Fady asked the GP about Mrs. Soad's ECG on the phone.
a.x: Asking about the ECG was unnecessary for a woman who felt well.
a.w: ECG changes mean urgent treatment.

a.o: Dr. Fady advised the GP to stop Mrs. Soad's spironolactone.
a.x: Her ramipril should have stopped instead of spironolactone.
a.w: Spironolactone raises potassium the most.

a.o: Dr. Fady gave the GP a potassium level for sending Mrs. Soad in.
a.x: Setting a level for sending her in was far too fussy.
a.w: A clear limit makes it safe to manage her at home.

t: New stoma sent home without the stoma nurse
s:
Mr. Hesham, 65, had bowel cancer surgery a week ago and now has a new stoma bag. He is eating well, his wound is healing and his pain is controlled.

Dr. Karim checked his blood tests, which were normal, and his stoma, which looked pink and healthy and was working.

He wrote his discharge letter, with plans for the cancer team follow-up, and gave him clot prevention injections for four weeks.

Mr. Hesham had not yet learned to change his bag by himself. His wife said she was frightened to touch it. The stoma nurse was on leave until Monday.

Dr. Karim sent him home on Friday without stoma training or a referral to the community stoma nurse.
h: sent him home on Friday without stoma training or a referral to the community stoma nurse

a.o: Dr. Karim sent Mr. Hesham home before he could manage his stoma.
a.x: He should have stayed until trained to care for his stoma.
a.w: Without training, stoma problems such as leaks, skin damage and dehydration are common and lead to readmission.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Hesham four weeks of clot prevention injections.
a.x: Clot prevention injections weren't needed once he could walk.
a.w: Clot risk stays high for weeks after cancer surgery.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked that Mr. Hesham's stoma looked pink and healthy.
a.x: The stoma's color was unnecessary to check before discharge.
a.w: A dark stoma means poor blood flow.

a.o: Dr. Karim planned Mr. Hesham's follow-up with the cancer team.
a.x: The cancer team follow-up was off topic at discharge.
a.w: Further treatment may be needed.

t: Cancer referral sent as routine
s:
Mrs. Amany, 61, came to the GP with blood in her urine three times in the past month. She has no pain or fever. She smoked for 30 years.

Dr. Ghada sent a urine test, which showed blood but no infection, and checked her kidney tests, which were normal.

She examined her belly, which was normal, and asked about weight loss, which Mrs. Amany did not have.

She wrote a referral to the urology team for a camera test of the bladder. The referral form had a box for "urgent suspected cancer" and a box for "routine".

Mrs. Amany said she was not worried, as the blood came and went. She works as a school secretary and asked if the test could wait until the holidays. Her husband had kidney stones that caused blood in his urine.

Dr. Ghada ticked the "routine" box, making the wait about four months.
h: Dr. Ghada ticked the "routine" box, making the wait about four months

a.o: Dr. Ghada ticked the routine box for Mrs. Amany's referral.
a.x: She should have sent an urgent suspected cancer referral.
a.w: Painless blood in the urine in a smoker over 45 may be bladder cancer. Delay can let it spread.

a.o: Dr. Ghada sent a urine test for infection from Mrs. Amany.
a.x: Her urine test was off topic, as she had no fever or pain.
a.w: Infection can cause blood in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Ghada checked Mrs. Amany's kidney tests at the same visit.
a.x: Her kidney tests were unnecessary for this.
a.w: Kidney disease can cause blood in the urine.

a.o: Dr. Ghada asked Mrs. Amany whether she had lost any weight lately.
a.x: Asking about weight loss was off topic for a urine problem.
a.w: Weight loss can be a sign of cancer.

t: Patient with C. difficile moved into an open bay
s:
Mrs. Wafaa, 74, has diarrhea from C. difficile and is in a side room on the medical ward. She still has loose stools four times a day. She is on oral vancomycin.

Dr. Ihab checked her fluid balance, her kidney tests and her belly, which was soft. Her diarrhea was slowly getting better.

He stopped her laxatives and her omeprazole.

The bed manager needed the side room for a new patient with flu. She asked if Mrs. Wafaa could move into a six-bed bay, as she was "improving". Two patients in that bay were on antibiotics after surgery.

Dr. Ihab agreed to move Mrs. Wafaa into the open bay to free the side room.
h: Dr. Ihab agreed to move Mrs. Wafaa into the open bay to free the side room

a.o: Dr. Ihab moved Mrs. Wafaa with active C. difficile into a bay.
a.x: She should have stayed in a side room, 48 hours clear.
a.w: C. difficile spores spread easily on hands and surfaces. Patients on antibiotics nearby are at high risk.

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mrs. Wafaa's laxatives while she had diarrhea.
a.x: Her laxatives should have carried on as before.
a.w: Laxatives make diarrhea worse and hide progress.

a.o: Dr. Ihab checked Mrs. Wafaa's kidney tests and fluid balance.
a.x: Her kidney tests were off topic for a woman with diarrhea.
a.w: Diarrhea can cause dehydration and kidney injury.

a.o: Dr. Ihab stopped Mrs. Wafaa's omeprazole along with her laxatives.
a.x: Her omeprazole was safe to carry on with the infection.
a.w: Acid-lowering drugs raise C. difficile risk.

t: Kept fasting all day for a delayed operation
s:
Mr. Gaber, 80, has diabetes and a broken hip. He was put on the morning theatre list and fasted from midnight. His operation was delayed because of emergencies.

Dr. Karim checked his blood tests and his sugar at 8 am, which was 7. He made sure he had good pain relief with a nerve block.

He checked his clot prevention and that his consent form was signed.

By 4 pm, Mr. Gaber still had not been to theatre. He was thirsty and his mouth was dry. His sugar was now 4.2. The theatre team said he might go at 6 pm, or tomorrow.

Dr. Karim told the nurse to keep him nil by mouth until theatre called, without checking with the theatre team or starting a drip.
h: told the nurse to keep him nil by mouth until theatre called, without checking with the theatre team or starting a drip

a.o: Dr. Karim kept Mr. Gaber nil by mouth all day, with no drip.
a.x: He should have allowed clear fluids and started a drip.
a.w: Long fasting in older people with diabetes causes dehydration, low sugar and confusion, and makes surgery riskier.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Gaber a nerve block for his broken hip pain.
a.x: A nerve block was unnecessary with morphine available.
a.w: It controls hip pain with less morphine.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked that Mr. Gaber's consent form was signed.
a.x: Checking his consent was premature before a theatre time.
a.w: He must be ready when theatre calls.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Gaber's clot prevention before surgery.
a.x: Clot prevention was unnecessary on the day of surgery.
a.w: A broken hip raises clot risk.

t: Broken bone found on X-ray after the patient left
s:
Miss Hend, 22, came into the ER after twisting her wrist while playing basketball. Dr. Karim examined her and found tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox at the base of her thumb.

He sent a wrist X-ray, which he read as normal. He gave her a wrist splint and pain relief.

He told her to come back if the pain got worse, and planned a clinic review in two weeks.

The next morning, the radiologist's report said there was a possible scaphoid fracture. The report went to the ER inbox. Miss Hend's phone number was on her record.

Dr. Karim saw the report on his next shift and filed it, without calling Miss Hend back or bringing her clinic visit forward.
h: filed it, without calling Miss Hend back or bringing her clinic visit forward

a.o: Dr. Karim filed Miss Hend's fracture report without acting on it.
a.x: He should have called her back the same day for a cast.
a.w: Scaphoid fractures can lose their blood supply and not heal. Reports after a patient leaves must be acted on.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Miss Hend a wrist splint and pain relief.
a.x: A splint was unnecessary for a wrist X-ray read as normal.
a.w: It protects a possible scaphoid fracture.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Miss Hend's anatomical snuffbox for tenderness.
a.x: The snuffbox was off topic for a twisted wrist in sport.
a.w: Tenderness there suggests a scaphoid fracture.

a.o: Dr. Karim planned a clinic review for Miss Hend in two weeks.
a.x: A clinic review was unnecessary after a normal X-ray.
a.w: Scaphoid fractures are often missed at first.

t: Follow-up promised but never booked
s:
Mr. Raafat, 55, came to the GP with a cough for three weeks. He smokes and had a little blood in his phlegm once. His chest sounded clear.

Dr. Ghada sent a chest X-ray, which was normal. She gave him stop-smoking advice and offered him a referral to the smoking clinic.

She told him that if the cough was still there in three weeks, he would need more tests, including a CT scan.

Mr. Raafat is often away for work and forgets appointments. He did not have a phone number on his record. Dr. Ghada said, "We'll see you in three weeks."

Dr. Ghada did not book a follow-up appointment or set a reminder to check on him.
h: Dr. Ghada did not book a follow-up appointment or set a reminder to check on him

a.o: Dr. Ghada never booked Mr. Raafat's follow-up in three weeks.
a.x: She should have booked the follow-up before he left.
a.w: Coughing up blood in a smoker needs follow-up. A normal X-ray doesn't rule out lung cancer, and he may be lost.

a.o: Dr. Ghada sent Mr. Raafat for a chest X-ray, which was normal.
a.x: The chest X-ray was unnecessary with a clear chest.
a.w: An X-ray is the first test for a cough with blood.

a.o: Dr. Ghada offered Mr. Raafat a referral to the smoking clinic.
a.x: The smoking clinic was off topic for a man with a cough.
a.w: Stopping smoking is the biggest help for his lungs.

a.o: Dr. Ghada listened to Mr. Raafat's chest at the first visit.
a.x: Listening to his chest was useless with an X-ray ordered.
a.w: Chest signs can point to infection or other causes.

t: Two teams argue while the patient waits
s:
Mr. Sherif, 70, came into the ER with confusion and a fall. His sodium is 118 and he has a cut on his head. His CT scan of the head was normal. He has lung cancer.

Dr. Karim started treatment, gave him a small dose of hypertonic saline as advised, and checked his sodium every four hours.

He asked the medical team to admit him. The medical registrar said it was a fall and should go to the surgeons. The surgical registrar said it was a sodium problem and should go to the medics.

Mr. Sherif had been in the ER for nine hours. His sodium checks were being missed. His daughter asked which doctor was in charge.

Dr. Karim left Mr. Sherif waiting while the teams argued, without asking the senior ER doctor to decide.
h: left Mr. Sherif waiting while the teams argued, without asking the senior ER doctor to decide

a.o: Dr. Karim left Mr. Sherif waiting while the two teams argued.
a.x: He should have asked the senior ER doctor to decide.
a.w: Disputes over who admits delay care. A very low sodium needs careful, regular checks, which get missed.

a.o: Dr. Karim gave Mr. Sherif a small dose of hypertonic saline.
a.x: Hypertonic saline was too risky for his low sodium.
a.w: A very low sodium with confusion needs careful correction.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Sherif's head CT scan after his fall.
a.x: The CT scan was unnecessary for a man with a low sodium.
a.w: A fall in an older person can cause a brain bleed.

a.o: Dr. Karim checked Mr. Sherif's sodium every four hours in the ER.
a.x: Checking his sodium every four hours was far too often.
a.w: Sodium must not rise too fast.
